project_spec.title: interpreter.ts — a stack language with a checker
project_spec.goal: Model a small language as a discriminated union of instructions, check the whole program before running any of it, and let an exhaustive `switch` — ending in `never` — be what forces you to handle every instruction you add.
requirements: The input is a program, one instruction per line: `push <int>`, `pop`, `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div` (integer division, truncating toward zero), `dup`, `swap`, `print`. Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored; line numbers count every line from 1.

Parse every line first. For each bad line print `line <n>: unknown instruction <word>` or `line <n>: push needs an integer` (also for any extra words: `line <n>: <word> takes no argument`). If there were any, print `not run` and stop.
Otherwise run it. `print` prints the top of the stack without popping. The first runtime error — `line <n>: stack underflow` or `line <n>: division by zero` — stops the program.
At the end (normal or after an error) print `stack: <bottom … top>` or `stack: empty`.
Represent instructions as a discriminated union and execute them with a `switch` that ends in a `never` check.
stretch: Add `jz <line>` and `jmp <line>` instructions — the `never` check shows you every switch that must learn them.
Report *all* runtime problems a static pass can find before running (like underflow on straight-line code).
rubric: No `any` anywhere — not even one hidden in a cast
Every function has a typed signature; locals are left to inference
Bad input is handled on purpose, not by accident
Names say what things are, not how they are stored
I could explain every line to someone else

weeks.title: Function Types, Type Tests & Checkpoint
weeks.goal: Read any function signature, test a type like you test a value — and prove the first three months stuck.

problems.note: Sliding window over a string — Weeks 4, 7, 9.
Review — canonical keys and a Map, first met in Week 9.
Careful pointer work and narrowing — Weeks 11, 12.
Prefix sums in a Map — Weeks 7, 9.
Review — a fast recap of the string toolkit, first met in Week 11.

weeks.project: Re-implement your Week 8 config reader from scratch without looking at it, then add type tests for it: `Expect<Equal<…>>` lines pinning its parsed type, and a `@ts-expect-error` line for a key it must reject.

quiz.question: `const nums = [3, 1, 2]; const sorted = nums.sort();` — what is `nums` afterwards?
options: [1, 2, 3] — sort mutates, and sorted is the same array
[1, 2, 3], but sorted is a separate array
quiz.explanation: `sort` is in place and returns the same reference. `[...nums].sort()` is the non-destructive form.

quiz.question: Which pair of values makes `a ?? b` and `a || b` disagree?
quiz.explanation: `0` is falsy but not nullish, so `||` returns 5 while `??` returns 0. This is the bug `??` was introduced to prevent.

quiz.question: You have `x: unknown` from JSON.parse. What is the safest next step?
options: Run it through a type predicate that checks every field you rely on
Use `any` so the checks stop complaining
quiz.explanation: A cast and an annotation both assert without checking. Only a predicate that actually inspects the data makes the type honest.

quiz.question: What single flag most changes what a type annotation means?
quiz.explanation: Without it, every type silently includes null and undefined, so no annotation can be trusted. It is the foundation the rest rests on.

quiz.question: Why prefer `@ts-expect-error` over `@ts-ignore`?
options: It errors once the problem is fixed, so the suppression cannot outlive its reason
quiz.explanation: `@ts-ignore` hides whatever the next line does, forever. `@ts-expect-error` fails when there is nothing left to suppress.

quiz.question: `const a = [1,2]; const b = a; b.push(3);` — what is `a.length`?
options: 3, because both names point at the same array
2, because push returns a new array
quiz.explanation: `const` fixes the binding, not the contents. Copying needs `[...a]` — the same distinction as `readonly` versus `const`.

quiz.question: Which is the safest way to handle a value of type `unknown`?
options: Narrow it with a check that inspects the data before use
Annotate the variable with the expected type
Assign it to an any-typed variable
quiz.explanation: Casts and annotations both assert without verifying. Only a real runtime check makes the resulting type honest.

quiz.question: Your program does `input.split("\n")` on `n` lines that end with a trailing newline, with no `trim()`. How long is the array?
options: `n + 1` — there's an empty string after the last newline
quiz.explanation: Splitting `"a\nb\n"` gives `["a", "b", ""]`. Trim first or filter empties.

quiz.question: What is the cheapest way to check two strings are anagrams?
options: Count letters (a Map or a 26-slot array) and compare the counts
Sort both and compare only the first letters
quiz.explanation: Counting is O(n); sorting both is O(n log n) and also fine.

quiz.question: Which of these is O(n log n)?
quiz.explanation: Comparison sorting is O(n log n); the others are O(n) or O(1).

quiz.question: `Math.max()` with no arguments?
quiz.explanation: The identity for max is −∞ — which is also what `Math.max(...[])` gives on an empty array.

quiz.question: Merging two sorted arrays in O(n + m) uses…
options: Two pointers, always taking the smaller head
quiz.explanation: Each step consumes one element, so the whole merge is linear.

quiz.question: A function returns `number | undefined`. What prints `0` when it's undefined, but keeps a real 0?
quiz.explanation: `??` defaults only on null/undefined. (`Number(undefined)` is `NaN`.)

quiz.question: `[..."stressed"].reverse().join("")`?
quiz.explanation: Spread into characters, reverse the array, join back into a string.

quiz.question: You need the index AND the ability to stop early. Which loop?
quiz.explanation: `forEach` and `map` can't `break`; `for…in` gives string keys.

quiz.question: What type does `words.map((w) => w.length)` have, for `words: string[]`?
quiz.explanation: `map` returns an array of whatever the callback returns.

quiz.question: Building a Set from an array, then filtering another array with `set.has` costs…
quiz.explanation: Building is O(n); each `has` is O(1), so the filter is O(m).

quiz.question: What happens when `// @ts-expect-error` sits above a line with no error?
options: It becomes an error itself: "Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive"
It suppresses errors on the next two lines
It disables checking for the file
quiz.explanation: That's its advantage over `@ts-ignore`: when the problem is fixed, it tells you to remove it (TS2578).

quiz.question: Which type describes something you call with `new`?
quiz.explanation: A construct signature is written with `new` in front. A class value has one, and so can any object type.

quiz.question: A slot expects `(value: number, index: number) => void`. Why does `(value) => …` fit?
options: Passing extra arguments to a function that ignores them is harmless
The compiler adds the missing parameter
It doesn't fit; you must declare both
quiz.explanation: A function that takes fewer parameters can always be called with more arguments; the rest are ignored.

quiz.question: What does `this: Account` in a parameter list do at runtime?
options: Nothing — it is erased; it only checks what `this` is at each call site
Adds a first parameter the caller must pass
Creates a new `Account` for each call
quiz.explanation: The `this` parameter is purely a type annotation. `describe("x")` still takes one argument.

quiz.question: Under `strict`, why can't `(e: "click") => void` be assigned to `(e: string) => void`?
options: The slot may pass any string, and the handler only accepts one
Literal types can't appear in parameters
Arrow functions can't be assigned to type aliases
It can; parameters are compared bivariantly
quiz.explanation: Parameters are checked contravariantly: the function must accept everything the slot might pass it.

quiz.question: What is different about an interface method declared as `accept(v: string): void` compared with `accept: (v: string) => void`?
options: The method form's parameters are checked bivariantly, so a narrower implementation slips through
The property form can't be implemented by a class
quiz.explanation: Method syntax keeps an old, deliberate unsoundness. Property syntax gets the strict, contravariant check.

quiz.question: Why is it `ReturnType<typeof parse>` and not `ReturnType<parse>`?
options: `parse` is a value; `typeof` lifts it into the type world
`typeof` calls the function to find its result
quiz.explanation: Utility types take types. `typeof parse` is the function's type.

quiz.question: When does `type _ = Expect<Equal<A, B>>` compile?
options: Only when A and B are the same type
When A is assignable to B
When B is a subtype of A
quiz.explanation: `Expect` requires `true`, and `Equal` is true only for identical types.

quiz.question: What does an unused `// @ts-expect-error` do?
options: It is itself a compile error (TS2578)
It disables checking for the whole file
quiz.explanation: That is what makes it a negative test: if the next line compiles, the directive fails.

quiz.question: Why do misuses under `@ts-expect-error` usually sit inside a function that is never called?
options: The line must compile-fail but must not run
The directive only works inside functions
quiz.explanation: The type checker sees the line; the runtime never executes it.

quiz.question: Why is `[A] extends [B] ? [B] extends [A] ? true : false : false` not an identity check?
quiz.explanation: Mutual assignability is weaker than identity; the generic-function trick in `Equal` is not.

quiz.question: What can a type test NOT tell you?
options: Whether the function returns the right values
quiz.explanation: Types are erased. Values need runtime tests.

quiz.question: What is `typeof unique<string>`?
options: The type of `unique` with its type parameter fixed to `string` (an instantiation expression)
quiz.explanation: Instantiation expressions (TS 4.7) let you test a generic function at a specific type.

quiz.question: What does `a.difference(b)` return?
options: A new set of the members of `a` that are not in `b`
It removes `b`'s members from `a` in place
Members in exactly one of the two
quiz.explanation: The set methods never mutate either operand.

quiz.question: Why can't you write `set.union([1, 2])`?
options: The argument must be set-like (`size`, `has`, `keys`), and an array isn't
quiz.explanation: Wrap it: `set.union(new Set([1, 2]))`.

quiz.question: How are keys compared in a `Set`?
options: SameValueZero — like `===`, but `NaN` equals `NaN`; objects by identity
quiz.explanation: Two equal-looking objects are two different members.

quiz.question: When do you need a `WeakMap` rather than a `Map`?
options: To attach data to objects without keeping them alive
When you need to iterate the entries
quiz.explanation: Entries disappear with their key; the price is no iteration and no `size`.

quiz.question: `Map.groupBy` versus `Object.groupBy`?
options: `Map.groupBy` keeps keys of any type; `Object.groupBy` turns them into property keys
quiz.explanation: Numbers, objects or booleans as keys call for the `Map` version.

quiz.question: `let d = "up"` — what type is `d`?
quiz.explanation: A `let` can be reassigned, so its literal widens.

quiz.question: `const o = { d: "up" }` — what is `o.d`?
quiz.explanation: Object properties are mutable and widen unless you use `as const` or annotate.

quiz.question: What does `as const` do to `[1, 2]`?
quiz.explanation: Literal element types, fixed length, readonly — and nothing at runtime.

quiz.question: `const SIZES = ["S", "M"] as const` — what is `(typeof SIZES)[number]`?
quiz.explanation: Indexing a tuple type with `number` gives the union of its element types.

quiz.question: Is `const x = input as Size` a validation?
options: No — it only tells the compiler to assume it
Yes, it throws on bad values
quiz.explanation: Check the value against the list at runtime to earn the type.

quiz.question: What changes if you write `function isPerson(x: unknown): boolean` instead of `: x is Person`?
options: The function still runs but no longer narrows x at the call site
x is narrowed to any instead of Person
quiz.explanation: Only the `x is T` return type carries narrowing information. With `: boolean` the compiler learns nothing from the `if`, so `x` stays `unknown` inside it.

quiz.question: `function isPerson(x: unknown): x is Person { return true; }` — what does TypeScript do?
options: Accepts it; the compiler trusts the predicate without verifying the body
Errors, because the body does not check any Person fields
Narrows to unknown instead, as a safety fallback
quiz.explanation: A type predicate is an unchecked promise. This is exactly why a predicate should test every field it claims — a sloppy one puts a hole straight through the type system.

quiz.question: What distinguishes `asserts x is string` from `x is string`?
options: The assertion narrows for the rest of the scope by throwing on failure, rather than returning a boolean to test
The assertion works on primitives only
The assertion is checked at runtime by TypeScript
There is no difference other than spelling
quiz.explanation: A predicate answers a question you branch on; an assertion function makes a demand — control only continues past the call when the value really is that type.

quiz.question: After `if (!user) return;`, what does the compiler know about `user`?
options: That it's truthy — `null` and `undefined` are gone
quiz.explanation: Early returns narrow everything after them.

quiz.question: What is `[1, undefined, 2].filter((x) => x !== undefined)` typed as (TS 5.5+)?
quiz.explanation: The arrow is inferred as a type predicate.

quiz.question: What does `asserts v is T` mean in a return type?
options: If the function returns at all, `v` is a `T` from then on
quiz.explanation: It narrows by throwing on failure.

quiz.question: When is a narrowed `let` NOT narrowed inside a callback (TS 5.4+)?
options: When the variable is assigned again after the callback is created
quiz.explanation: The callback might run after that later assignment. Copy the narrowed value to a `const`.

quiz.question: `typeof null` is…
quiz.explanation: Check `v === null` before trusting a `typeof v === "object"` test.

quiz.question: Why must the discriminant be a literal type rather than `string`?
options: Only distinct literal types let the compiler rule out the other union members
String discriminants are slower at runtime
TypeScript forbids string-typed properties in unions
Literal types are required for JSON serialization
quiz.explanation: Narrowing works by elimination: `kind === \"circle\"` can only exclude the rect member if that member's `kind` is the literal `\"rect\"`. With `kind: string` both members still match.

quiz.question: You add a `{ kind: "triangle"; b: number; h: number }` member. What does the `const exhaustive: never = s` line do?
options: It becomes a compile error in every switch that has not handled the new kind
It silently accepts the new member
It throws at runtime when a triangle arrives
It narrows the triangle to never so the switch keeps working
quiz.explanation: That is the point of the pattern: `s` in `default` is now the triangle member, which is not assignable to `never`, so the compiler walks you to every place that needs a new case.

quiz.question: Which is the real advantage of a tagged union over one object with all fields optional?
options: Each branch statically guarantees which fields exist, removing the undefined checks
It uses less memory at runtime
It allows more than one field to be required
It survives JSON.stringify, which optional fields do not
quiz.explanation: With all-optional fields every access needs a runtime guard and the compiler cannot tell a circle from a rect. The tag makes the impossible combinations unrepresentable.

quiz.question: What can you do with a value of type `unknown` before narrowing it?
options: Pass it around or store it — nothing that reads from it
Nothing; it can't even be stored
quiz.explanation: It's the safe top type: everything fits in, nothing comes out unchecked.

quiz.question: What is the return type of a function that always throws?
quiz.explanation: It never produces a value.

quiz.question: Why does `const unhandled: never = s` in a `default` branch catch missing cases?
options: If a case is missing, `s` isn't `never` there, and the assignment fails to compile
quiz.explanation: The type left after all narrowing must be empty.

quiz.question: Which values does the type `{}` accept?
options: Anything except `null` and `undefined` — including numbers and strings
quiz.explanation: Use `object` for non-primitives, `Record<string, never>` for truly empty objects.

quiz.question: A slot typed `() => void` receives `() => 5`. Is that allowed?
options: Yes — `void` means the result is ignored
quiz.explanation: That's why `forEach` callbacks can return things.

exam.title: Checkpoint: word frequency report
exam.prompt: The input is a line of words. Print the three most frequent words as `word=count`, one per line, breaking ties alphabetically; then the number of distinct words. Fewer than three distinct words prints only what exists.
exam.hint: Count in a Map, then sort the entries by count descending with an alphabetical tie-break.

tests.input: a b a c b a
the cat the dog the cat
c b a c b a d

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: which week's tool handles "count how often each word appears"?
flashcards.back: A `Map<string, number>` with the `(get(k) ?? 0) + 1` idiom — then sort the entries by count, breaking ties by key.

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: how do you sort entries by count descending, then alphabetically?
flashcards.back: `entries.sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1] || a[0].localeCompare(b[0]))`.

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: reading a JSON record from untrusted input — the three steps?
flashcards.back: Parse into `unknown`, check the shape with a type predicate, then use the narrowed value.

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: string, number or array — which methods mutate?
flashcards.back: Strings and numbers never. Arrays do for `push`, `pop`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`; prefer the copying versions.

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: what does `const` protect, and what doesn't it?
flashcards.back: It stops reassigning the binding; it does not stop mutating the object or array it points to.

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: the fastest way to test membership repeatedly?
flashcards.back: Build a `Set` once, then `set.has(x)` is O(1) — `array.includes` is O(n) each time.

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: where do default values belong — `||` or `??`?
flashcards.back: `??`, unless you really mean to replace every falsy value, including `0` and `""`.

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: how do you avoid mutating an argument inside a function?
flashcards.back: Copy first (`[...xs]`, `{ ...obj }`), or type the parameter `readonly` so the compiler refuses.

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: sliding window over a string — what is the state?
flashcards.back: A left pointer and a map or set of what is inside the window; the right pointer extends it, the left shrinks it.

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: prefix sums answer which question in O(1)?
flashcards.back: The sum of any range `[i, j)`: `prefix[j] - prefix[i]`.

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: when is `!` (non-null assertion) acceptable?
flashcards.back: When you have just proved non-null in a way the compiler can't follow — e.g. right after `map.has(k)` for `map.get(k)!`.

flashcards.front: Checkpoint: why diff a rewrite against your old version?
flashcards.back: Each difference you can justify is something you now understand; each one you can't is something to go and look up.

flashcards.front: Write the type of a callable object that also has a `label: string`.
flashcards.back: `{ (x: number): string; label: string }` — a call signature plus a property.

flashcards.front: Write the type of "something you call with `new` and a number to get a `Shape`".
flashcards.back: `new (size: number) => Shape` — a construct signature. A class value has one.

flashcards.front: A slot wants `(value, index) => void`. May you pass `(value) => value * 2`?
flashcards.back: Yes: fewer parameters are fine, and a `void` slot accepts any return value — it is simply ignored.

flashcards.front: Why is `(e: "click") => void` not assignable to `(e: string) => void` under `strict`?
flashcards.back: Parameters are checked contravariantly: the slot may pass any string, and the handler only accepts one.

flashcards.front: What makes `type _ = Expect<Equal<A, B>>` a test?
flashcards.back: `Expect` only accepts `true`, and `Equal` is `true` only for identical types — so the line compiles only when the claim holds.

flashcards.front: What does an unused `@ts-expect-error` do?
flashcards.back: It is itself an error (TS2578) — which is exactly what makes it a negative test.

flashcards.front: Is `(x: number) => void` assignable to `(x: number, i: number) => void`?
flashcards.back: Yes — a function taking fewer parameters can always be called with more; the extras are ignored.

flashcards.front: What is a construct signature?
flashcards.back: `new (args) => T`: the type of something you call with `new`, such as a class value.

flashcards.front: What does a `this` parameter compile to?
flashcards.back: Nothing — it's erased, but every call is checked for the right `this`.

flashcards.front: How do you write a type test for a misuse?
flashcards.back: Put `// @ts-expect-error` on the line above it; if the line compiles, the unused directive is itself an error (TS2578).

flashcards.front: Why pair type tests with runtime tests?
flashcards.back: Type tests prove shapes, not values — a correctly typed function can still return the wrong number.

flashcards.front: What is `typeof fn<string>`?
flashcards.back: An instantiation expression: the generic function's type with `T` fixed to `string`.

project_spec.title: config.ts — the config reader, from scratch
project_spec.goal: Rebuild the Week 8 config reader without looking at it, the way you would now: every input line is untrusted, every value is validated against a schema, every problem is reported with its line number, and the parsed result has an exact type. (Stretch: pin that type down with `Expect<Equal<…>>` tests.)
requirements: The input is an INI-style file: `key = value` lines, `[section]` headers, blank lines and `#` comments. Line numbers count every line from 1.

Top-level keys: `name` (required, non-empty), `port` (integer 1-65535, default 3000), `debug` (`yes/no/true/false/on/off`, default `false`), `tags` (comma-separated, trimmed, empty items dropped; default none). A `[db]` section may set `host` (required when the section appears) and `port` (default 5432).

Report, sorted by line: `line <n>: expected key = value`, `line <n>: unknown section [<s>]` (its keys are then skipped), `line <n>: unknown key <k>`, `line <n>: duplicate key <k>`, `line <n>: port must be an integer from 1 to 65535`, `line <n>: debug must be yes or no`. Then the missing ones, unnumbered: `name is required`, `db.host is required`.
With any problem, print them all and then `invalid config (<k> problems)` (`problem` when there is one).

Otherwise print `name: `, `port:

`, `debug: `, `tags: ` or `tags: (none)`, and `db: :` or `db: (none)`.

Make the schema data (key → validator) so adding a key is one line.

Every function has a typed signature; locals are left to inference
Bad input is handled on purpose, not by accident
Names say what things are, not how they are stored
I could explain every line to someone else

weeks.title: The Toolchain: tsconfig, Modules & Declarations
weeks.goal: Configure the compiler on purpose, split code into modules, and describe the code you do not own.

problems.note: Absence as a first-class case — under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`.
Boundary conditions on an index scan, with every read honest.
An empty input is a real case — decide what it means.

weeks.project: Take your Week 8 config reader and make it clean under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`: rewrite every index access to handle `undefined` honestly, split the parsing and the printing into their own modules, and write a `.d.ts` for one helper you pretend is an untyped library.

quiz.question: What does a `.d.ts` file emit at build time?
options: Nothing — it only describes types the runtime is assumed to provide
A module that must be imported
quiz.explanation: Declaration files are pure description. Declaring something the runtime lacks gives a ReferenceError with no compile-time warning.

quiz.question: Why must module augmentation use `interface` rather than `type`?
options: Interfaces merge across declarations; type aliases cannot be reopened
type is illegal inside declare module
Interfaces are erased and types are not
quiz.explanation: Declaration merging is interface-only, and it is what lets you ADD a field to a library type instead of shadowing it.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a default export and a named export?
options: A default can be imported under any name, which makes it easy to rename inconsistently
A default is faster to load
A module may have several defaults
quiz.explanation: Named exports keep one canonical spelling across the codebase, which is why many style guides prefer them for anything but a single obvious entry point.

quiz.question: What does `import type { X } from "./x"` guarantee?
options: The import is erased entirely, so no runtime module dependency is created
X must be a type alias, not an interface
The module is loaded but unused
quiz.explanation: It makes the type-only intent explicit, avoiding a runtime import that a bundler would otherwise have to keep — the point of `verbatimModuleSyntax`.

quiz.question: What does `strictPropertyInitialization` flag?
options: Class fields that aren't definitely assigned by the constructor
quiz.explanation: A field typed `string` must be initialised, assigned in the constructor, or declared `field!: string`.

quiz.question: What does `useUnknownInCatchVariables` change?
quiz.explanation: Anything can be thrown, so `unknown` is the honest type. It's part of `strict`.

quiz.question: What does `noImplicitReturns` report?
options: Functions where some code paths return a value and others fall off the end
quiz.explanation: It catches the forgotten `return` in one branch.

quiz.question: What is `arr[5]` at runtime for a three-element `number[]`?
quiz.explanation: Out-of-range reads return `undefined`. Only `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` makes the type admit it.

quiz.question: What does `target` in tsconfig control?
options: Which JavaScript syntax version the output uses
quiz.explanation: Newer syntax is down-levelled for older targets. `lib` is the separate setting for available built-in types.

quiz.question: What does `lib` in tsconfig control?
options: Which built-in declarations exist — e.g. `es2022` or `dom`
quiz.explanation: Without `dom`, `document` doesn't exist; with an older `lib`, newer methods don't type-check.

quiz.question: `export default function f() {}` — how can another file import it?
quiz.explanation: A default export has no fixed name at the import site.

quiz.question: What does `import * as m from "./m"` give you?
options: A namespace object holding every export
A copy of the file's source
quiz.explanation: Access them as `m.name`.

quiz.question: What does `export { a as b }` do?
options: Exports the local `a` under the public name `b`
quiz.explanation: Aliasing on export lets a module choose its public names.

quiz.question: `declare const x: number; console.log(x);` — with nothing else defining `x`, what happens at runtime?
quiz.explanation: `declare` only tells the compiler the value exists elsewhere. If it doesn't, the runtime disagrees.

quiz.question: How do you declare types for an untyped package `"lib"`?
quiz.explanation: An ambient module declaration describes the package's exports.

quiz.question: What does `verbatimModuleSyntax` require?
options: Type-only imports to be written with `import type`
All imports to use file extensions
quiz.explanation: Imports without `type` are kept in the output, so a type-only one must say so or the runtime would try to load it.

quiz.question: What does `esModuleInterop` mainly affect?
quiz.explanation: It lets `import fs from "fs"` work against a CommonJS module that has no real default export.

quiz.question: Which is a `.d.ts` declaration for a function `add`?
options: `export declare function add(a: number, b: number): number;`
`export function add(a, b) { return a + b; }`
`export type add(a: number, b: number): number;`
quiz.explanation: Declarations have signatures and no bodies.

quiz.question: Why can circular imports bite at runtime?
options: One module may run before the other has finished initialising its exports
quiz.explanation: An import from a half-initialised module can be `undefined` (or in its temporal dead zone) when first used.

quiz.question: What does `isolatedModules` guarantee?
options: Each file can be transpiled on its own, without type information from other files
Each file runs in its own process
Every file has a default export
quiz.explanation: Single-file tools (esbuild, SWC, Node's stripping) need this: e.g. re-exporting a type must use `export type`.

quiz.question: What does `export type { User }` do at runtime?
quiz.explanation: Type-only exports and imports exist only for the compiler.

quiz.question: Under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, what is `const [first] = xs` typed as for `xs: string[]`?
quiz.explanation: Destructuring reads an index, so the flag adds `undefined` (a tuple's fixed positions are exempt).

quiz.question: What does `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` forbid?
options: Assigning `undefined` explicitly to an optional property not typed `| undefined`
quiz.explanation: It separates "absent" from "present but undefined".

quiz.question: `moduleResolution: bundler` vs `nodenext` — which fits a Node app without a bundler?
quiz.explanation: `nodenext` follows Node's own rules (file extensions, `exports`); `bundler` mirrors how bundlers resolve.

quiz.question: What does `strictNullChecks` change about the meaning of `string`?
options: With it on, `string` excludes null and undefined — absence must be written explicitly
quiz.explanation: With the flag off, every type silently includes null and undefined, so no annotation can be trusted. It is the flag the rest of the type system's usefulness rests on.

quiz.question: What does `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` do?
options: Gives `arr[i]` the type `T | undefined`, reflecting that the index may be out of range
Throws at runtime on an out-of-range index
Requires every array access to use .at()
quiz.explanation: It tells the truth about indexing. It is not part of `strict`, and it is usually the most disruptive flag to enable in an existing codebase — and the most valuable.

quiz.question: Why prefer `@ts-expect-error` over `@ts-ignore`?
options: It errors once the underlying problem is fixed, so the suppression cannot outlive its reason
It only works in test files
quiz.explanation: `@ts-ignore` silently hides whatever the next line does forever. `@ts-expect-error` fails when there is no longer an error, forcing the comment to be removed.

quiz.question: Why does a file using `declare global` usually need `export {};`?
options: It forces the file to be a module, which `declare global` requires
It prevents the globals from leaking
It is a convention with no effect
quiz.explanation: A file with no imports or exports is a script, and its top-level declarations are already global — so `declare global` is only meaningful (and only legal) inside a module.

quiz.question: Which of these survives type stripping unchanged?
options: `function f<T>(x: T): T { return x as T; }`
quiz.explanation: Generics and `as` are only deleted. The other three generate runtime code, so a stripper rejects them.

quiz.question: What does `--erasableSyntaxOnly` do?
options: Reports every construct that would need code generation, such as `enum` and parameter properties
quiz.explanation: It makes the type checker agree with a stripper about what can run.

quiz.question: Why does `verbatimModuleSyntax` require `import type` for type-only imports?
options: A stripper can't tell which imports are types, so the source must say which ones to delete
quiz.explanation: The rule is: what you write is what runs. A type-only import is deleted; any other import is kept.

quiz.question: `const Level = { A: 1, B: 2 } as const; type Level = (typeof Level)[keyof typeof Level];` — what is the type `Level`?
quiz.explanation: `keyof typeof Level` is the keys; indexing by them gives the values' literal types.

quiz.question: Why can't you write `x instanceof User` when `User` is an interface?
options: Interfaces are erased — nothing named `User` exists at runtime
quiz.explanation: `instanceof` needs a runtime constructor. Test a value (`in`, a tag, a validator) instead.

quiz.question: What does `const n = "5" as unknown as number; console.log(n + 1)` print?
quiz.explanation: Assertions never convert. The value is still a string, so `+` concatenates.

quiz.question: In TypeScript 6.0, what is `strict` if a tsconfig doesn't mention it?
quiz.explanation: 6.0 flipped the default. A project that wants the old behaviour has to say `"strict": false`.

quiz.question: Which option did TypeScript 6.0 deprecate?
quiz.explanation: Use `nodenext` for Node and `bundler` for bundled apps.

quiz.question: What does `"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"` do in TypeScript 7.0?
options: Nothing useful — the deprecated options are removed and are errors
quiz.explanation: It is a 6.0 transition aid. 7.0 has no switch to bring the options back.

quiz.question: What is TypeScript 7.0?
options: The compiler ported to Go — same `typescript` package and `tsc` command, roughly 10× faster
A new language with different syntax
quiz.explanation: The language is the same; the implementation is native.

quiz.question: Which flag is NOT part of `strict`?
quiz.explanation: It's valuable but disruptive, so it is opt-in. So is `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`.

quiz.question: A 6.0 project doesn't list `types`. What happens to the `@types/node` package it has installed?
options: It isn't loaded — the default is now `[]`, so it must be listed
It's an error to have it installed
quiz.explanation: 6.0 changed the default from 'every installed @types package' to none; add `"types": ["node"]`.

flashcards.front: What does `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` add?
flashcards.back: `undefined` to the type of every index read — `xs[i]` becomes `T | undefined`, `record[key]` becomes `V | undefined`.

flashcards.front: Name four flags `strict` turns on.
flashcards.back: `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictPropertyInitialization` (also `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, `alwaysStrict`, `strictBindCallApply`).

flashcards.front: What does `noImplicitAny` catch?
flashcards.back: Parameters and variables whose type would silently fall back to `any` (TS7006, TS7005).

flashcards.front: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` — what changes?
flashcards.back: `{ x?: number }` no longer accepts `x: undefined` explicitly — only a missing `x`.

flashcards.front: Why is `skipLibCheck` common?
flashcards.back: It skips type-checking `.d.ts` files, which speeds builds and avoids errors in third-party types — at the cost of hiding real ones.

flashcards.front: TS2532 "Object is possibly 'undefined'" — the usual source under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`?
flashcards.back: An element access like `xs[0]` or `row[i]` — an index read that might be out of range.

flashcards.front: Named export vs default export?
flashcards.back: `export function f` is imported as `{ f }` under that exact name; a default export is imported under any name. Named exports refactor more safely.

flashcards.front: What is `import type` for?
flashcards.back: Importing only types. The import is erased entirely, which strip-only runners and `verbatimModuleSyntax` rely on.

flashcards.front: What is a `.d.ts` file?
flashcards.back: A declaration file: types only, no implementation — how types are described for JavaScript code.

flashcards.front: What does `declare` mean?
flashcards.back: "This exists at runtime, trust me" — it describes a value without creating it, e.g. `declare const VERSION: string`.

flashcards.front: How do you type an untyped JavaScript module?
flashcards.back: Write `declare module "lib" { export function f(x: number): string; }` in a `.d.ts` file.

flashcards.front: What is module augmentation?
flashcards.back: Reopening an existing module's declarations to add members: `declare module "lib" { interface Options { extra?: boolean } }`.

flashcards.front: What does `declare global` do?
flashcards.back: Adds declarations to the global scope from inside a module file.

flashcards.front: Why can a barrel file (`index.ts` re-exporting everything) hurt?
flashcards.back: It can create circular imports and pull the whole folder into every importer.

flashcards.front: What is a circular import's typical symptom?
flashcards.back: A value is `undefined` at the moment it's used, because its module hadn't finished evaluating.

flashcards.front: Why does `namespace` not run in Node's type-stripping mode?
flashcards.back: A namespace emits a real object and code — it isn't erasable. Use ES modules instead.

flashcards.front: What is `moduleResolution: "bundler"` for?
flashcards.back: Resolving imports the way modern bundlers do: extensionless relative imports allowed, `package.json` `exports` respected.

flashcards.front: What does type stripping do with `enum Color { Red }`?
flashcards.back: Refuses to run it: an `enum` generates an object, so it isn't erasable. Use an `as const` object plus a derived type.

flashcards.front: `const Level = {…} as const; type Level = …` — how is the type written?
flashcards.back: `type Level = (typeof Level)[keyof typeof Level];` — the union of the object's values.

flashcards.front: Why must type-only imports say `import type` under `verbatimModuleSyntax`?
flashcards.back: A stripper can't tell types from values, so the source must mark which imports to delete.

flashcards.front: TypeScript 6.0's new default for `strict`?
flashcards.back: `true` — and `module` defaults to `esnext`, `types` to `[]`, `target` to the current ES year.

flashcards.front: Name three options TypeScript 6.0 deprecated.
flashcards.back: Any of: `target: es5`, `moduleResolution: node`/`classic`, `baseUrl`, `outFile`, `module: amd/umd/systemjs/none`, `esModuleInterop: false`.

flashcards.front: What is TypeScript 7.0?
flashcards.back: The compiler ported to Go (July 2026): same `tsc`, about 10× faster; the 6.0 deprecations are errors, and it ships no compiler API yet.

project_spec.goal: The arc project's fourth version: the ledger read under every flag this month turns on, and split into modules the way a real project is. quiz.question: `const el = {} as { id: string }; el.id.length` — what happens?

options: Compile error: `y` is an excess property
quiz.explanation: A fresh literal with unknown keys is almost always a typo (TS2353).

quiz.question: `function len(x: { length: number }) { … }` — is `len("abc")` allowed?
options: Yes — a string has a numeric `length`
quiz.explanation: Structural typing: anything with the right members fits.

quiz.question: Can an instance of `class A { x = 1 }` be used where `class B { x = 1 }` is expected?
options: Yes — they have the same structure
quiz.explanation: Classes compare structurally, as long as neither has private or protected members.

quiz.question: What makes two structurally identical classes incompatible?
quiz.explanation: Private members are compared by where they were declared, which makes classes that have them nominal.

quiz.question: Is `(x: string) => void` assignable to `(x: string | number) => void`?
options: No — the target may call it with a number it can't handle
quiz.explanation: Parameters are contravariant: the substitute must accept at least everything the original accepts.

quiz.question: Is `(x: string | number) => void` assignable to `(x: string) => void`?
options: Yes — it accepts everything it will be given, and more
Only if it returns a value
quiz.explanation: Accepting a wider parameter type is always safe.

quiz.question: Why write `const ROUTES = { … } as const satisfies Record<string, string>`?
options: To keep a read-only, literal-typed object while still checking its shape
To convert it to a Map
quiz.explanation: `as const` freezes the literal types; `satisfies` validates them without widening.

quiz.question: What does `x as unknown as T` do?
options: Forces any conversion past the compiler — a double assertion with no check
quiz.explanation: It exists for genuine escape hatches; treat it as a code-review red flag.

quiz.question: When is `as` reasonable?
options: When you know something the compiler can't — and you've checked it, or it's a well-understood API
quiz.explanation: `as` is a claim. Prefer narrowing or validation when a check is possible.

quiz.question: What does `satisfies` check against a union target like `"a" | "b"`?
options: That the value is one of the members, keeping the literal type
quiz.explanation: `const x = "a" satisfies "a" | "b"` is typed `"a"`.

quiz.question: Do excess-property checks apply to a variable passed to a function?
options: No — only to fresh object literals
quiz.explanation: Structural typing admits objects with extra properties once they're in a variable.

quiz.question: Why does TypeScript use structural rather than nominal typing?
options: JavaScript code routinely uses plain objects of the right shape, not declared classes
quiz.explanation: Typing "duck typing" is the whole point.

quiz.question: A function takes `{ name: string }`. Can you pass a `Date` with a `name` property added?
options: Yes, if it has a string `name`
No, Date isn't an object type
quiz.explanation: Only the required members matter.

quiz.question: Is a `readonly` property assignable to a mutable one of the same type?
quiz.explanation: That's why a readonly view isn't a guarantee someone else can't mutate the object.

quiz.question: Is `readonly string[]` assignable to `string[]`?
options: No — the mutable type has methods the readonly one lacks
quiz.explanation: Array readonly-ness *is* checked, because `push` and friends differ.

quiz.question: What does `in out T` declare?
options: `T` is invariant — both consumed and produced
quiz.explanation: Variance annotations: `out` covariant, `in` contravariant, both invariant.

quiz.question: Why is a callback parameter typed `(x: Animal) => void` more flexible for callers?
options: It accepts any animal, so it fits slots expecting handlers for dogs, cats, …
quiz.explanation: Contravariance: a handler of the supertype works wherever a handler of a subtype is needed.

quiz.question: What is `const el = document as any` in a codebase a sign of?
options: Type checking turned off at that point — every use of `el` is unchecked
quiz.explanation: `any` spreads: anything derived from it is `any` too.

quiz.question: What does `satisfies` do to the variable's declared type?
options: Nothing — the variable keeps its inferred type
quiz.explanation: It checks, it doesn't annotate.

quiz.question: Which reports a missing property in a literal: annotation, `satisfies`, or `as`?
quiz.explanation: `as` only requires the two types to overlap, so a literal missing a required property is accepted.

quiz.question: Can you assign `{ x: 1 }` to `{ x: number; y?: number }`?
options: Yes — optional properties may be absent
quiz.explanation: Optional means "may be missing".

quiz.question: How does TypeScript compare two function types' return types?
options: Covariantly — the source's return must be assignable to the target's
quiz.explanation: A function returning `Dog` fits a slot expecting a function returning `Animal`.

quiz.question: Why is `interface` method syntax `m(x: T): void` looser than `m: (x: T) => void`?
options: Method parameters are checked bivariantly for compatibility
quiz.explanation: Prefer property syntax for callback members you want checked strictly.

quiz.question: What is the risk of `JSON.parse(text) satisfies User`?
options: It compiles and checks nothing — `JSON.parse` returns `any`, which satisfies every type
quiz.explanation: `satisfies` is compile-time only; untrusted data needs a runtime check.

quiz.question: What makes `private` members affect assignability?
options: A class with a private member is compatible only with instances of that same class declaration
quiz.explanation: The one nominal corner of TypeScript's class types.

quiz.question: What does `satisfies` do that a type annotation does not?
options: It validates the value against the type while keeping the value's own narrower inferred type
It validates the value at runtime
It widens the value to the given type
quiz.explanation: An annotation replaces the inferred type; `satisfies` only checks against it. That is how you keep literal key and tuple information while still enforcing a contract.

quiz.question: With `const routes = { home: "/" } satisfies Record<string, string>`, what is `keyof typeof routes`?
quiz.explanation: The inferred object type is preserved, so its keys are the literal union of what was actually written. With a plain `Record<string, string>` annotation it would have been `string`.

quiz.question: Does `satisfies` help validate JSON arriving from a network call?
options: No — it is erased at compile time and checks nothing at runtime
Yes, it throws when the shape does not match
Yes, but only in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Like every type-level construct it disappears before the code runs. Runtime data still needs a type predicate or a schema validator.

quiz.question: `const bad: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, label: "home" };` errors, but assigning the same object through a variable does not. Why?
options: The excess property check only applies to fresh object literals assigned directly
Variables are always typed as any
The variable version is also an error, just reported later
label is a reserved property name
quiz.explanation: TypeScript treats a directly-assigned literal as a place where extra keys are almost certainly typos, so it checks them. Once the object is widened into a variable, ordinary structural assignability applies.

quiz.question: Two unrelated aliases `type A = { id: number }` and `type B = { id: number }`. Is `const b: B = someA;` legal?
options: Yes — structural typing compares shapes, not declaration names
No — they are different named types
Only when both are interfaces rather than type aliases
quiz.explanation: Nothing links A and B by name, but they have identical members, so each is assignable to the other. This is the core difference from Java's nominal `implements`.

quiz.question: What makes a class NOT purely structural in TypeScript?
options: Having private or protected members, which only match members from the same declaration
quiz.explanation: Private and protected members are tied to their declaring class, so two classes with identical-looking private fields are not interchangeable — the one nominal corner of the type system.

quiz.question: `Dog` is assignable to `Animal`. Which is assignable to which for `type Getter<T> = () => T`?
quiz.explanation: A getter produces `T`, so it is covariant: same direction as `Dog → Animal`.

quiz.question: And for `type Handler<T> = (x: T) => void`?
quiz.explanation: A handler consumes `T`: contravariant. A handler of any animal can handle a dog.

quiz.question: Why is passing `Dog[]` where `Animal[]` is expected unsound?
options: The receiver can push a non-dog into your array
quiz.explanation: TypeScript allows it for convenience; `readonly Animal[]` makes it genuinely safe.

quiz.question: What variance does `{ get(): T; set(v: T): void }` have in `T`?
quiz.explanation: It both produces and consumes `T`, so only the exact same `T` fits.

quiz.question: What does `interface Source<out T>` do?
options: Declares `T` covariant, and the compiler checks that `T` is only produced
quiz.explanation: Variance annotations are checked, erased documentation.

quiz.question: Which declaration gets the strict, contravariant parameter check under `strictFunctionTypes`?
quiz.explanation: Method syntax stays bivariant; property syntax with a function type is checked contravariantly.

flashcards.front: What does `as T` actually do?
flashcards.back: Nothing at runtime. It tells the compiler "trust me, this is a T" — a claim, not a conversion.

flashcards.front: When is `x as unknown as T` needed?
flashcards.back: When the two types don't overlap enough for a direct `as` (TS2352). Its ugliness is deliberate — it flags a dangerous claim.

flashcards.front: `: T` vs `as T` vs `satisfies T` on an object literal?
flashcards.back: `: T` checks and widens to `T`; `as T` asserts with little checking; `satisfies T` checks but keeps the literal's own, narrower type.

flashcards.front: Why use `satisfies` on a config table?
flashcards.back: You get errors for a wrong shape *and* keep the literal keys, so `keyof typeof table` is the exact key union.

flashcards.front: What is structural typing?
flashcards.back: Compatibility by shape, not by name: any value with the required members fits, whatever it was declared as.

flashcards.front: A variable with extra properties is assigned to a narrower type. What happens to the extras at runtime?
flashcards.back: They stay. The type just stops mentioning them — `Object.keys` still lists them.

flashcards.front: Why are excess-property errors only reported for literals?
flashcards.back: A fresh literal can't be used anywhere else, so an extra key is almost certainly a typo. A variable may legitimately have more.

flashcards.front: Why is `Dog[]` assignable to `Animal[]` a hole in the type system?
flashcards.back: Arrays are treated covariantly, so you can push a plain `Animal` through the `Animal[]` view into what is really a `Dog[]`.

flashcards.front: Contravariance in one sentence?
flashcards.back: A function that accepts `Animal` can stand in for one that accepts `Dog` — not the other way round.

flashcards.front: Why are methods declared with method syntax riskier than function-typed properties?
flashcards.back: Method parameters are checked bivariantly even under `strictFunctionTypes`, so an unsafe override compiles.

flashcards.front: TS1360 — cause?
flashcards.back: A `satisfies` check failed: the expression does not satisfy the type named after it.

flashcards.front: Why test membership with `Object.hasOwn(obj, k)` instead of `k in obj`?
flashcards.back: `in` also sees inherited properties — `"toString" in {}` is `true`.

flashcards.front: Covariant, contravariant, invariant — in one line each?
flashcards.back: Producers keep the subtype direction; consumers reverse it; things that do both need an exact match.

flashcards.front: Is `Dog[]` assignable to `Animal[]`? Is that safe?
flashcards.back: Yes, and no: arrays are covariant for convenience, but the receiver can push a non-dog. `readonly Animal[]` is the safe version.

flashcards.front: `(a: Animal) => void` vs `(d: Dog) => void` — which fits where the other is expected?
flashcards.back: The `Animal` handler fits a `Dog` slot, not the reverse (parameters are contravariant).

flashcards.front: What does `interface Source<out T>` promise?
flashcards.back: `T` only comes out of a `Source`; the compiler checks the body and rejects members that take a `T` in.

flashcards.front: Why does `interface Box<out T> { set(v: T): void }` compile?
flashcards.back: Method syntax is bivariant, so the check misses it; `set: (v: T) => void` is caught (TS2636).

flashcards.front: How do you make an object property safe to widen?
flashcards.back: Mark it `readonly` in the wider type, so nothing can write a supertype value through it.

weeks.title: Branded Types & Immutability
weeks.goal: Make validated values a type, and stop accidental mutation at the boundary.

problems.note: Build a new array rather than editing in place.
Compare the in-place and copying solutions honestly.

weeks.project: Write an `ids.ts` with branded `UserId` and `OrderId`, validating parsers for both, and a `readonly` lookup table that cannot be mutated by callers.

quiz.question: What does a brand cost at runtime?
options: Nothing — the intersection is erased and the value stays a plain string
A hidden property on each value
quiz.explanation: That is the appeal over a wrapper class: nominal safety with zero runtime representation.

quiz.question: What does `readonly string[]` prevent?
options: Calling mutating methods and assigning to indices
quiz.explanation: It is a compile-time restriction on the array's own operations. `const` only stops rebinding the variable.

quiz.question: Does `Object.freeze` give you a deeply immutable object?
options: No — it is shallow; nested objects remain mutable
quiz.explanation: Freezing one level is the runtime counterpart to `Readonly<T>`, which is also shallow. Deep immutability needs a recursive helper.

quiz.question: `type UserId = string & { __brand: "UserId" }; const id: UserId = "u1";` — result?
options: Compile error: a plain string isn't a `UserId`
quiz.explanation: The brand is the point: only your constructor, with its one cast, can make a `UserId`.

quiz.question: Can a `UserId` be passed to a function expecting a plain `string`?
options: Yes — a brand is a subtype of `string`
Only if the function is generic
quiz.explanation: Branding restricts which values *become* a `UserId`, not where one can go.

quiz.question: `const a = Object.freeze([1, 2]); a.push(3);` — does it compile?
options: Yes, but it throws at runtime
Yes, and the push is silently ignored
quiz.explanation: The type of a frozen array has no mutators, so the compiler stops you before the runtime would.

quiz.question: `const o = Object.freeze({ inner: { n: 1 } }); o.inner.n = 2;` — what happens?
options: It compiles and works — `freeze` is shallow
quiz.explanation: Only `o`'s own properties are frozen; `inner` is an ordinary object.

quiz.question: With `x: Readonly<{ a: { b: number } }>`, is `x.a.b = 2` allowed?
quiz.explanation: `x.a` can't be reassigned, but the object it points to is still mutable.

quiz.question: What is structural sharing?
options: A new version of a data structure reusing the unchanged parts of the old one
Two variables pointing at one object
quiz.explanation: It makes immutable updates cheap: changing one field copies only the path to it.

quiz.question: How do you add `x` to an array without mutating it?
quiz.explanation: Spread builds a new array; `push` changes the original.

quiz.question: How do you remove the element at index `i` without mutating?
quiz.explanation: `splice` mutates; `delete` leaves a hole.

quiz.question: How do you update one field of an object immutably?
quiz.explanation: `Object.assign(obj, …)` writes into `obj`; spreading into a new literal doesn't.

quiz.question: What does a `unique symbol` brand give you over a string-literal brand?
options: It can't be forged by writing the property name by hand
quiz.explanation: Every `unique symbol` declaration is its own type, so no other code can produce a matching key.

quiz.question: Is `as const` deep?
options: Yes — nested object and array literals become readonly too
quiz.explanation: `as const` applies recursively to the whole literal expression (unlike `Readonly<T>`).

quiz.question: What is the smallest brand you can write?
quiz.explanation: The phantom property only exists in the type; a `unique symbol` key makes it unforgeable outside the module.

quiz.question: Does a branded `Cents` still support arithmetic?
options: Yes, but the result is a plain `number` — re-brand it through a function
quiz.explanation: `a + b` on two `Cents` gives `number`; wrap arithmetic in helpers that return `Cents`.

quiz.question: What does `ReadonlyArray<T>` lack compared with `T[]`?
quiz.explanation: Non-mutating methods (`map`, `slice`, `toSorted`) are all still there.

quiz.question: What does `Readonly<T>` do to nested objects?
quiz.explanation: A `DeepReadonly` needs a recursive mapped type (week 20).

quiz.question: What does `Object.freeze` return, typed?
quiz.explanation: The type reflects the shallow freeze.

quiz.question: In strict mode, what happens on assigning to a frozen object's property?
quiz.explanation: Modules are strict, so the failure is loud. In sloppy scripts it's silent.

quiz.question: How do you sort an array without mutating it?
quiz.explanation: Or `[...xs].sort(compare)` before ES2023.

quiz.question: Why is aliasing a common source of mutation bugs?
options: Two variables refer to the same object, so a change through one is seen through the other
quiz.explanation: Immutable updates avoid the question entirely.

quiz.question: What does `{ ...state, user: { ...state.user, name } }` do?
options: Copies the path to the change and shares everything else
quiz.explanation: Structural sharing: new objects only where something changed.

quiz.question: A smart constructor returns `Email | undefined`. What should the caller do with `undefined`?
options: Handle the invalid case explicitly — report or reject it
quiz.explanation: The type forces the decision to be made, which is the point.

quiz.question: Why not validate an email with a `boolean` function?
options: The knowledge is thrown away; later code can't tell a checked string from an unchecked one
quiz.explanation: Parse into a branded type instead.

quiz.question: Does `const` make an array immutable?
options: No — it prevents rebinding; `push` still works
quiz.explanation: Use `readonly` types (or `as const` for literals).

quiz.question: What does `as const` on an array literal make it?
options: A readonly tuple of literal types
quiz.explanation: Types only — nothing is frozen at runtime.

quiz.question: What's the cost of a brand compared with a wrapper class?
options: Zero runtime cost; a wrapper allocates an object and needs unwrapping
quiz.explanation: Brands are erased; the value is still a plain string or number.

quiz.question: Can two brands with the same symbol-less `__brand` string be confused?
options: Yes — `{ __brand: "Id" }` in two modules is the same type
quiz.explanation: A module-private `unique symbol` avoids accidental collisions.

quiz.question: Which update to `const arr: readonly number[]` compiles?
quiz.explanation: Build a new array.

quiz.question: What is persistent data structure sharing good for?
options: Cheap copies: undo/redo, time travel and snapshots without copying everything
quiz.explanation: Each version shares unchanged parts with the previous one.

quiz.question: Why validate at the boundary rather than in every function?
options: Inside the boundary, precise types carry the guarantee; checking again is noise and drift
quiz.explanation: Parse once, then trust.

quiz.question: Why should the constructor function be the ONLY place that writes `as UserId`?
options: It concentrates the unchecked assertion in one validated spot, so the type genuinely implies the invariant
TypeScript only allows one cast per type
Casting elsewhere is a runtime error
The compiler tracks how many casts a program contains
quiz.explanation: The brand is only as trustworthy as the assertions that create it. Scattering casts around means the type no longer proves anything.

quiz.question: How can you check at runtime whether a value is a `UserId`?
options: You cannot directly — you must re-run the validation the constructor performs
quiz.explanation: Since the brand is erased there is nothing to inspect. Runtime questions about a branded value always come back to re-checking the underlying data.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a validator and a parser?
options: A parser returns a more precise type that records the check; a validator returns a boolean
A validator throws, a parser doesn't
quiz.explanation: The parser's return type carries the knowledge forward, so nothing downstream has to recheck.

quiz.question: What does `declare const Brand: unique symbol` emit at runtime?
quiz.explanation: It only creates a type-level unique symbol to key the brand property.

quiz.question: Where should the `as Email` cast appear?
options: Once, inside the parser, right after the check
quiz.explanation: Concentrating the cast in the smart constructor is what makes the brand trustworthy.

quiz.question: Why is `readonly [number, ...number[]]` useful?
options: Its first element is never `undefined`, so code taking it needs no emptiness check
It is faster than an array
quiz.explanation: The non-emptiness is proven once, at construction, and carried in the type.

quiz.question: A parser trims and lower-cases emails. Why?
options: So equal addresses become equal strings — normalising is part of parsing
quiz.explanation: Returning the canonical form removes a whole class of duplicate bugs.

quiz.question: Where in a program should parsing happen?
options: At the boundary, where untyped input enters — once
In every function that uses the value
quiz.explanation: Inside the boundary, the precise types carry the guarantee.

exam.title: Branded money
exam.prompt: Brand `Cents` and `Dollars`. The input is `n` then `n` amounts in cents. Print the running total in cents after each, then the final total in dollars (cents / 100). Only a validating constructor may produce a branded value; reject negatives by printing `invalid` for that line and skipping it.
exam.hint: Return `Cents | null` from the constructor so the caller must handle bad input; the cast inside it is the single place the brand is applied.

types.title: Part 1 — a reusable brand
types.prompt: Write `Brand<T, B>`: a `T` that carries the tag `B` in a property keyed by the `unique symbol` `brand`, so that a plain `number` is not a `UserId`, a `UserId` is not an `OrderId`, and both are still usable as numbers.
types.hint: A brand is an intersection: the base type `&` an object type nobody else can produce.
hints: A brand is an intersection: the base type `&` an object type nobody else can produce.
`T & { readonly [brand]: B }` — the computed key uses the `unique symbol` declared above.

flashcards.front: What is a branded type?
flashcards.back: A primitive intersected with a tag: `type Cents = number & { readonly __brand: "Cents" }`, so a plain `number` is not accepted where `Cents` is expected.

flashcards.front: How should branded values be created?
flashcards.back: By one validating constructor that returns `Cents | null` (or throws) — the only place the `as Cents` cast appears.

flashcards.front: Does a brand exist at runtime?
flashcards.back: No — it is purely a type. A `Cents` is an ordinary number when the program runs.

flashcards.front: What does `readonly` on a property prevent?
flashcards.back: Assigning to it through that type (TS2540). It does not deep-freeze, and it does not exist at runtime.

flashcards.front: `readonly number[]` vs `ReadonlyArray<number>`?
flashcards.back: The same type; both drop `push`, `pop`, `sort` and the other mutators.

flashcards.front: What does `Object.freeze` do that `readonly` doesn't?
flashcards.back: It is enforced at runtime. But it is shallow, and a write to a frozen property fails silently in sloppy mode and throws only in strict mode.

flashcards.front: What is aliasing, and why is it a bug source?
flashcards.back: Two names for one object. Mutating through one changes what the other sees — the fix is copying, or making mutation impossible.

flashcards.front: How do you update one element of an array immutably?
flashcards.back: `xs.with(i, value)` (ES2023) or `xs.map((x, j) => (j === i ? value : x))`.

flashcards.front: How does an undo stack stay cheap with immutable state?
flashcards.back: Each state is a new value that shares unchanged parts with the old one, so keeping history is just keeping references.

flashcards.front: What is `Readonly<T>`?
flashcards.back: A mapped type that marks every property of `T` `readonly` — one level deep only.

flashcards.front: Why prefer parsing to validating?
flashcards.back: A parser returns a narrower type (`Email`, not `string`), so later code can't forget the check was done — the type carries the proof.

flashcards.front: TS2540 — cause?
flashcards.back: "Cannot assign to 'x' because it is a read-only property."

flashcards.front: Validator vs parser, in one line?
flashcards.back: A validator returns `true`/`false` and forgets; a parser returns a more precise type (`Email`) that proves the check happened.

flashcards.front: How do you declare an unforgeable brand?
flashcards.back: `declare const B: unique symbol; type Email = string & { readonly [B]: true };` — kept private to the module.

flashcards.front: What does a `unique symbol` brand cost at runtime?
flashcards.back: Nothing: `declare` emits no code and the intersection is erased — the value is a plain string.

flashcards.front: Where does the one `as Email` belong?
flashcards.back: Inside the smart constructor, immediately after the check that justifies it.

flashcards.front: How do you type a list that can't be empty?
flashcards.back: `readonly [T, ...T[]]` — its first element is always present.

flashcards.front: Why normalise inside the parser?
flashcards.back: So equal values become equal (trimmed, lower-cased, integer cents) and duplicates can't sneak in.

project_spec.title: ids.ts — branded ids and a read-only store
project_spec.goal: Parse users and orders into branded `UserId`/`OrderId` values and integer cents, reject every bad row, and answer queries from a store that callers cannot mutate. A user id where an order id belongs is a compile error — and, from the query input, a clear message.
requirements: The input has three sections separated by lines containing only `---`: users (`<userId> <name>`), orders (`<orderId> <userId> <amount>`), queries.

A `UserId` is `U-` and three digits; an `OrderId` is `O-` and four; an amount has at most two decimals. Report bad rows as they are read: `bad user line: <line>`, `bad order line: <line>`, `duplicate id <id>`, `order <id>: unknown user <userId>`.

Queries: `user <id>` → `<name>: <k> orders, $<total>` (`order` for one); `order <id>` → `<id> by <name>: $<amount>`; `top` → the user with the highest total, `<name> $<total>` (earliest id on a tie; `none` if no orders). A missing id prints `no user <id>` / `no order <id>`; an id of the wrong kind or format prints `not a user id <x>` / `not an order id <x>`.
Store users and orders in `ReadonlyMap`s keyed by the branded ids, built once and never changed afterwards.
Money is printed with two decimals.
stretch: Make the maps impossible to mutate even through a cast by freezing them — and explain why that is not the same guarantee.
Add `refund <orderId> <amount>` producing a new store rather than editing the old one.
rubric: No `any` anywhere — not even one hidden in a cast
Every function has a typed signature; locals are left to inference
Bad input is handled on purpose, not by accident
Names say what things are, not how they are stored
I could explain every line to someone else

Only a validating constructor may produce a `Kelvin` (a finite number, not below 0); print `invalid` for any other line. Convert each valid reading to `Celsius` (K − 273.15) and print it to 2 decimal places; then print the mean Celsius of the valid readings to 2 places, or `none`.
exam_alternates.hint: The constructor returns `Kelvin | null`; nothing else may assert a number into a brand.

weeks.title: Composition & Utility Types
weeks.goal: Build types out of other types instead of restating them.

problems.note: Sort, then fold — with a well-typed interval.
A variant of the same model.
The simplest form of the pattern.

weeks.project: Model a `Task` type, then derive `TaskDraft` (no id), `TaskPatch` (all optional) and `TaskSummary` (a few fields) with `Omit`, `Partial` and `Pick` rather than three hand-written types.

quiz.question: What does `Omit<T, K>` do?
options: Produces T without the properties named in K
Makes the properties in K optional
Keeps only the properties in K
quiz.explanation: `Pick` keeps, `Omit` removes. `Omit` is defined in terms of `Pick` and `Exclude`.

quiz.question: How do you combine two object types?
options: An intersection: A & B, or interface B extends A
quiz.explanation: An intersection requires BOTH sets of members. A union means 'one or the other', which is the opposite of combining.

quiz.question: What is `Record<string, number>`?
options: An object type with string keys and number values
A tuple of a string and a number
A union of string and number
quiz.explanation: `Record` is a mapped type: `{ [P in K]: V }`. Note that a string-keyed Record loses literal key checking.

quiz.question: `Partial<T>` makes every property optional. What is its inverse?
quiz.explanation: `Required<T>` is `{ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }` — the `-?` strips the optional modifier the source type had.

quiz.question: What does `A & B` mean for two object types?
options: A value must satisfy BOTH — it has all members of A and of B
A value must satisfy either one
quiz.explanation: Intersection combines requirements. It is unions that mean 'one or the other', which is the opposite of what people first expect from the & symbol.

quiz.question: What is `Exclude<"a" | "b" | "c", "b">`?
quiz.explanation: `Exclude` filters a union with a distributive conditional type. `Omit` is the object-level cousin, built from Exclude and Pick.

quiz.question: `Partial<{ a: number }>`?
quiz.explanation: Every property becomes optional.

quiz.question: `Required<{ a?: number }>`?
quiz.explanation: The `?` is removed.

quiz.question: `Pick<{ a: 1; b: 2 }, "a">`?
quiz.explanation: `Pick` keeps the named keys.

quiz.question: `Record<"x" | "y", boolean>`?
quiz.explanation: One property per member of the key union.

quiz.question: `Extract<"a" | "b" | 1, string>`?
quiz.explanation: `Extract` keeps the members assignable to the second argument.

quiz.question: `NonNullable<string | null | undefined>`?
quiz.explanation: Both `null` and `undefined` are removed.

quiz.question: `Parameters<(a: number, b: string) => void>`?
quiz.explanation: A labelled tuple of the parameter types.

quiz.question: `ReturnType<() => Promise<number>>`?
quiz.explanation: It's the declared return type — the promise itself.

quiz.question: `Awaited<ReturnType<() => Promise<number>>>`?
quiz.explanation: `Awaited` unwraps the promise.

quiz.question: What is the type of `a` in `{ a: number } & { a: string }`?
quiz.explanation: No value is both a number and a string, so the property's type is `never`.

quiz.question: What is `Omit<{ a: 1; b: 2 }, "c">`?
options: `{ a: 1; b: 2 }` — `Omit` accepts keys that don't exist
quiz.explanation: `Omit`'s key parameter is unconstrained, so a typo silently does nothing. `Pick` would reject it.

quiz.question: Why does `Pick<T, "typo">` fail while `Omit<T, "typo">` compiles?
options: `Pick` constrains keys to `keyof T`; `Omit` takes any key
quiz.explanation: Wrap it in your own `StrictOmit<T, K extends keyof T>` if you want the check.

quiz.question: What does `ReturnType<typeof f>` require?
options: `typeof` — `f` is a value, and utilities take types
quiz.explanation: `ReturnType<f>` is an error.

quiz.question: What is `Parameters<typeof f>[0]`?
quiz.explanation: An indexed access on the parameter tuple.

quiz.question: What does `Readonly<Pick<User, "id" | "name">>` produce?
options: A type with just `id` and `name`, both readonly
quiz.explanation: Utilities compose.

quiz.question: What does `NoInfer<T>` (TS 5.4) do in a signature?
options: Stops that position from contributing to inferring `T`
quiz.explanation: Useful for defaults and fallbacks.

quiz.question: What is composition over inheritance, in types?
options: Building types by combining smaller ones (`&`, `Pick`, mapped types) instead of deep `extends` chains
quiz.explanation: Small pieces are easier to reuse and to change.

quiz.question: What's a risk of `Partial<T>` as a function parameter everywhere?
options: Required data can go missing without the compiler noticing
quiz.explanation: Use it for patches and options, not for complete records.

quiz.question: A `Record<"a" | "b", number>` literal is missing `b`. Result?
options: A compile error — every key is required
quiz.explanation: `Record` over a finite union demands every key.

quiz.question: What does `Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>` give?
quiz.explanation: It unwraps recursively, as `await` does.

quiz.question: What does `InstanceType<typeof MyClass>` give?
options: The type of an instance of `MyClass`
quiz.explanation: Useful when all you have is the class value.

quiz.question: What does `ConstructorParameters<typeof Date>` describe?
quiz.explanation: The constructor counterpart of `Parameters`.

quiz.question: Where should a validator's schema live relative to the type?
options: The type should be derived from the schema — one source of truth
Separately, kept in sync by hand
quiz.explanation: Two descriptions drift; one can't.

quiz.question: What does `Required<T>` do to `x?: number | undefined`?
options: Makes `x` required and removes the `undefined` added by `?`
quiz.explanation: It's the `-?` modifier in a mapped type.

quiz.question: What is `Extract<"a" | "b" | "c", "a" | "z">`?
quiz.explanation: Only members of the first union that fit the second survive.

quiz.question: A `TaskPatch = Partial<Omit<Task, "id">>` — can a patch change the id?
options: No — `id` isn't in the patch type
quiz.explanation: Types make the rule part of the API.

quiz.question: When is a hand-written type better than a derived one?
options: When it's a deliberate contract that must not change just because the source does
quiz.explanation: Public API types are often pinned on purpose.

quiz.question: What does spreading a `Partial<Options>` with `{ width: undefined }` into defaults do?
quiz.explanation: Filter out undefined values or use `??` per field.

quiz.question: Why derive the type from the schema rather than write both?
options: Two descriptions drift apart; one description can't
quiz.explanation: The validator is the source of truth, and `Infer` computes the type from it.

quiz.question: What does `Infer<typeof User>` give you when `User = obj({ name: str() })`?
quiz.explanation: `Infer` extracts the `T` from a `Schema<T>`.

quiz.question: `const user = JSON.parse(text) as User` — what has been checked?
options: Nothing; the assertion is a promise, erased at runtime
Only the types of the values
quiz.explanation: Assertions never check. A schema does.

quiz.question: Why should a validator collect every issue instead of stopping at the first?
options: So whoever sent bad data can fix all of it in one pass
quiz.explanation: One error at a time makes fixing data a slow loop.

quiz.question: Where should `User.parse` be called?
options: At the boundary where the data enters the program
In every function that uses a user
quiz.explanation: Parse once; inside the boundary the type carries the guarantee.

quiz.question: Which existing libraries work this way?
quiz.explanation: They are schema libraries whose validators also produce static types.

exam.title: Typed patch API
exam.prompt: Tasks are `id|title|done|tags` lines (`done` is `true`/`false`, tags comma-separated, possibly empty) after a count `n`; then a count `m` and `m` patches `id;key=value;key=value…`. A patch may set `title` (non-empty, trimmed), `done` (`true`/`false` only) and `tags` (comma-separated; empty clears them). It may never touch `id`, and an unknown key rejects it. A patch applies completely or not at all. Print `#<id>: updated <keys>` (the keys comma-joined in the order given, `nothing` for none), `#<id>: rejected, <reason>` (`id cannot change`, `unknown field <key>`, `title cannot be empty`, `done must be true or false`), or `#<id>: no such task`. Then every task by id as `id | title | done-or-open | tags-or--`. Type the patch as a utility type of `Task`, and parse it into a `Result`.
exam.hint: `Partial<Omit<Task, "id">>` is the patch. Build it field by field into a `Result`, and only apply it once every field has parsed.
