types.title: Part 1 — make some keys required
types.prompt: Write `WithRequired<T, K>`: `T` with the keys in `K` made required (and no longer `undefined`), every other property exactly as it was. `K` must be a key of `T`. Compose it from utility types.
types.hint: Split `T` in two: the keys you are changing, and the rest.
hints: Split `T` in two: the keys you are changing, and the rest.
`Omit<T, K>` keeps the rest untouched; `Required<Pick<T, K>>` makes the chosen ones required. Intersect them.
types.starter: type WithRequired<T, K extends keyof T> = ____;
types.solution: type WithRequired<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K> & Required<Pick<T, K>>;

flashcards.front: What does `Partial<T>` do?
flashcards.back: Makes every property of `T` optional — the natural type for an update or patch.

flashcards.front: `Pick<T, K>` vs `Omit<T, K>` — which checks its keys?
flashcards.back: `Pick` requires `K extends keyof T` (a typo is TS2344). `Omit` accepts any key, so a typo omits nothing, silently.

flashcards.front: Does `Omit<User, "password">` remove `password` at runtime?
flashcards.back: No. `return { ...user }` typed as the `Omit` still contains the password. You must actually delete or not copy it.

flashcards.front: What is `Record<K, V>`?
flashcards.back: An object type with keys `K` and values `V`: `Record<"a" | "b", number>` is `{ a: number; b: number }`.

flashcards.front: `Exclude<U, X>` vs `Extract<U, X>`?
flashcards.back: `Exclude` removes the union members assignable to `X`; `Extract` keeps only those.

flashcards.front: What does `NonNullable<T>` remove?
flashcards.back: `null` and `undefined` from `T`.

flashcards.front: How do you get a function's return type without repeating it?
flashcards.back: `ReturnType<typeof fn>`. And `Parameters<typeof fn>` gives its parameter tuple.

flashcards.front: What does `Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>` give?
flashcards.back: `number` — `Awaited` unwraps promises recursively, like `await` does.

flashcards.front: What does `Required<T>` do?
flashcards.back: Removes `?` from every property of `T`.

flashcards.front: Why derive `TaskDraft` from `Task` instead of writing it out?
flashcards.back: One source of truth: add a field to `Task` and every derived type updates. Hand-written copies drift apart.

flashcards.front: Composition over inheritance — in one line?
flashcards.back: Build behaviour by combining small functions and objects, rather than extending a class hierarchy.

flashcards.front: TS2344 — cause?
flashcards.back: A type argument doesn't satisfy its constraint, e.g. `Pick<User, "nope">`.

flashcards.front: Why derive a type from a schema instead of writing both?
flashcards.back: Two descriptions drift; with `type T = Infer<typeof Schema>` there is only one.

flashcards.front: `JSON.parse(text) as User` — what did it check?
flashcards.back: Nothing. An assertion is erased; only a runtime validator checks.

flashcards.front: What does a schema's `parse` return?
flashcards.back: Either the typed value or the issues — a result union such as `{ ok: true; value } | { ok: false; issues }`.

flashcards.front: Why collect every validation issue?
flashcards.back: So the sender can fix all of them in one pass instead of one per round trip.

flashcards.front: Name three libraries built on the schema-first idea.
flashcards.back: Zod, Valibot and ArkType.

flashcards.front: Where do you call a schema's `parse`?
flashcards.back: Once, at the boundary where untrusted data enters; inside, the inferred type carries the guarantee.

practice.title: A draft has no id yet
practice.prompt: Derive `TaskDraft` from `Task` — everything except `id` — with a utility type rather than by writing the fields out.
practice.hint: Which utility type removes keys?
hints: Which utility type removes keys?
`Omit<T, K>` keeps every property of `T` except those in `K`.
practice.starter:
type Task = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean; tags: string[] };
type TaskDraft = ____;
practice.solution:
type Task = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean; tags: string[] };
type TaskDraft = Omit<Task, "id">;

practice.title: A patch may change any field but the id
practice.prompt: `TaskPatch` is what an update accepts: any subset of the fields, except `id`, which never changes. Build it by composing two utility types.
practice.hint: Two steps: drop `id`, then make what is left optional.
hints: Two steps: drop `id`, then make what is left optional.
`Partial<Omit<Task, "id">>`.
practice.starter:
type Task = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean; tags: string[] };
type TaskPatch = ____;
practice.solution:
type Task = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean; tags: string[] };
type TaskPatch = Partial<Omit<Task, "id">>;

practice.title: Only what the list view needs
practice.prompt: The task list shows just `id` and `title`. Derive `TaskSummary` from `Task`.
practice.hint: Which utility keeps only the keys you name?
hints: Which utility keeps only the keys you name?
`Pick<T, K>` — and `K` can be a union of keys.
practice.starter:
type Task = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean; tags: string[] };
type TaskSummary = ____;
practice.solution:
type Task = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean; tags: string[] };
type TaskSummary = Pick<Task, "id" | "title">;

practice.title: A total for every status
practice.prompt: `Totals` must have exactly one number per status — no more, no fewer. Build it from `Status`.
practice.hint: You want an object type whose keys are the members of a union.
hints: You want an object type whose keys are the members of a union.
`Record<K, V>`.
practice.starter:
type Status = "open" | "blocked" | "done";
type Totals = ____;
practice.solution:
type Status = "open" | "blocked" | "done";
type Totals = Record<Status, number>;

practice.title: Which statuses are final
practice.prompt: From `Status`, derive `Finished`: every status except `"idle"` and `"loading"`.
practice.hint: `Omit` works on object keys; you are filtering a union.
hints: `Omit` works on object keys; you are filtering a union.
`Exclude<Union, Removed>`.
practice.starter:
type Status = "idle" | "loading" | "done" | "error";
type Finished = ____;
practice.solution:
type Status = "idle" | "loading" | "done" | "error";
type Finished = Exclude<Status, "idle" | "loading">;

practice.title: Name what a factory makes
practice.prompt: `makeUser` is the single source of truth for a user's shape. Derive `User` from it, so the two can never drift apart.
practice.hint: A utility type can read a function's return type.
hints: A utility type can read a function's return type.
It takes a *type*, and `makeUser` is a value — lift it with `typeof`.

practice.title: What does an async function give you?
practice.prompt: `loadScores` is async. Derive `Scores` — the value you get *after* awaiting it — from the function itself.
practice.hint: `ReturnType` gives you `Promise<number[]>` — one step short.
hints: `ReturnType` gives you `Promise<number[]>` — one step short.
Unwrap the promise with `Awaited<…>`.

practice.title: Reading a Partial field
practice.prompt: What type does TypeScript already infer for `t`? Annotate `check` with exactly that type — not merely one that fits.
practice.hint: `Partial` makes every property optional.
hints: `Partial` makes every property optional.
An optional property reads as `T | undefined`.

practice.title: A key that isn't there
practice.prompt:
The compiler rejects this program:

    error TS2344: Type '"titel"' does not satisfy the constraint 'keyof Task'.

Fix the cause.
practice.hint: `Pick` only accepts keys the type has.
hints: `Pick` only accepts keys the type has.
Fix the spelling.

practice.title: A spread that erased the default
practice.prompt: Print the window width: the given number, or 800 when the input is empty. It prints `undefined` for empty input.
practice.hint: Spreading `{ width: undefined }` sets `width` to `undefined` — it doesn't skip it.
hints: Spreading `{ width: undefined }` sets `width` to `undefined` — it doesn't skip it.
Fall back explicitly with `??`.

problem_set.title: Apply patches to a task

hints: `Partial<Omit<Task, "id">>` is exactly "any subset of the fields except the id".

problem_set.title: Fill in the defaults — carefully
problem_set.prompt: Window options have defaults `{ width: 800, height: 600, title: "Untitled", resizable: true, theme: "light" }`. Each input line is a JSON object of overrides (a `Partial<Options>`). Then print the resolved `<width>x<height> "<title>" resizable=<bool> theme=<theme>`. Note that a spread of `{ width: undefined }` would *erase* the default.
problem_set.hint: Copy an override only when it is present *and* valid; a key set to `undefined` or `null` must not reach the spread.

project_spec.title: tasks.ts — a typed task API with validation
project_spec.goal: Build the core of a task service: one `Task` model, and every other shape — the create payload, the patch, the list summary — derived from it with utility types. Every JSON body is validated from `unknown`, and every problem is reported at once.
requirements: `Task` is `{ id, title, done, priority, tags }` with priority `low`/`normal`/`high`. Derive `TaskDraft = Pick<Task, "title"> & Partial<Pick<Task, "priority" | "tags">>` and `TaskPatch = Partial<Omit<Task, "id">>`.

`create <json>`: title a non-empty string (required), priority one of the three (default `normal`), tags an array of strings (default none), no other keys. Print `created #<id>` (ids start at 1) or `create rejected: ` and every problem — `title: required`, `title: must be text`, `priority: must be low, normal or high`, `tags: must be a list of strings`, `unknown field <k>` — joined by `; `.

`patch <id> <json>`: the same rules for any subset of `title`, `done` (boolean, else `done: must be true or false`), `priority`, `tags`; `id: cannot change` if `id` is present. Print `patched #<id> (<changed fields in input order>)`, `patch #<id>: nothing to change` for an empty patch, `patch rejected: …`, or `no task #<id>`. `delete <id>` prints `deleted #<id>` or `no task #<id>`.
`list` prints each task by id: `#<id> [x] <title> (<priority>)` plus ` #tag` for each tag (`[ ]` when not done), or `(no tasks)`.
`summary` prints `open <a>, done <b>, high=<h> normal=<n> low=<l>`.
stretch: Rewrite the validation with the week's schema library, so `TaskDraft` is `Infer<typeof TaskDraftSchema>`.
Add `undo`, keeping each version of the store immutable (week 16).
rubric: No `any` anywhere — not even one hidden in a cast
Every function has a typed signature; locals are left to inference
Bad input is handled on purpose, not by accident
Names say what things are, not how they are stored
I could explain every line to someone else

quiz.question: When is a generic the WRONG tool?
options: When the body never uses T — a plain parameter type is clearer
When there is more than one type parameter
quiz.explanation: A type parameter used once and never related to anything else adds noise without adding a guarantee.

quiz.question: `function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined` — what does `first([1, 2])` return, type-wise?
quiz.explanation: `T` is inferred as `number`; the `| undefined` covers the empty array.

quiz.question: `function len<T extends { length: number }>(x: T) { … }` — what is `len(5)`?
quiz.explanation: The constraint rejects arguments without a numeric `length`.

quiz.question: `class Box<T> { value: T; constructor(v: T) { this.value = v; } }` — what is `new Box(3).value`'s type?
quiz.explanation: `T` is inferred from the constructor argument and widened to `number` for the mutable field.

quiz.question: `first<string>([1])` — result?
quiz.explanation: An explicit type argument fixes `T`, and the argument must match it.

quiz.question: What does `function merge<A, B>(a: A, b: B): A & B` promise?
options: A value with every property of both
quiz.explanation: `A & B` is an intersection: it has all members of both.

quiz.question: `get(user, "nme")` where `get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K)` — result?
options: Compile error: `"nme"` isn't a key of the user type
quiz.explanation: The `keyof` constraint turns a typo into an error at the call.

quiz.question: In `Promise<T>`, what is `T`?
options: The type of the value the promise resolves with
quiz.explanation: Rejections are untyped (`any`/`unknown`); only the fulfilment value is in the type.

quiz.question: You write a helper that only counts elements. Should it be `count<T>(xs: T[])` or `count(xs: unknown[])`?
options: `count(xs: unknown[])` — `T` would appear only once and link nothing
It makes no difference to callers, so either
quiz.explanation: A type parameter earns its place by connecting two positions (input and output). Otherwise `unknown` says the same thing more simply.

quiz.question: With `function f<const T extends readonly string[]>(xs: T)`, what is `T` for `f(["a", "b"])`?
quiz.explanation: A `const` type parameter (TS 5.0) infers as if the caller had written `as const`.

quiz.question: `function wrap<T>(x: T) { return [x]; }` — what is the inferred return type?
quiz.explanation: An array literal infers an array type, not a tuple, unless asked otherwise.

quiz.question: What does `NoInfer<T>` do in `function pick<T extends string>(options: T[], fallback: NoInfer<T>)`?
options: Makes `T` come from `options` only, so a `fallback` not in the list is an error
quiz.explanation: Without it, `pick(["a", "b"], "c")` would widen `T` to include `"c"` (TS 5.4).

quiz.question: When is a generic default like `<T = string>` used?
options: When `T` can be neither inferred nor is it passed explicitly
quiz.explanation: Inference and explicit arguments both take priority over the default.

quiz.question: `class Stack<T> { items: T[] = []; }` — what is `new Stack()`?
quiz.explanation: With nothing to infer from and no default, a type parameter becomes `unknown`. Write `new Stack<number>()`.

quiz.question: For `f<T>(x: T[]): T`, what is `f([1, "a"])`?
quiz.explanation: The array literal's element type is the union, so `T` is too.

quiz.question: Are `Array<T>` and `T[]` different types?
options: No — two spellings of the same type
quiz.explanation: `ReadonlyArray<T>` is `readonly T[]`.

quiz.question: Does `T extends object` accept arrays?
quiz.explanation: Constrain further (e.g. `Record<string, unknown>`) if you mean plain objects.

quiz.question: How do you annotate a variable that holds a generic function?
quiz.explanation: The type parameter list goes at the start of the function type.

quiz.question: How do you require a type argument to satisfy two constraints?
quiz.explanation: An intersection means "both".

quiz.question: What does `<T extends unknown>` constrain?
options: It forces `T` to be an object
quiz.explanation: It is the same as `<T>`.

quiz.question: Why is `function parse<T>(json: string): T` a warning sign?
options: `T` appears only in the return type — the caller picks it, so it's an unchecked cast
quiz.explanation: Return `unknown` and validate, or take a schema that produces the type.

quiz.question: Can a default refer to an earlier type parameter: `<T, U = T[]>`?
quiz.explanation: Defaults are evaluated left to right.

quiz.question: What are the conventional names `T`, `K`, `V`, `E`?
quiz.explanation: Use descriptive names (`TItem`) when there are several.

quiz.question: In `<T extends string>`, what does `extends` mean?
quiz.explanation: A constraint, not inheritance.

quiz.question: Why are generic classes like `Stack<T>` better than `Stack` of `unknown`?
options: Callers get back the type they put in, with no casts
quiz.explanation: `pop()` on a `Stack<number>` returns `number | undefined`.

quiz.question: What does `Map<K, V>` need two type parameters for?
options: The key type and the value type are independent
It doesn't; the second is optional
quiz.explanation: `Map<string, number[]>`, for example.

quiz.question: What does `function merge<A extends object, B extends object>(a: A, b: B)` ensure that plain `<A, B>` doesn't?
options: Both arguments are objects, so spreading them makes sense
quiz.explanation: Constraints document and enforce the assumptions the body makes.

quiz.question: When does inference fail and require an explicit type argument?
options: When nothing in the call mentions the type parameter — e.g. `new Map()` or `useState([])`
quiz.explanation: Give inference something, or say the type yourself.

quiz.question: What is a generic *constraint* for, in one line?
options: To let the body use members every allowed `T` must have
quiz.explanation: `T extends { length: number }` lets the body read `.length`.

quiz.question: What is `function wrap<T>(x: T): { value: T }` for `wrap("a")` with a `const` result?
quiz.explanation: The literal widens when inferred for an unconstrained `T`; a `const` type parameter would keep `"a"`.

quiz.question: Why does `Promise<T>` need a type parameter?
options: It describes what the promise will eventually hold
quiz.explanation: `await` on a `Promise<T>` gives a `T`.

quiz.question: Why is `function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T` better than `function longest(a: { length: number }, b: { length: number }): { length: number }`?
options: The generic returns the caller's exact type instead of collapsing it to { length: number }
The generic is faster at runtime
The non-generic version does not compile
quiz.explanation: Both accept the same arguments. The difference is on the way out: the generic hands back `string` for strings, while the plain signature loses everything except `.length`.

quiz.question: In `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`, what is `T[K]`?
options: An indexed access type — the type of the property named K on T
An array of T indexed by K
quiz.explanation: `T[K]` looks up a property type by name, which is what lets one signature return `string` for `\"name\"` and `number` for `\"age\"`.

quiz.question: What does the default in `function makeBox<T = string>(value: T)` actually do?
options: It supplies T only when inference has nothing to infer from
It makes the value parameter optional
It coerces the argument to string
quiz.explanation: A type-parameter default is not a value default. `makeBox(1)` still infers `T = number`; the default matters for cases like `const b: Box = ...` where no argument drives inference.

quiz.question: What is `T` in `wrap(42)` for `function wrap<T>(x: T)`?
quiz.explanation: Inferred type arguments widen literals like a `let` does, unless the parameter is `const` or constrained.

quiz.question: What does a `const` type parameter change?
options: Arguments are inferred as if written with `as const`, keeping literal and tuple types
quiz.explanation: Added in TS 5.0: `<const T extends readonly string[]>`.

quiz.question: What is `NoInfer<T>` for?
options: Stopping one argument from contributing to `T`, so it is only checked against it
Disabling type checking for an argument
quiz.explanation: TS 5.4. Typical use: a fallback or default that must be one of the inferred options.

quiz.question: `box([])` infers `T` as?
quiz.explanation: There is no element to infer from. Write `box<string>([])`.

quiz.question: Why is `function log<T>(x: T): void` a smell?
options: `T` appears once, so it relates nothing — it's just `unknown`
quiz.explanation: Type parameters exist to connect types: an input to an output, or two inputs.

quiz.question: When does a type parameter default like `<T = string>` apply?
options: When no type argument is given and nothing can be inferred
quiz.explanation: Inference wins when it has candidates; the default fills the gap when it doesn't.

flashcards.front: What problem do generics solve?
flashcards.back: Reusing code across types without losing precision: `first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined` returns a `number` for a `number[]`, not `any`.

flashcards.front: How are type arguments usually supplied?
flashcards.back: Inferred from the arguments: `first([1, 2])` infers `T = number`. Pass them explicitly only when inference can't see them.

flashcards.front: What does `<T extends { id: string }>` mean?
flashcards.back: `T` can be any type, as long as it has a string `id` — so the body may use `x.id`.

flashcards.front: What does `K extends keyof T` give you?
flashcards.back: A key that really exists on `T`, so `obj[key]` is typed `T[K]` — the value type for that exact key.

flashcards.front: Smell: a type parameter used only once. Why?
flashcards.back: It adds nothing — `<T>(x: T): void` is just `(x: unknown): void`. A generic earns its place by linking two positions.

flashcards.front: What is a generic default?
flashcards.back: `<T = string>` — the type used when `T` is neither passed nor inferable.

flashcards.front: Why might `T extends object` surprise you?
flashcards.back: Arrays and functions are objects too, so they satisfy it.

flashcards.front: What does TS2322 "'T' could be instantiated with an arbitrary type" mean?
flashcards.back: You returned a specific type where the caller chose `T`. The body must work for *every* `T`, not just the one you had in mind.

flashcards.front: What does a `const` type parameter do (TS 5.0)?
flashcards.back: `<const T>` infers literal types for arguments, as if the caller wrote `as const` — `f(["a", "b"])` infers `readonly ["a", "b"]`.

flashcards.front: What is `NoInfer<T>` for (TS 5.4)?
flashcards.back: Blocking inference from one argument, so `T` is decided by the others — e.g. a default value that must match the options list.

flashcards.front: How do you type a generic `groupBy`?
flashcards.back: `function groupBy<T, K extends PropertyKey>(xs: T[], key: (x: T) => K): Map<K, T[]>`.

flashcards.front: Generic class — how is `T` fixed?
flashcards.back: At construction: `new Stack<number>()`, or inferred from constructor arguments.

flashcards.front: Where do inferred type arguments come from?
flashcards.back: Candidates from the arguments (and the contextual return type); literals widen unless the parameter is `const` or constrained.

flashcards.front: What does `<const T extends readonly unknown[]>` do?
flashcards.back: Infers the argument as if written with `as const` — exact tuples and literal types (TS 5.0).

flashcards.front: What is `NoInfer<T>` for?
flashcards.back: Excluding one argument from inference so it is only checked against `T` — e.g. a fallback that must be one of the options (TS 5.4).

flashcards.front: `box([])` gives `T` = ?
flashcards.back: `never` — nothing to infer from. Write `box<string>([])`.

flashcards.front: When does a default type argument `<T = string>` apply?
flashcards.back: Only when there is no explicit argument and nothing to infer.

flashcards.front: A type parameter that appears once — what's wrong?
flashcards.back: It relates nothing to anything; use `unknown` (or a real constraint) instead.

project_spec.goal: Write a small generic `Collection<T>` class whose methods keep the element type through a pipeline — `map` changes it, `filter` and `sortBy` keep it, `groupBy` produces a `Map` — and drive it from commands. The same class serves numbers and words, which is the point of making it generic.
requirements: The first input line is `numbers <n…>` or `words <w…>`; each later line is one step applied to the current collection: `map double|square|length|upper`, `filter even|odd|long` (`long` = length > 3), `sortBy value|length`, `unique`, `take <n>`, `chunk <n>`, `groupBy length|parity`, `first`, `count`.

`map`, `filter`, `sortBy`, `unique` and `take` print the new collection space-separated (or `(empty)`); `first` prints the first item or `none`; `count` prints the size. A step that doesn't apply to the current element type (e.g. `map upper` on numbers) prints `cannot <step> <numbers|words>` and changes nothing.
`chunk <n>` prints the chunks as `[a b] [c]`; `groupBy` prints `<key>: <items>` per group in first-seen order. Neither changes the collection.
Implement `Collection<T>` with generic methods — `map<U>(fn: (x: T) => U): Collection<U>` and friends — so that the element type is tracked at every step.
`sortBy` is stable and ascending; `length` compares the printed length of each item.
stretch: Add `reduce<U>(fn: (acc: U, x: T) => U, start: U): U` and a `sum` step that only type-checks for `Collection<number>` (hint: a `this` parameter, `sum(this: Collection<number>)`).
Make `Collection` iterable (`[Symbol.iterator]`) — week 24 teaches how.

weeks.title: keyof, typeof & Indexed Access
weeks.goal: Derive types from values so one source of truth drives both.

problems.note: Applied: a keyed store with a typed accessor.

weeks.project: Write a `settings.ts` where one `as const` object defines the defaults, and every getter, setter and key union is derived from it — adding a setting should require exactly one edit.

quiz.question: What is `(typeof levels)[number]` when `const levels = ["a", "b"] as const`?
quiz.explanation: `as const` keeps the elements literal, and indexing the tuple type by `number` unions them — the standard derive-a-union idiom.

quiz.question: What is `keyof Record<string, number>`?
quiz.explanation: `keyof` on an index signature gives the index type, and numeric keys are also valid string keys — which is why it includes `number`.

quiz.question: `keyof { a: 1; b: 2 }`?
quiz.explanation: `keyof` produces the union of property names.

quiz.question: With `type P = { name: string; age: number }`, what is `P["age"]`?
quiz.explanation: An indexed access type looks up the property's type.

quiz.question: With `type P = { name: string; age: number }`, what is `P[keyof P]`?
quiz.explanation: Indexing with the key union gives the union of all value types.

quiz.question: `const o = { x: 1 };` — what is `typeof o`?
quiz.explanation: The property is mutable, so it widens to `number`. (In an expression, `typeof o` would be the string `"object"`.)

quiz.question: `const arr = [1, "a"];` — what is `(typeof arr)[number]`?
quiz.explanation: Without `as const`, the element type is widened.

quiz.question: Does `keyof string[]` include `number`?
options: Yes — along with `length`, `push` and the other array members
quiz.explanation: Arrays have numeric index keys as well as named properties.

quiz.question: `const COLORS = { red: "#f00" } as const;` — what is `(typeof COLORS)["red"]`?
quiz.explanation: `as const` keeps the literal value type.

quiz.question: With `type P = { name: string; age: number }`, what does `P["missing"]` give?
quiz.explanation: Indexed access requires a key that exists on the type.

quiz.question: With `type P = { name: string; age: number }`, what is `P["name" | "age"]`?
quiz.explanation: Indexing with a union of keys distributes over them.

quiz.question: Why write `ReturnType<typeof f>` rather than `ReturnType<f>`?
options: `ReturnType` takes a type, and `f` is a value — `typeof` lifts it
quiz.explanation: Values and types live in different namespaces; `typeof` bridges from value to type.

quiz.question: When is `Object.keys(o) as (keyof typeof o)[]` safe?
options: When you built `o` yourself and know it carries no extra keys
quiz.explanation: The cast asserts there are no extra keys — true for a literal you control, not for data from outside.

quiz.question: What does `keyof` produce for a type with a `[key: string]: V` index signature?
quiz.explanation: Numeric keys are converted to strings, so they're allowed too.

quiz.question: What is `keyof any`?
quiz.explanation: Every possible key type — also spelled `PropertyKey`.

quiz.question: What is `keyof unknown`?
quiz.explanation: Nothing is known to be a key of an unknown value.

quiz.question: What is `[1, 2]["length"]` as a type?
quiz.explanation: A tuple's length is a literal type.

quiz.question: What is `string[]["length"]`?
quiz.explanation: An array's length isn't known statically.

quiz.question: What is `Record<string, number>[string]`?
quiz.explanation: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` affects reading values in code, not the type expression `T[string]`.

quiz.question: Does `keyof { a?: 1 }` include `a`?
options: Yes — optional keys are still keys
quiz.explanation: `keyof` lists declared properties whether or not they're optional.

quiz.question: How do you get the type of every value in an object type `T`?
quiz.explanation: There's no `valueof`; index by all the keys at once.

quiz.question: What is `typeof` of a function value in a type position?
options: Its full function type, with parameters and return
quiz.explanation: Type-position `typeof` gives a type; the runtime operator gives a string.

quiz.question: With `const T = ["a", "b"] as const`, what is `(typeof T)[0]`?
quiz.explanation: A readonly tuple has a type per position.

quiz.question: What does `(typeof CONFIG)["db"]["port"]` read?
options: An error — only one level is allowed
quiz.explanation: Indexed accesses chain.

quiz.question: What is `PropertyKey`?
quiz.explanation: The built-in alias for any valid key.

quiz.question: How do you test whether `"id"` is a key of `T` at the type level?
quiz.explanation: Type-level membership is assignability to the key union.

quiz.question: What does `keyof` a class instance type include?
quiz.explanation: `#private` and `private` members aren't in `keyof`.

quiz.question: For a function parameter typed `key: keyof T`, what may a caller pass?
options: Only the literal names of `T`'s keys (or a variable of that union)
quiz.explanation: Typos become compile errors.

quiz.question: Why is `get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]` better than `(obj: T, key: keyof T): T[keyof T]`?
options: The return type follows the specific key instead of being the union of all value types
quiz.explanation: A separate `K` remembers which key was passed.

quiz.question: What is `Parameters<typeof Math.max>`?
quiz.explanation: `Math.max` takes a rest parameter of numbers.

quiz.question: Why does deriving `type Size = (typeof SIZES)[number]` beat writing the union by hand?
options: Adding a size to the array updates the type automatically
quiz.explanation: One source of truth.

quiz.question: What does `keyof` a tuple type include besides its indexes?
quiz.explanation: Tuples are arrays; use `T[number]` for the elements.

quiz.question: `const levels = ["a", "b"];` — with no `as const` — what is `(typeof levels)[number]`?
quiz.explanation: Without `as const` the array widens to `string[]`, so indexing it by number yields `string` — the literal information is gone before the type-level trick can use it.

quiz.question: How does the type-position `typeof` differ from the runtime `typeof` operator?
options: The type-position one lifts a value into a type; the runtime one returns a string at execution time
They are the same operator used in two places
The type-position one only works on classes
The runtime one is removed by the compiler
quiz.explanation: They share a keyword and nothing else. `type S = typeof settings` computes a type; `typeof x === \"string\"` is a runtime check that happens to also narrow.

quiz.question: `type U = { tags: string[] }`. What is `U["tags"][number]`?
quiz.explanation: `U["tags"]` is `string[]`; indexing an array type by `number` gives its element type.

quiz.question: `const S = ["a", "b"] as const; type T = (typeof S)[number];` — `T` is?
quiz.explanation: `as const` keeps the literals; `[number]` unions the tuple's elements.

quiz.question: What does `User["id" | "email"]` give?
options: The union of both properties' types
An error — keys must be single
quiz.explanation: Indexing with a union key distributes over it.

quiz.question: Why does `Object.keys(obj)` return `string[]` and not `(keyof T)[]`?
options: At runtime an object can have more keys than its type lists
quiz.explanation: Structural typing admits objects with extra properties, so `keyof T` would be a lie.

quiz.question: What is `keyof { [k: string]: number }`?
quiz.explanation: Numeric keys are allowed on a string index signature (they become strings at runtime).

quiz.question: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K)` — what should it return?
quiz.explanation: The indexed access type follows the specific key passed in.

types.title: Part 1 — a two-level lookup type
types.prompt: Write `Get<T, A, B>`: the type of `obj[a][b]` for `obj: T`. `A` must be a key of `T`, and `B` a key of `T[A]` — so a key from the wrong section is rejected.
types.hint: Each type parameter is constrained by the one before it.
hints: Each type parameter is constrained by the one before it.
`A extends keyof T`, `B extends keyof T[A]`, and the result is the indexed access `T[A][B]`.
types.solution: type Get<T, A extends keyof T, B extends keyof T[A]> = T[A][B];

flashcards.front: What does `keyof T` produce?
flashcards.back: The union of `T`'s property names: `keyof { a: 1; b: 2 }` is `"a" | "b"`.

flashcards.front: What is an indexed access type?
flashcards.back: `T[K]` — the type of property `K` on `T`. `Person["age"]` is `number`.

flashcards.front: How do you get the element type of an array type?
flashcards.back: `T[number]` — `string[][number]` is `string`.

flashcards.front: Type-position `typeof` vs runtime `typeof`?
flashcards.back: In a type (`typeof defaults`) it takes a variable's static type; in an expression it returns a runtime string like `"number"`.

flashcards.front: How do you derive a key union from an object value?
flashcards.back: `keyof typeof settings`.

flashcards.front: How do you get the union of an object's value types?
flashcards.back: `T[keyof T]`.

flashcards.front: `keyof` an object with a string index signature?
flashcards.back: `string | number` — number keys are allowed too, because JavaScript turns them into strings.

flashcards.front: What is `PropertyKey`?
flashcards.back: `string | number | symbol` — everything that can be an object key.

flashcards.front: How is `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, k: K): T[K]` better than returning `any`?
flashcards.back: The return type follows the key: `get(user, "age")` is a `number`, `get(user, "name")` a `string`.

flashcards.front: Why is `Object.keys(obj) as (keyof T)[]` a white lie?
flashcards.back: At runtime the object may have extra keys; the cast is fine only when you control how the object was built.

flashcards.front: `keyof {}`?
flashcards.back: `never` — an empty object type has no known keys.

flashcards.front: TS7053 — cause?
flashcards.back: Indexing an object with a `string` its type doesn't declare an index signature for: "Element implicitly has an 'any' type…".

flashcards.front: `User["role"]`?
flashcards.back: An indexed access type: the type of `User`'s `role` property.

flashcards.front: Element type of `string[][]`'s inner arrays?
flashcards.back: `string[][][number][number]` — or just `string`; `[number]` reads an array's element type.

flashcards.front: `(typeof X)[number]` for `const X = ["a", "b"] as const`?
flashcards.back: `"a" | "b"` — a union from a constant list.

flashcards.front: `User["id" | "email"]`?
flashcards.back: The union of both properties' types — a union key gives a union.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't `Object.keys` return `(keyof T)[]`?
flashcards.back: Objects can have more keys at runtime than their type lists; `string[]` is the honest type.

flashcards.front: The typed property read, as a signature?
flashcards.back: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`.

weeks.title: Mapped Types
weeks.goal: Transform every property of a type at once — and build what the type describes.

problems.note: Applied: a projection over a frequency table.

weeks.project: Reimplement `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick` and `Omit` from scratch in a `utils.d.ts`, then check each against the built-in with a type-level test.

quiz.question: What does `{ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }` produce?
options: Every property made required — the built-in Required<T>
A union of T's property types
quiz.explanation: The `-` prefix strips a modifier the source had. `-readonly` does the same for readonly.

quiz.question: What is `keyof (A | B)`?
options: The keys A and B have in COMMON
quiz.explanation: Only shared keys are safe to access on a value that might be either — a frequent surprise when mapping over a union.

quiz.question: `{ [K in "a" | "b"]: K }`?
quiz.explanation: Each key maps to its own literal.

quiz.question: Which built-in is `{ readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }`?
quiz.explanation: It adds `readonly` to every property.

quiz.question: Which built-in is `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`?
quiz.explanation: It adds `?` to every property.

quiz.question: What does `{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null }` describe?
options: `T` with every field also allowed to be `null`
quiz.explanation: A mapped type can transform each value type.

quiz.question: What happens when a homomorphic mapped type is applied to an array type?
options: It produces an array (or tuple) type, mapping the elements
It maps the array's method names
It produces an object with numeric keys
quiz.explanation: Mapped types over `keyof T` treat arrays and tuples specially, so `Partial<[number, string]>` is `[number?, string?]`.

quiz.question: What does the `-?` modifier do?
quiz.explanation: `-?` is how `Required<T>` is built.

quiz.question: What does `[K in keyof T as K extends `` `_${string}` `` ? never : K]` do?
options: Drops every key starting with an underscore
Adds an underscore to every key
quiz.explanation: Remapping a key to `never` removes it.

quiz.question: Is `Record<K, V>` itself a mapped type?
options: No, it's built in to the compiler
quiz.explanation: Most utility types are ordinary mapped or conditional types you could write yourself.

quiz.question: Which modifiers does a homomorphic mapped type (over `keyof T`) keep from `T`?
quiz.explanation: That's why `Partial<Readonly<T>>` is still read-only.

quiz.question: `keyof (A & B)`?
quiz.explanation: An intersection has every key of both. (`keyof (A | B)` is the reverse: only the shared keys.)

quiz.question: What does `{ [K in keyof T]: () => T[K] }` produce for `T = { a: number }`?
quiz.explanation: Each value type is wrapped in a function type.

quiz.question: Why does `DeepReadonly` need recursion?
options: `Readonly` only covers the top level; nested objects need the same treatment
quiz.explanation: `{ readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }` walks every level.

quiz.question: What is `Partial<string>`?
quiz.explanation: Homomorphic mapped types pass primitives through.

quiz.question: What is `Readonly<string[]>`?
quiz.explanation: Mapped types over arrays and tuples produce arrays and tuples.

quiz.question: What is `{ [K in string]: number }`?
quiz.explanation: Mapping over `string` itself gives a string index signature.

quiz.question: What is `Partial<A | B>`?
quiz.explanation: A homomorphic mapped type on a type parameter distributes over unions.

quiz.question: What does `-readonly` do?
quiz.explanation: `Mutable<T>` is `{ -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }`.

quiz.question: What is `{ -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }` for `T = readonly [1, 2]`?
quiz.explanation: Tuples stay tuples; the modifier is removed.

quiz.question: What is `+?` in a mapped type?
quiz.explanation: `+` is the explicit form; `-` removes.

quiz.question: How is `Pick<T, K>` written as a mapped type?
options: `{ [P in K]: T[P] }` with `K extends keyof T`
quiz.explanation: Mapping over the chosen keys only.

quiz.question: What does `{ [K in keyof T as Uppercase<string & K>]: T[K] }` make of `{ a: 1 }`?
quiz.explanation: Key remapping with an intrinsic string type.

quiz.question: How do you keep only the string-valued properties of `T`?
options: `{ [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K] }`
quiz.explanation: Filter keys by their value type in the `as` clause.

quiz.question: What does `{ [K in keyof T]: T[K][] }` produce?
options: Each property becomes an array of its type
quiz.explanation: Mapped types can transform every value type.

quiz.question: Do mapped types keep an index signature of `T`?
quiz.explanation: `Partial<Record<string, number>>` is `{ [x: string]: number | undefined }`-like.

quiz.question: Why does `DeepPartial` need a special case for arrays?
options: Otherwise arrays become objects with optional numeric keys and methods
quiz.explanation: Recurse into the element type instead.

quiz.question: What makes a mapped type "homomorphic"?
options: It maps over `keyof T` for some `T`, preserving `T`'s structure and modifiers
It maps over a union of literals
quiz.explanation: Homomorphic mapped types keep `?`, `readonly`, arrays and tuples.

quiz.question: What is `Record<"a" | "b", number>` written as a mapped type?
quiz.explanation: `Record<K, V> = { [P in K]: V }`.

quiz.question: What does `Required<Partial<T>>` give back?
quiz.explanation: `-?` undoes `?`.

quiz.question: Can a mapped type add keys that weren't in `T`?
options: Only by renaming them with `as` (or intersecting with another type)
quiz.explanation: The output keys come from the keys you map over.

quiz.question: What is the result of a mapped type whose every key maps to `never` via `as`?
quiz.explanation: No keys survive.

quiz.question: In a mapped type's `as` clause, what happens to a key you map to `never`?
options: The property is removed from the result — this is how Omit works
quiz.explanation: Key remapping to `never` drops the entry entirely, which is exactly the mechanism behind filtering utilities like `Omit`.

quiz.question: You define `type Getters<T>` that renames keys to `getName`, `getAge`. What exists at runtime?
options: Nothing — you must still build the object yourself; the type only describes it
An object with those methods, generated by the compiler
A proxy that forwards property access
The original object with extra prototype methods
quiz.explanation: Mapped types are erased like every other type. They describe the shape your runtime code is obliged to produce, usually ending in a cast where the loop finishes.

quiz.question: What does `as` do in `{ [K in keyof T as NewKey]: … }`?
options: Chooses a new key for each property
quiz.explanation: The `as` clause computes the output key from the input key `K`.

quiz.question: How do you remove a key in a mapped type?
options: Map it to `never` in the `as` clause
quiz.explanation: A key of `never` produces no property. (A value of `never` would keep the key, with an unusable type.)

quiz.question: Why write `Capitalize<string & K>` instead of `Capitalize<K>`?
options: `keyof T` can include `number` and `symbol`, and `Capitalize` only accepts strings
quiz.explanation: The intersection keeps only string keys.

quiz.question: What is `` `get${Capitalize<"first_name">}` ``?
quiz.explanation: `Capitalize` upper-cases only the first character.

quiz.question: Does `{ [K in keyof T as …]: T[K] }` keep `?` and `readonly` modifiers?
options: Yes — it's still homomorphic over `keyof T`
quiz.explanation: Add `-?` or `-readonly` to remove them explicitly.

quiz.question: A value is assigned to a remapped type that omits `password`. Is the password gone?
options: No — types are erased; the object is unchanged
quiz.explanation: Remove keys at runtime (rest destructuring), then type the result.

exam.title: Build what the mapped type describes
exam.prompt: `Getters<T>` renames each key to `getX` returning that property's type. The input is a name. Build the getters object at runtime for `{ name, size: 5 }`, then print `getName()`, `getSize()`, and the getter keys sorted and comma-joined.
exam.hint: The mapped type is erased — the loop has to produce the renamed keys itself, and the cast at the end is where you assert it matched.

types.title: Part 1 — a validator for every field
types.prompt: Write `Validators<T>`: for every property of `T` — optional ones included — a type guard `(value: unknown) => value is …` for that property's type. An optional property's guard accepts `undefined` too, and every validator is required.
types.hint: A homomorphic mapped type over `keyof T` keeps `readonly` — and `?`, unless you remove it.
hints: A homomorphic mapped type over `keyof T` keeps `readonly` — and `?`, unless you remove it.
`-?` removes the optionality; `T[K]` of an optional property already includes `undefined`.
types.solution: type Validators<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: (value: unknown) => value is T[K] };

flashcards.front: What is a mapped type?
flashcards.back: A type built by looping over keys: `{ [K in keyof T]: … }`.

flashcards.front: How would you write `Partial<T>` yourself?
flashcards.back: `type MyPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`.

flashcards.front: How do you remove `readonly` or `?` in a mapped type?
flashcards.back: With a minus modifier: `{ -readonly [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }`.

flashcards.front: What is key remapping?
flashcards.back: An `as` clause renaming keys: `` { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] } ``.

flashcards.front: How do you filter keys out in a mapped type?
flashcards.back: Remap the unwanted ones to `never`: `[K in keyof T as T[K] extends Function ? never : K]`.

flashcards.front: What is a homomorphic mapped type?
flashcards.back: One that maps over `keyof T` directly; it preserves `T`'s `readonly` and `?` modifiers.

flashcards.front: How would you write `Pick<T, K>` yourself?
flashcards.back: `type MyPick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] }`.

flashcards.front: How would you write `Record<K, V>` yourself?
flashcards.back: `type MyRecord<K extends PropertyKey, V> = { [P in K]: V }`.

flashcards.front: Why does `Readonly<T>` not protect nested objects?
flashcards.back: It maps one level only. A `DeepReadonly` recurses: `{ readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }`.

flashcards.front: Why does `string & K` appear inside `Capitalize<…>` in a remap?
flashcards.back: `keyof T` may include `number` and `symbol`; `Capitalize` accepts only strings, so intersecting keeps the string keys.

flashcards.front: Do mapped types exist at runtime?
flashcards.back: No. If you need the object they describe, you build it yourself — the type only checks that you did.

flashcards.front: What does `{ [K in "a" | "b"]: number }` produce?
flashcards.back: `{ a: number; b: number }`.

flashcards.front: What does the `as` clause in a mapped type do?
flashcards.back: Computes each output key from the input key `K` — renaming, or filtering with `never`.

flashcards.front: How do you drop a key in a mapped type?
flashcards.back: Map it to `never` in the `as` clause: `[K in keyof T as Test<K> extends true ? never : K]`.

flashcards.front: `Capitalize<string & K>` — why the `string &`?
flashcards.back: `keyof T` may include number and symbol keys; `Capitalize` only accepts strings.

flashcards.front: What is `` `get${Capitalize<"first_name">}` ``?
flashcards.back: `"getFirst_name"` — only the first letter changes.

flashcards.front: Do `readonly` and `?` survive `{ [K in keyof T as …]: T[K] }`?
flashcards.back: Yes — mapping over `keyof T` keeps the modifiers; `-readonly` / `-?` remove them.

flashcards.front: A remapped type omits `password`; is it gone from the object?
flashcards.back: No — types are erased; remove it at runtime (rest destructuring) and then type the result.

project_spec.title: store.ts — a typed store with watchers and undo
project_spec.goal: A small state container: `createStore<T>(initial)` returns typed `get`/`set` keyed by `keyof T`, per-key watchers, snapshots and undo. Mapped types describe the watcher table and the change events, so a watcher for `count` receives numbers and nothing else.
requirements: State is `{ count: number; user: string; dark: boolean }`, starting `{ count: 0, user: "guest", dark: false }`.

Commands: `get <key>` prints `<key> = <value>`; `set <key> <text>` converts by the key's current type (a bad number/boolean prints `bad value for <key>`); `inc <key> [n]` adds n (default 1) to a number (`<key> is not a number` otherwise); `toggle <key>` flips a boolean (`<key> is not a boolean`); unknown keys print `unknown key <k>`.
`watch <key>` / `unwatch <key>`: while watched, every change to the key prints `<key>: <old> -> <new>` (a set to the same value is not a change and prints nothing).
`undo` restores the state before the last change (and notifies watchers), or prints `nothing to undo`; `snapshot` prints the state as JSON.
Type the watcher table as a mapped type `{ [K in keyof T]?: (from: T[K], to: T[K]) => void }` and `set` as `<K extends keyof T>(key: K, value: T[K])`.
stretch: Add `select<K extends keyof T>(...keys: K[]): Pick<T, K>`.
Generate `setCount`/`setUser`/`setDark` methods with the week's key remapping.
rubric: No `any` anywhere — not even one hidden in a cast
Every function has a typed signature; locals are left to inference
Bad input is handled on purpose, not by accident
Names say what things are, not how they are stored
I could explain every line to someone else

weeks.title: Conditional Types & infer
weeks.goal: Branch on types and pattern-match their structure.

problems.note: Applied: `k[...]` nests arbitrarily deep — unwrap the inner layer before the outer one, as `infer` does.

weeks.project: Write a `types.ts` implementing `ReturnType`, `Parameters`, `Awaited` and `Exclude` yourself, with a comment on each explaining where `infer` binds.

quiz.question: `type NonNil<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T`. What is `NonNil<string | null>`?
quiz.explanation: T is naked, so the conditional distributes: `string` takes the else branch, `null` becomes `never`, and `never` vanishes from a union.

quiz.question: What is `IsString<any>` for `type IsString<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no"`?
quiz.explanation: `any` is assignable to everything and nothing simultaneously, so a conditional over it resolves to the union of both branches.

quiz.question: `type IsArr<T> = T extends unknown[] ? true : false;` — what is `IsArr<string[]>`?
quiz.explanation: `string[]` is assignable to `unknown[]`.

quiz.question: `type IsArr<T> = T extends unknown[] ? true : false;` — what is `IsArr<string[] | number>`?
quiz.explanation: A naked type parameter distributes over the union, checking each member separately.

quiz.question: `type Elem<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : never;` — what is `Elem<number[]>`?
quiz.explanation: `infer E` captures the element type.

quiz.question: `type Elem<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : never;` — what is `Elem<string>`?
quiz.explanation: `string` isn't an array, so the false branch runs.

quiz.question: `type First<T> = T extends [infer F, ...unknown[]] ? F : never;` — `First<[1, 2]>`?
quiz.explanation: `F` captures the first element of the tuple.

quiz.question: `type First<T> = T extends [infer F, ...unknown[]] ? F : never;` — what is `First<[]>`?
quiz.explanation: An empty tuple doesn't match `[infer F, ...unknown[]]`.

quiz.question: `type Args<T> = T extends (...a: infer A) => unknown ? A : never;` — `Args<(x: string) => void>`?
quiz.explanation: Rest-parameter position infers a tuple — this is how `Parameters` works.

quiz.question: `Exclude<string | number | boolean, number>`?
quiz.explanation: Members assignable to `number` are removed.

quiz.question: `[never] extends [never] ? 1 : 2`?
quiz.explanation: Wrapped in a tuple there's no distribution, and `[never]` is assignable to itself.

quiz.question: `type T = any extends string ? 1 : 2`?
quiz.explanation: `any` as the checked type takes both branches.

quiz.question: Where may `infer` appear?
options: Only in the `extends` clause of a conditional type
quiz.explanation: It declares a variable for the pattern being matched.

quiz.question: `type Unbox<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? Unbox<V> : T;` — `Unbox<Promise<Promise<1>>>`?
quiz.explanation: The recursion peels one promise per step until none are left.

quiz.question: What is `boolean extends true ? 1 : 2`?
quiz.explanation: No type parameter, so no distribution: `boolean` as a whole isn't assignable to `true`.

quiz.question: For `type D<T> = T extends true ? 1 : 2`, what is `D<boolean>`?
quiz.explanation: `boolean` is `true | false`, and a type parameter distributes.

quiz.question: What is `never extends string ? 1 : 2` (written directly, not through a type parameter)?
quiz.explanation: `never` is assignable to everything; only a *type parameter* given `never` returns `never`.

quiz.question: With `type I<T> = T extends { a: infer U; b: infer U } ? U : never`, what is `I<{ a: string; b: number }>`?
quiz.explanation: Several candidates for one `infer` in covariant positions are unioned.

quiz.question: And when the same `infer U` appears in two *parameter* positions?
quiz.explanation: Contravariant positions combine with `&` — the trick behind `UnionToIntersection`.

quiz.question: What is `NonNullable<string | null>`?
quiz.explanation: Defined today as `T & {}`.

quiz.question: What is `Extract<string | number, number | boolean>`?
quiz.explanation: Members of the first union assignable to the second.

quiz.question: What is `ReturnType<() => void>`?
quiz.explanation: It reads the declared return type.

quiz.question: How do you detect `any` at the type level?
quiz.explanation: Only `any` makes `1 & T` accept `0`.

quiz.question: When is a conditional type on a type parameter *deferred*?
options: While the parameter is still generic — it's resolved when `T` is known
quiz.explanation: Inside a generic function body, `T extends string ? … : …` stays unresolved.

quiz.question: Why does an implementation returning a conditional type usually need a cast?
options: The compiler can't resolve the conditional for a generic `T` inside the body
quiz.explanation: Overloads are the common alternative.

quiz.question: What is `Awaited<string>`?
quiz.explanation: Non-promises pass through unchanged.

quiz.question: With `T = string | number`, is `[T] extends [string]` true?
quiz.explanation: Wrapped in a tuple, the union is checked as a whole.

quiz.question: What is `Exclude<"a" | "b", string>`?
quiz.explanation: Both members are strings, so both are excluded.

quiz.question: Where does `infer` get its candidate in `T extends (x: infer P) => void ? P : never`?
quiz.explanation: `infer` can sit anywhere a type can in the pattern.

quiz.question: Why write `T extends unknown ? … : never` deliberately?
options: To force distribution over a union `T`
quiz.explanation: It maps a transformation over each member.

quiz.question: What does `T extends readonly unknown[]` accept that `T extends unknown[]` doesn't?
quiz.explanation: Match `readonly` so `as const` values work too.

quiz.question: What is `Parameters<(x: string, y?: number) => void>`?
quiz.explanation: Optional parameters stay optional in the tuple.

quiz.question: What does `infer` do inside a conditional type?
options: Binds a fresh type variable to whatever type matched at that position
Forces TypeScript to re-infer the whole expression
Declares a default for the type parameter
Converts a value into a type
quiz.explanation: `T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T` matches T against 'array of something' and names that something `U` — pattern matching on the type's structure.

quiz.question: How do you stop a conditional type from distributing over a union?
options: Wrap both sides in a tuple: [T] extends [U] ? X : Y
Use an interface instead of a type alias
quiz.explanation: Distribution requires a bare type parameter on the left. Putting it inside a tuple makes it non-naked, so the check runs once against the whole union.

quiz.question: `type F<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never`. What is `F<string | number>`?
quiz.explanation: A naked type parameter distributes over the union.

quiz.question: How do you stop a conditional type from distributing?
options: Wrap both sides in a tuple: `[T] extends [U]`
quiz.explanation: `[T]` isn't a naked type parameter, so the union is checked as a whole.

quiz.question: A distributive conditional type is given `never`. The result is?
quiz.explanation: `never` is the empty union: zero members, zero results.

quiz.question: How is `IsNever<T>` written?
quiz.explanation: The distributive version would return `never` for `never`.

quiz.question: What does `infer U extends string` do?
options: Captures `U` only if it is a `string`, and types it as one in the true branch
quiz.explanation: The constraint is part of the match (TS 4.7+).

quiz.question: Why is `Exclude<"a" | "b", "a">` equal to `"b"`?
options: Each member is tested; `"a"` becomes `never` and vanishes from the union
String literals are compared by length
It's a special case in the compiler
quiz.explanation: `type Exclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T` — distribution does the work.

exam.title: Unwrap and compact
exam.prompt: Write `Unwrap<T>` (element type of an array, else T) and `NonNil<T>` (drops null/undefined from a union). The input is a line of tokens where `-` means null. Print the first non-null token or `(none)`, then the compacted tokens space-separated or `(none)`, then how many were dropped.
exam.hint: Both types are erased, so each function ends in a cast — the type describes what the runtime branch is obliged to produce.

types.title: Part 1 — resolve a function or a promise
types.prompt: Write `Resolved<T>`: if `T` is a function, its return type; otherwise if it is a `Promise`, the value it resolves to (one level); otherwise `T` itself. It must distribute over unions.
types.hint: Two conditional types, the second in the false branch of the first.
hints: Two conditional types, the second in the false branch of the first.
`T extends (...args: never[]) => infer R ? R : T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T` — a naked `T` distributes.
types.solution: type Resolved<T> = T extends (...args: never[]) => infer R ? R : T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T;

flashcards.front: What is a conditional type?
flashcards.back: `T extends U ? X : Y` — a type-level if/else that picks `X` when `T` is assignable to `U`.

flashcards.front: What does `infer` do?
flashcards.back: Declares a type variable to be captured by the match: `T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T` extracts the promise's value type.

flashcards.front: How would you write `ReturnType` yourself?
flashcards.back: `type MyReturn<F> = F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never`.

flashcards.front: What is a distributive conditional type?
flashcards.back: When the checked type is a naked type parameter, a union input is split and each member is checked separately: `Exclude` works this way.

flashcards.front: How do you stop distribution?
flashcards.back: Wrap both sides in tuples: `[T] extends [U] ? X : Y`.

flashcards.front: What does a distributive conditional return for `never`?
flashcards.back: `never` — an empty union distributes over zero members.

flashcards.front: How would you write `Exclude<T, U>` yourself?
flashcards.back: `type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T`.

flashcards.front: How do you get the element type of an array, or `T` itself if it isn't one?
flashcards.back: `type Unwrap<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : T`.

flashcards.front: What does `infer U extends string` add (TS 4.7)?
flashcards.back: A constraint on the inferred type: the branch matches only if what `U` captures is a `string`.

flashcards.front: Why does a function returning a conditional type usually need a cast inside?
flashcards.back: The compiler can't evaluate the conditional for an unresolved generic `T`, so it can't check your return value against it.

flashcards.front: How do you test whether `T` is `never`?
flashcards.back: `[T] extends [never] ? true : false` — the bare `T extends never` distributes and returns `never`.

flashcards.front: How would you write `Awaited` for one level?
flashcards.back: `type Unpromise<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T`.

flashcards.front: `T extends unknown ? T[] : never` given `string | number`?
flashcards.back: `string[] | number[]` — a naked type parameter distributes over the union.

flashcards.front: What switches distribution off in `T extends U ? X : Y`?
flashcards.back: Wrapping both sides in a tuple: `[T] extends [U] ? … : …`.

flashcards.front: A distributive conditional type given `never`?
flashcards.back: `never` — the empty union has no members to map.

flashcards.front: How is `IsNever<T>` written?
flashcards.back: `[T] extends [never] ? true : false`.

flashcards.front: `infer U extends string` — what's different from `infer U`?
flashcards.back: The branch only matches if the captured type is a `string`, and `U` is known to be one.

flashcards.front: `ReturnType` of an overloaded function?
flashcards.back: The last overload's return type — `infer` sees only the last signature.

practice.title: Exclude, by hand
practice.prompt: Implement `MyExclude<T, U>`: the members of union `T` not assignable to `U`.

Return `never` for the members you want gone.
practice.starter: type MyExclude<T, U> = ____;
practice.solution: type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;

`F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never`.
practice.starter: type MyReturnType<F> = ____;
practice.solution: type MyReturnType<F> = F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;

hints: Capture the rest-parameter position.
`(...args: infer P) => any`.

practice.title: Unwrap every promise

hints: Capture the promise's value with `infer`.
Then recurse on what you captured.
practice.starter: type Unpromise<T> = ____;
practice.solution: type Unpromise<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? Unpromise<V> : T;

practice.title: Element type, or the type itself

hints: Match against an array type and capture its element.
`(infer E)[]` — note the parentheses.

practice.solution: type Unwrap<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : T;

practice.title: The last element of a tuple
practice.prompt: Implement `Last<T>`: the type of a tuple's last element, `never` for an empty tuple.

hints: A variadic tuple pattern can put the rest *first*.
`[...unknown[], infer L]`.
practice.starter: type Last<T extends unknown[]> = ____;
practice.solution: type Last<T extends unknown[]> = T extends [...unknown[], infer L] ? L : never;

practice.title: Is it never?
practice.prompt: Implement `IsNever<T>`: `true` exactly when `T` is `never`.
practice.hint: `T extends never ? … : …` distributes over zero members and returns `never` itself.
hints: `T extends never ? … : …` distributes over zero members and returns `never` itself.
Wrap both sides in a one-element tuple to stop distribution.
practice.starter: type IsNever<T> = ____;
practice.solution: type IsNever<T> = [T] extends [never] ? true : false;

practice.title: The success type of a Result
practice.prompt: `Result` is a discriminated union. Implement `OkValue<R>`: the `value` type of its success member.
practice.hint: Distribution runs the condition once per member.

Match the success member's shape and `infer` its `value`.

type Result<T, E = string> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };
type OkValue<R> = ____;
practice.solution:
type Result<T, E = string> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };
type OkValue<R> = R extends { ok: true; value: infer V } ? V : never;

Fix the cause.

problem_set.title: Flatten to the bottom
problem_set.prompt: Write `flattenDeep<T>(xs: readonly T[]): FlattenDeep<T>[]` where `FlattenDeep<T> = T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? FlattenDeep<E> : T`. First print `sample <…>` — the flattened constant `[[1, [2, [3]]], [4]]`, typed `number[]` straight from the call. problem_set.title: A type-level `if`
problem_set.prompt: Write `If<C, T, F>`: `T` when the condition `C` is `true`, `F` when it's `false`.
problem_set.hint: A conditional type on `C`.
hints: A conditional type on `C`.
`boolean` is `true | false`, so it distributes to both branches.
problem_set.starter: type If<C extends boolean, T, F> = ____;
problem_set.solution: type If<C extends boolean, T, F> = C extends true ? T : F;

problem_set.title: The first parameter's type
problem_set.prompt: Write `FirstArg<F>`: the type of a function's first parameter, `never` for a function with no parameters, and `never` for anything that isn't a function.
problem_set.hint: Capture the whole parameter list with `infer P`, then take its first element with a second `infer`.
hints: Capture the whole parameter list with `infer P`, then take its first element with a second `infer`.
problem_set.starter: type FirstArg<F> = ____;
problem_set.solution: type FirstArg<F> = F extends (...args: infer P) => unknown ? (P extends [infer A, ...unknown[]] ? A : never) : never;

problem_set.title: FlattenDeep, as a type
problem_set.prompt: Write `FlattenDeep<T>`: the innermost element type of an array nested to any depth; non-arrays are left unchanged.
problem_set.hint: If it's an array of `E`, flatten `E`; otherwise stop.
hints: If it's an array of `E`, flatten `E`; otherwise stop.
Distribution handles the union case for you.
problem_set.starter: type FlattenDeep<T> = ____;
problem_set.solution: type FlattenDeep<T> = T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? FlattenDeep<E> : T;

problem_set.title: Is it a union?
problem_set.prompt: Write `IsUnion<T>`: `true` if `T` is a union of two or more members, else `false` (`never` is not a union).
problem_set.hint: Keep an undistributed copy of `T` in a second parameter with a default.
hints: Keep an undistributed copy of `T` in a second parameter with a default.
Inside a distributive branch, `T` is one member; if the full union isn't assignable to it, there was more than one.
problem_set.starter: type IsUnion<T, U = T> = ____;
problem_set.solution: type IsUnion<T, U = T> = [T] extends [never] ? false : T extends unknown ? ([U] extends [T] ? false : true) : never;

problem_set.title: Union to intersection
problem_set.prompt: Write `UnionToIntersection<U>`: `A | B` becomes `A & B`. (The trick: put each member in a function *parameter* position, then `infer` from the union of those functions.)
problem_set.hint: Distribute `U` into a union of functions `(x: A) => void | (x: B) => void`.
hints: Distribute `U` into a union of functions `(x: A) => void | (x: B) => void`.
Inferring a parameter type from a union of functions gives the intersection — parameters are contravariant.
problem_set.starter: type UnionToIntersection<U> = ____;
problem_set.solution: type UnionToIntersection<U> = (U extends unknown ? (x: U) => void : never) extends (x: infer I) => void ? I : never;

project_spec.title: commands.ts — a dispatcher typed from its handlers
project_spec.goal: Declare command handlers once; derive each command's argument types with `Parameters`, describe each argument's runtime kind with a mapped conditional type, and let the dispatcher parse text into correctly typed arguments before calling the handler.
requirements: Handlers: `add(a: number, b: number)` → the sum; `greet(name: string, times: number)` → `hello <name>` repeated `times` times, joined by `, ` (`(no greeting)` for none); `flip(flag: boolean)` → the negation; `upper(text: string)` → upper-cased; `between(x: number, lo: number, hi: number)` → `true` if lo ≤ x ≤ hi.

Each input line is `<command> <args…>`. Parse each argument by its declared kind — numbers must be finite, booleans `true`/`false` — and print the handler's result, or `<command> expects <n> arguments`, `argument <i> of <command> must be a <kind>` (1-based, the first bad one), or `unknown command <c>`.
`help` prints every command with its argument kinds, in declaration order, like `add(number, number)`.

Derive `ArgsOf<N> = Parameters<Handlers[N]>` and a signature table typed with a mapped conditional type (`number` → `"number"`, …) so a handler whose parameters change breaks the table at compile time.
Only one cast is allowed: the final call of a handler with its parsed argument list.
stretch: Add optional parameters (`greet(name, times = 1)`) and make the signature table say which arguments may be omitted.
Type `dispatch` so that a *call in code* like `dispatch("add", 1, "x")` is a compile error.
rubric: No `any` anywhere — not even one hidden in a cast
Every function has a typed signature; locals are left to inference
Bad input is handled on purpose, not by accident
Names say what things are, not how they are stored
I could explain every line to someone else

quiz.question: Where can `Capitalize<T>` be used?
options: Only inside template literal types — it is a compiler intrinsic
quiz.explanation: `Capitalize`, `Uppercase`, `Lowercase` and `Uncapitalize` live purely in the type system. Capitalizing a real string is still your own code.

quiz.question: Why is `type Bad = Bad | string` an error while `type Json = string | Json[]` is fine?
options: A recursive alias must go through an object, array or function
type aliases cannot be recursive at all
quiz.explanation: `Bad` refers to itself with nothing to defer into. Wrapping the recursion in `Json[]` gives the checker a structure to expand lazily.

quiz.question: What does `T extends readonly [unknown, ...infer Rest]` accomplish?
options: Peels the first tuple element and binds the rest, enabling recursion
Checks T is a readonly array
quiz.explanation: It is the type-level head/tail destructure — the shrinking step every recursive tuple algorithm needs.

quiz.question: Which string does `` `id-${number}` `` accept?
quiz.explanation: `${number}` matches anything that parses as a number, fractions included.

quiz.question: `Uppercase<"ab">`?
quiz.explanation: The intrinsic string types transform literal types.

quiz.question: `` type H<S> = S extends `${infer X}${infer R}` ? X : never; `` — what is `H<"abc">`?
quiz.explanation: An `infer` followed by another placeholder captures a single character.

quiz.question: `` type Trim<S> = S extends ` ${infer R}` ? Trim<R> : S; `` — `Trim<"  x">`?
quiz.explanation: Each recursive step removes one leading space.

quiz.question: What does `` `${string}` `` match?
quiz.explanation: It's equivalent to `string` on its own; it's useful as part of a larger pattern.

quiz.question: Which is a valid recursive type for a tree?
quiz.explanation: The recursion sits inside an object type, so it's deferred and well-founded.

quiz.question: `` `${Uppercase<"get">}_${"a" | "b"}` ``?
quiz.explanation: Only the first part is uppercased; the union distributes over the second.

quiz.question: `Capitalize<"hello world">`?
quiz.explanation: Only the very first character is changed.

quiz.question: What does `` "42" extends `${infer N extends number}` ? N : never `` give (TS 4.8+)?
quiz.explanation: An `infer … extends number` constraint in a template parses the matched text into a number literal.

quiz.question: Why is `type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [k: string]: Json }` allowed?
options: The self-references sit inside array and object types, so they're resolved lazily
Because it has a base case
quiz.explanation: A bare `type Bad = Bad | string` has nothing to defer and is rejected.

quiz.question: What is `` `${boolean}` ``?
quiz.explanation: A union placeholder produces one string per member.

quiz.question: What is `Uppercase<"a" | "b">`?
quiz.explanation: The intrinsic string types distribute over unions.

quiz.question: What is `Uncapitalize<"Hello">`?
quiz.explanation: Only the first character changes.

quiz.question: With `` type Sp<S> = S extends `${infer A},${infer B}` ? [A, B] : never ``, what is `Sp<"a,b,c">`?
quiz.explanation: The first `infer` takes the shortest match; the last takes the rest.

quiz.question: Is `"prefix-"` assignable to `` `prefix-${string}` ``?
options: Only if the suffix is a number
quiz.explanation: Pattern placeholders can be empty.

quiz.question: What is `` `${1 | 2}px` ``?
quiz.explanation: Numbers in unions are stringified per member.

quiz.question: How do you compute a tuple's length type?
quiz.explanation: For tuples it's a literal like `3`.

quiz.question: How do you append to a tuple type?
quiz.explanation: Variadic tuple types spread other tuples.

quiz.question: Why is type-level arithmetic with tuples "a toy"?
options: It builds tuples of that length, so it's limited to small numbers and is slow
quiz.explanation: Fine for lengths of a few hundred; not for real numbers.

quiz.question: What does `--generateTrace` help with?
options: Finding which types make type checking slow
quiz.explanation: Load the output in a trace viewer.

quiz.question: What's a sign a recursive type should be simplified?
options: It hits TS2589, makes the editor lag, or nobody can read it
It has more than one parameter
quiz.explanation: Complexity has a cost at every call site.

quiz.question: What does `` S extends `${infer H}${infer R}` ? H : never `` give for `S = ""`?
options: `never` — an empty string has no first character
quiz.explanation: Each `infer` without a delimiter matches at least one character.

quiz.question: How do you recurse over each character of a string type?
quiz.explanation: Peel one character per step.

quiz.question: Can an interface refer to itself?
quiz.explanation: Self-reference through properties is fine for both.

quiz.question: Why does `` `${Entity}:${Action}` `` beat a hand-written list of event names?
options: It stays in step with the two unions and can't miss a combination
quiz.explanation: Derive, don't duplicate.

quiz.question: What is `Lowercase<string>` useful for?
options: Describing "any lower-case string" as a pattern type
quiz.explanation: Intrinsic types work on non-literal strings too, as patterns.

quiz.question: What limit applies to the number of members in a union?
quiz.explanation: Template literals over several unions reach it quickly.

quiz.question: What does `Capitalize<"hello world">` return?
quiz.explanation: One character, not one per word.

quiz.question: How many members does `` type T = `${"a" | "b"}-${"x" | "y" | "z"}` `` have?
quiz.explanation: Interpolating unions produces the cross product — 2 × 3 = 6 literal types. This growth is also why deeply nested templates can blow the compiler's limits.

quiz.question: Why does `function toSize(v: number, u: Unit): Size { return `${v}${u}` as Size; }` need the cast?
options: A template built from a runtime `number` widens to `string`, which the compiler cannot prove matches the pattern
Casts are always required when returning template literals
Unit is a union, and unions cannot be interpolated
quiz.explanation: Type-level interpolation over `${number}` works on literal types. A runtime value produces an ordinary `string`, so you assert the invariant your code maintains.

quiz.question: In `type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends object ? DeepReadonly<T[K]> : T[K] }`, what is the base case?
options: A property whose type is not an object, which stops the recursion
quiz.explanation: The conditional decides at each property whether to recurse. Primitives take the else branch and terminate that path.

quiz.question: What does TS2589 mean?
options: Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite
A union has too many members
A type is used before it is declared
A generic has too many parameters
quiz.explanation: Usually a non-tail-recursive type, or genuinely infinite recursion.

quiz.question: Which recursive type can go deepest?
options: One whose recursive call is the whole branch, with the result carried in an accumulator
One wrapped in a tuple spread
quiz.explanation: Tail-recursive conditional types are evaluated iteratively, up to 1,000 steps.

quiz.question: A template literal of six 10-member unions is…
options: A million members — TS2590, too complex to represent
quiz.explanation: Unions in template literals multiply. Use a pattern like `` `${number}` ``.

quiz.question: `Split<string>` with no special case returns `[string]`. Why is that wrong?
options: A plain `string` has nothing to parse; the honest answer is `string[]`
quiz.explanation: Check `string extends S` first.

quiz.question: Which is cheaper for the checker?
options: `type C = A & B & …` with many parts
quiz.explanation: Interfaces are cached by name; large intersections are recomputed.

quiz.question: When is complex type-level code worth it?
options: When it catches real mistakes at many call sites of a widely used API
quiz.explanation: Otherwise a plain type and a runtime check are cheaper to read and to check.
