types.title: Part 1 — join a tuple of strings
types.prompt: Write `Join<T, S>`: the string literal made by joining the tuple of string literals `T` with the separator `S`. An empty tuple joins to `""`.
types.hint: Take the tuple apart with `[infer H, ...infer R]` and recurse on the rest.
hints: Take the tuple apart with `[infer H, ...infer R]` and recurse on the rest.
One element left means no separator after it; an empty tuple gives `""`.
types.starter:
type Join<T extends string[], S extends string> =
  ____;
types.solution:
type Join<T extends string[], S extends string> =
  T extends [infer H extends string, ...infer R extends string[]]
    ? R extends [] ? H : `${H}${S}${Join<R, S>}`
    : "";

flashcards.front: What is a template literal type?
flashcards.back: A string type built from other types: `` `${Entity}:${Action}` `` — every combination of the two unions.

flashcards.front: How many members does `` `${"a" | "b"}-${"x" | "y" | "z"}` `` have?
flashcards.back: Six — template literals take the cartesian product of the unions.

flashcards.front: Name the four intrinsic string types.
flashcards.back: `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`, `Uncapitalize`.

flashcards.front: How do you parse a string type?
flashcards.back: Match it with `infer` in a template: `` S extends `${infer Head}/${infer Rest}` ? … : … ``.

flashcards.front: How do you extract `"id"` from the route `"/users/:id"` at the type level?
flashcards.back: Recursively match `` `${string}:${infer P}/${infer Rest}` `` (and a final `` `${string}:${infer P}` ``), collecting each `P` into a union.

flashcards.front: What is a recursive type?
flashcards.back: One that refers to itself: `type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [k: string]: Json }`.

flashcards.front: What is TS2589?
flashcards.back: "Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite" — a recursive type went past the compiler's depth limit.

flashcards.front: How do you reverse a tuple type?
flashcards.back: `type Reverse<T extends unknown[]> = T extends [infer H, ...infer R] ? [...Reverse<R>, H] : []`.

flashcards.front: How do you get a tuple's length as a type?
flashcards.back: `T["length"]` — for `[1, 2, 3]` it is the literal `3`.

flashcards.front: What happens when you recurse on plain `string` instead of a literal?
flashcards.back: It never matches a specific pattern, so the result collapses to a wide type (usually `string` or `never`).

flashcards.front: What is `Paths<T>` used for?
flashcards.back: Typing dotted paths into an object (`"a.b.c"`) so a `get(obj, path)` helper rejects paths that don't exist.

flashcards.front: Why keep type-level programs small?
flashcards.back: They slow the compiler, error messages grow unreadable, and depth limits bite. Reach for them where they remove real bugs.

flashcards.front: What does TS2589 mean?
flashcards.back: Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite — usually recursion that isn't a tail call.

flashcards.front: How do you let a recursive type go deeper?
flashcards.back: Make it tail-recursive: carry the result in an accumulator so the recursive call is the whole branch (up to 1,000 steps).

flashcards.front: What is TS2590?
flashcards.back: A union too complex to represent (over 100,000 members) — often a template literal of several unions.

flashcards.front: Why check `string extends S` in a string-parsing type?
flashcards.back: A plain `string` has nothing to parse; return the general type (`string[]`) instead of a wrong tuple.

flashcards.front: Cheaper for the checker: interface extends or a big intersection?
flashcards.back: `interface … extends` — named interfaces are cached; intersections are recomputed.

flashcards.front: When is advanced type-level code worth it?
flashcards.back: When it catches real mistakes at many call sites of a widely used API; otherwise prefer a simple type and a runtime check.

project_spec.title: events.ts — a typed event catalogue (arc: typed-kit)
project_spec.goal: The Month 5 arc project: an event bus whose event names come from a catalogue, whose payloads are checked per event at runtime, and whose subscriptions support one-shot handlers and `entity:*` wildcards. Event names are a template literal type built from the catalogue.
requirements: The catalogue: `user:created { name: string }`, `user:deleted { id: number }`, `order:placed { id: number; total: number }`, `order:shipped { id: number }`. Event names are typed as `` `${Entity}:${Action}` `` restricted to these four.

Commands: `on `, `once ` (removed after its first delivery), `off `, `emit `. A pattern is an event name or `:*`; anything else prints `bad pattern

`.

`emit` checks the event name (`unknown event <e>`), parses the JSON and validates it against that event's payload shape (`bad payload for <event>`), then prints one line per delivery in subscription order: `<sub> got <event> <summary>` where the summary is `name=<n>`, `id=<i>` or `id=<i> total=<t>`; with no deliveries, `<event> unheard`.
`stats` prints each event name in catalogue order with how many times it was emitted successfully: `<event>: <n>`.
Payload validators are declared per event in a mapped type `{ [E in EventName]: (v: unknown) => v is Payloads[E] }`.
stretch: Make `emit` type-safe in code: `emit("order:placed", { id: 1 })` should fail to compile for the missing `total`.
Collect the Month 5 helpers — `groupBy`, `Paths`, `DeepReadonly`, `RouteParams`, this emitter — into one `typed-kit` file with type tests.
rubric: No `any` anywhere — not even one hidden in a cast
Every function has a typed signature; locals are left to inference
Bad input is handled on purpose, not by accident
Names say what things are, not how they are stored
I could explain every line to someone else

weeks.title: Classes & Encapsulation
weeks.goal: Use classes where they pay — real privacy, invariants and accessors.

problems.note: Two structures kept in step behind one interface.

weeks.project: Write an `account.ts` with a `BankAccount` class whose balance is `#private`, exposing `deposit`, `withdraw` (rejecting overdrafts) and a computed `balance` getter.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `#count` and `private count`?
options: `#` is enforced by the JavaScript engine; `private` is erased at compile time
`#` cannot be used in generic classes
quiz.explanation: A `private` field is visible to any JavaScript that ignores the types. A `#` field is genuinely inaccessible from outside the class.

quiz.question: Why do arrow-function class fields fix the `this` problem?
options: They capture `this` from the instance at construction rather than at call time
They are bound by the compiler
They cannot be detached from the object
quiz.explanation: Passing `obj.method` as a callback loses the receiver. An arrow field closes over `this` when the instance is built, so it travels with the function.

quiz.question: What does a `get` accessor let you do?
options: Expose a computed value through property syntax
quiz.explanation: Getters compute on access; `set` accessors are the ones that validate assignment. `readonly` is a separate modifier.

quiz.question: When should you NOT reach for a class?
options: When the thing is plain data with no invariant to protect
When there is more than one instance
quiz.explanation: Data with no behaviour is better as a plain object plus functions — it stays serializable and structurally typed.

quiz.question: Why does `const f = obj.method; f();` often break?
options: `this` is lost when the method is detached from its receiver
Methods cannot be assigned to variables
It only breaks in strict mode
quiz.explanation: A plain method call binds `this` from the call site. An arrow-function class field, or an explicit bind, keeps the receiver attached.

quiz.question: What does `readonly` on a class field prevent?
options: Mutating the object the field points at
quiz.explanation: It is a compile-time restriction on reassigning the field. The object it references can still be mutated freely.

quiz.question: `class A { #x = 1; static read(a: A) { return a.#x; } }` — allowed?
options: Yes — code inside the class can read `#x` on any `A`
quiz.explanation: Private names are scoped to the class body, not to one instance.

quiz.question: `class A { private x = 1 }` — `new A().x` from outside?
options: Compile error, but at runtime the property is there
quiz.explanation: `private` is checked by the compiler only. `#x` is the runtime-private version.

quiz.question: In a subclass constructor, `this.y = 1; super();` — result?
options: Error: `super()` must be called before `this` is used
quiz.explanation: The object doesn't exist until the parent constructor has run (TS17009).

quiz.question: Where do `static` members live?
options: On the class itself, not on instances
quiz.explanation: Access them as `ClassName.member`.

quiz.question: Can a `readonly` class field be assigned in the constructor?
options: Yes — only after construction is it fixed
quiz.explanation: `readonly` fields may be set at the declaration or in the constructor.

quiz.question: Does `implements I` give a class any code from `I`?
options: No — an interface has no implementation; it only checks
quiz.explanation: `implements` is a check. Inheritance of code comes from `extends`.

quiz.question: Assigning to a property that has a `get` but no `set`?
quiz.explanation: A getter without a setter is typed `readonly` (TS2540).

quiz.question: In a `static` method, what does `this` refer to?
quiz.explanation: That's why `this.create()` works inside a static factory.

quiz.question: `({ x: 1, y: 2 }) instanceof Point` for a class `Point { x = 0; y = 0 }`?
quiz.explanation: `instanceof` checks the prototype chain, not the shape. Structural typing is compile-time only.

quiz.question: Which is composition rather than inheritance?
quiz.explanation: The car *has* an engine instead of *being* one — swap it without touching a hierarchy.

quiz.question: `class A { static count = 5 }` and `class B extends A {}` — what is `B.count`?
quiz.explanation: Subclasses inherit static members through the constructor's prototype chain.

quiz.question: In `static make() { return new this(); }` called as `B.make()` on a subclass `B`, what is created?
quiz.explanation: `this` in a static method is the constructor it was called on.

quiz.question: What does `protected` allow that `private` doesn't?
quiz.explanation: Both are compile-time only; `#` fields are runtime-private.

quiz.question: Does a subclass constructor have to call `super()` before using `this`?
quiz.explanation: Using `this` first is a compile error and a runtime ReferenceError.

quiz.question: What does `implements` add at runtime?
quiz.explanation: Interfaces are erased.

quiz.question: A class `C` has a `#secret` field. Can another instance of `C` read it?
options: Yes — privacy is per class, not per instance
quiz.explanation: Methods of `C` may read `#secret` on any `C`.

quiz.question: Why is an accessor pair (`get`/`set`) better than a public field for validated state?
options: The setter can reject bad values while callers keep simple property syntax
quiz.explanation: Encapsulation without changing the call sites.

quiz.question: What is a mixin in TypeScript?
options: A function that takes a class and returns a subclass adding behaviour
quiz.explanation: `const Timestamped = <T extends new (...a: any[]) => object>(Base: T) => class extends Base { … }`.

quiz.question: When is a closure-based object (a factory returning functions) better than a class?
options: When you want true privacy and no `this` — small objects passed around as callbacks
quiz.explanation: Each call gets its own captured variables.

quiz.question: What does `override` add at runtime?
options: Nothing — it's erased; the compiler checks it
A copy of the base method
quiz.explanation: Like `private` and `abstract`, it only exists for the checker.

quiz.question: Can an `abstract` class have a constructor?
options: Only if it has no abstract members
quiz.explanation: It just can't be called with `new` directly.

quiz.question: What does `accessor x = 1` (with standard decorators) declare?
options: An auto-accessor: a getter/setter pair over a private backing field
quiz.explanation: Designed so decorators can intercept reads and writes.

quiz.question: What does `abstract area(): number` in a base class require?
quiz.explanation: Missing it is TS2515; the base class itself can't be instantiated (TS2511).

quiz.question: What does the `override` keyword catch?
options: A method meant to replace a base member when no such member exists (e.g. a typo)
quiz.explanation: TS4113. `--noImplicitOverride` makes the keyword required.

quiz.question: How do you stop callers from constructing invalid instances?
options: A `private constructor` plus a `static` factory that validates
quiz.explanation: The factory is the only door, and it can refuse.

quiz.question: Why is calling an overridable method from a constructor risky?
options: Subclass fields aren't initialised yet when the base constructor runs
quiz.explanation: The override sees `undefined` fields.

quiz.question: `private` vs `#private`?
options: `private` is checked only by the compiler; `#private` is enforced at runtime
quiz.explanation: `#` fields are part of JavaScript.

quiz.question: When is composition better than inheritance?
options: When you want to reuse behaviour without coupling to a base class's internals
quiz.explanation: Pass collaborators in; keep `extends` for stable is-a relationships.

quiz.question: What does a standard method decorator receive?
options: The original method and a context object
quiz.explanation: `(value, context)` — `context` has `kind`, `name`, `static`, `private` and `addInitializer`.

quiz.question: `@a @b method() {}` — which decorator is applied first?
quiz.explanation: Decorators are applied bottom-up; the top one's wrapper runs outermost.

quiz.question: What is `@retry(3)`?
options: A decorator factory: `retry(3)` returns the decorator that is applied
quiz.explanation: The outer call takes configuration.

quiz.question: Why can't type stripping run decorators?
options: They execute code at class definition, so deleting them would delete behaviour
quiz.explanation: Like `enum` and parameter properties, they aren't erasable.

quiz.question: Which is the experimental (legacy) method decorator signature?
quiz.explanation: Enabled by `--experimentalDecorators`; different from the standard.

quiz.question: How must a method-decorator wrapper call the original?
options: With the same `this` — e.g. `target.call(this, ...args)` in a `function` wrapper
quiz.explanation: An arrow wrapper can't receive the instance as `this`.

exam.title: Bank account with invariants
exam.prompt: Write a `BankAccount` class with a `#balance`, a `deposit`, a `withdraw` that refuses overdrafts, and a `balance` getter. The input is `n` then `n` commands (`deposit n`, `withdraw n`). Print the balance after each command, printing `refused` instead when a withdrawal would overdraw, then the final balance.
exam.hint: The invariant lives inside the class: withdraw is the only path that reduces #balance, and it refuses rather than going negative.

flashcards.front: `private` vs `#private`?
flashcards.back: `private` is compile-time only — the field is a normal property at runtime. `#field` is truly private, enforced by JavaScript.

flashcards.front: What is a class invariant?
flashcards.back: A rule that holds after every public method, e.g. "balance is never negative". Private state plus checked methods enforce it.

flashcards.front: What does `implements` check?
flashcards.back: That the class has every member of the interface. It does not inherit anything or change the class's type.

flashcards.front: When does `protected` make sense?
flashcards.back: When a subclass needs access but outside code shouldn't — it means nothing without a subclass.

flashcards.front: What does `override` guard against?
flashcards.back: Typos and base-class renames: with `noImplicitOverride`, a method that doesn't really override anything is an error.

flashcards.front: Can you instantiate an `abstract` class?
flashcards.back: No (TS2511). It exists to be extended; `abstract` methods have to be implemented by subclasses.

flashcards.front: Why can a detached method crash?
flashcards.back: `const f = obj.method; f()` calls it with `this` undefined. Bind it, wrap it in an arrow, or define it as an arrow field.

flashcards.front: Why are parameter properties (`constructor(private x: number)`) graded by type-check only here?
flashcards.back: They emit an assignment, so they aren't erasable — Node's strip-only mode refuses them.

flashcards.front: What does a getter give you over a plain field?
flashcards.back: A computed, read-only view: `get balance() { return this.#balance; }` — callers can read, not write.

flashcards.front: Classes are structural too — what does that mean?
flashcards.back: An object literal with the same public members is assignable to the class type; `instanceof` is the check that really needs the class.

flashcards.front: When is a discriminated union better than a class hierarchy?
flashcards.back: When the set of variants is closed and you mostly *switch* on them — exhaustiveness checking beats virtual dispatch there.

flashcards.front: What is a static factory?
flashcards.back: `static from(raw: string): Account | null` — a named constructor that can validate and fail, which `new` cannot.

flashcards.front: What does `abstract` on a method require?
flashcards.back: Every concrete subclass implements it (TS2515 otherwise); the abstract class itself can't be constructed (TS2511).

flashcards.front: What does the `override` keyword protect against?
flashcards.back: Renaming or misspelling: overriding a member the base doesn't have is TS4113.

flashcards.front: How do you stop invalid instances being constructed?
flashcards.back: A `private constructor` behind a `static` factory that validates and returns `undefined` or a `Result`.

flashcards.front: Why not call an overridable method from a base constructor?
flashcards.back: Subclass fields are initialised after the base constructor runs, so the override sees `undefined`.

flashcards.front: What is a standard decorator, in one line?
flashcards.back: A function `(value, context) => replacement?` applied to a class member or class at definition time.

flashcards.front: Why can't this app's runner execute `@decorators`?
flashcards.back: They run code at class definition, so type stripping can't delete them, and Node doesn't implement the syntax yet.

project_spec.title: account.ts — accounts that protect their invariants
project_spec.goal: A small bank built from classes whose invariants can't be bypassed: accounts are created only through a validating factory, balances live in `#private` fields, a savings account overrides withdrawal rules, and a transfer either happens completely or not at all.
requirements: `open <kind> <owner> <amount>` creates a `checking` or `savings` account (ids `A1`, `A2`, … in order) through a static factory; bad input prints `refused: <reason>` — `unknown kind`, `owner required`, `amount must be a whole number >= 0`.

`deposit <id> <n>`, `withdraw <id> <n>`: amounts are positive whole numbers. Checking accounts may go down to -100 (an overdraft); savings may not go below 0 and allow at most 3 withdrawals (`refused: withdrawal limit`). Print the new balance, or `refused: insufficient funds`/`refused: no account <id>`/`refused: bad amount`.
`transfer <from> <to> <n>` moves money only if the withdrawal succeeds — then prints `ok <from>=<balance> <to>=<balance>` — otherwise the refusal and no change.
`interest` adds 2% (rounded down) to every savings account with a positive balance and prints `interest paid <total>`; `statement` prints every account as `<id> <kind> <owner> <balance>` in id order.
Use an abstract `Account` with `#balance`, subclasses that override a `canWithdraw` rule, and a private constructor behind `Account.open`.
stretch: Add a `history` per account (every successful operation), readable but not writable from outside.
Replace the string refusals with a `Result` type and `Error` subclasses (week 25).
rubric: No `any` anywhere — not even one hidden in a cast
Every function has a typed signature; locals are left to inference
Bad input is handled on purpose, not by accident
Names say what things are, not how they are stored
I could explain every line to someone else

weeks.title: Iterators, Generators & Generic Data Structures
weeks.goal: Produce values lazily and build containers that feel built-in.

problems.note: A container with an interface contract.

weeks.project: Write a `lazy.ts` with generator-based `range`, `map`, `filter`, `take` and `chunk`, then use them to process an infinite sequence without materialising it.

quiz.question: What does `yield*` do?
options: Delegates to another iterable, yielding all its values in place
Yields an array of the remaining values
quiz.explanation: It forwards every value from the inner iterable as if written inline — the standard way to compose generators.

quiz.question: `function* g() { yield 1; yield 2; }` — `[...g()]`?
quiz.explanation: Spreading drains the generator.

quiz.question: `function* g() { yield 1; yield 2; }` — what does the third `next()` on one `g()` iterator return?
quiz.explanation: After the last `yield` the generator returns, and further calls report `done`.

quiz.question: Is a generator's `return` value visited by `for…of`?
quiz.explanation: `for…of` stops at `done: true` and ignores its `value`.

quiz.question: Stack vs queue order?
options: Stack is last-in first-out; queue is first-in first-out
Stack is FIFO; queue is LIFO
quiz.explanation: Stacks drive DFS and undo; queues drive BFS and scheduling.

quiz.question: Why use a ring buffer for a queue?
options: O(1) enqueue and dequeue without shifting elements
quiz.explanation: Head and tail indices wrap around a fixed array.

quiz.question: In an array-backed binary heap, where are the children of index `i`?
quiz.explanation: And the parent is `Math.floor((i - 1) / 2)`.

quiz.question: Cost of inserting at the head of a singly linked list?
quiz.explanation: Point the new node at the old head and update `head`.

quiz.question: What does iterating a `Map` with `for…of` yield?
quiz.explanation: Destructure them: `for (const [k, v] of map)`.

quiz.question: `Iterable<T>` vs `Iterator<T>`?
options: An iterable has `[Symbol.iterator]()`, which returns an iterator; an iterator has `next()`
An iterator has `[Symbol.iterator]`, an iterable has `next`
quiz.explanation: `for…of` asks the iterable for a fresh iterator, then calls `next()` until done.

quiz.question: Why a generic `Stack<T>` instead of a `Stack` that stores `any`?
options: So `pop()` returns `T | undefined` and callers keep their types
quiz.explanation: With `any`, every value that comes out has lost its type.

quiz.question: `function* g() { const x = yield 1; yield x * 2; }` — `it.next(); it.next(21).value` is?
quiz.explanation: The argument to `next` becomes the value of the paused `yield`. The first `next`'s argument is ignored.

quiz.question: A `for…of` loop over a generator `break`s early. What runs?
quiz.explanation: `break` calls the iterator's `return()`.

quiz.question: What does `[...(function* () { yield* [1, 2]; return 3; })()]` give?
quiz.explanation: The `return` value is not part of iteration.

quiz.question: What does iterating a `Map` directly (`for (const x of map)`) yield?
quiz.explanation: Same as `map.entries()`.

quiz.question: What is `Generator<T, TReturn, TNext>`'s `TNext`?
options: The type of values passed into `next()`
quiz.explanation: Most generators leave it `unknown` or `undefined`.

quiz.question: How do you traverse a tree in order with a generator?
quiz.explanation: `yield*` delegates to the recursive calls.

quiz.question: Why is a linked list's `shift` O(1) but an array's O(n)?
options: The list just moves its head pointer; the array re-indexes every element
quiz.explanation: For queue-heavy code, use a real queue or a ring buffer.

quiz.question: What makes `Iterator.from(x)` useful?
options: It gives any iterable the iterator helpers
quiz.explanation: Plain iterables don't carry `map`, `take` and friends.

quiz.question: What does `iter.drop(2)` do?
options: Skips the first two values lazily
Removes two values from the source
Sorts and drops the two smallest
quiz.explanation: Like `slice(2)`, but lazy.

quiz.question: What is the cost of building a heap by pushing n items one by one?
quiz.explanation: A bottom-up heapify can do it in O(n), but push-by-push is fine for most uses.

quiz.question: Why does a priority queue beat re-sorting an array after each insert?
options: Each insert/remove is O(log n) instead of O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: Sorting is right only when you need the whole order once.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `flatMap` on an iterator and on an array?
options: The iterator version is lazy; both flatten one level
quiz.explanation: Iterator `flatMap` expects the callback to return an iterable.

quiz.question: What happens the second time you iterate the SAME generator object?
options: Nothing is produced — a generator object is exhausted after one pass
It yields the values in reverse
quiz.explanation: The generator holds its own position. If callers may iterate more than once, hand back a function that creates a fresh generator each time.

quiz.question: Why does `take(naturals(), 4)` terminate even though `naturals()` never ends?
options: Generators are lazy — naturals only computes a value when take asks, and take stops asking
TypeScript detects the infinite loop and bounds it
naturals() is evaluated eagerly up to a default limit
The spread operator caps at 1000 elements
quiz.explanation: Laziness is the point: production is driven entirely by consumption. Spreading `naturals()` directly, with no `take`, really would hang.

quiz.question: Why should `pop()` be typed `T | undefined` rather than `T`?
options: An empty stack really does return undefined, and the type should say so
Generic methods cannot return a bare T
undefined is required for iteration to work
quiz.explanation: Typing it as `T` is a lie that hands the caller an `undefined` the compiler swears is a real value — precisely the class of bug the type system exists to prevent.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `#items` and `private items`?
options: `#items` is private at runtime too; `private` is erased and the field is visible in JavaScript
`#items` cannot be used in a generic class
quiz.explanation: `#` is a real JavaScript private field enforced by the engine. `private` is a compile-time-only marker, so anything ignoring the types can still reach the value.

quiz.question: Why does a generic `SortedList<T>` take a comparator instead of constraining `T extends Comparable`?
options: T is erased at runtime, so ordering must be supplied as a function the class can call
Comparable does not exist in the TypeScript standard library
Constraints cannot be used on classes
Comparators are faster than interface dispatch
quiz.explanation: Both parts are true — there is no built-in Comparable — but the underlying reason is erasure: nothing about `T` survives to run, so the behaviour has to be passed in as a value.

quiz.question: Which of these is lazy?
quiz.explanation: Iterator `map` returns a new iterator and runs nothing until pulled.

quiz.question: What does `take(n)` do to the pipeline?
options: Stops pulling from the source after `n` values
quiz.explanation: It's what makes infinite sources safe.

quiz.question: You call `toArray()` twice on the same iterator. The second result?
options: An empty array — the iterator was consumed
quiz.explanation: Iterators are single-use cursors.

quiz.question: How do you use the helpers on a value typed `Iterable<T>`?
quiz.explanation: `Iterable<T>` only promises `[Symbol.iterator]`.

quiz.question: How do you make a class work with `for…of`?
options: Implement `[Symbol.iterator]()`, often as a generator method
quiz.explanation: `*[Symbol.iterator]() { … yield … }`.

quiz.question: Which call hangs?
quiz.explanation: Spreading tries to collect everything.

quiz.question: Where is the smallest item in a min-heap stored in an array?
quiz.explanation: The heap property puts the minimum at the root.

quiz.question: What are the children of index `i`?
quiz.explanation: Its parent is `(i - 1) >> 1`.

quiz.question: Cost of `push` and `pop`?
quiz.explanation: Each walks one root-to-leaf path.

quiz.question: How do you get the k smallest of n values in O(n log k)?
options: A max-heap capped at k items, popping when it exceeds k
quiz.explanation: Its top is the largest kept value — the one to evict.

quiz.question: Are heaps stable for equal priorities?
options: No — add an insertion counter to the comparison if order matters
quiz.explanation: Swaps reorder equal items.

quiz.question: What does the comparator `(a, b) => b - a` produce?
quiz.explanation: Negative when `a` is larger, so larger items come out first.

exam.title: Lazy pipeline over an infinite source
exam.prompt: Write generators `naturals`, `filter`, `map` and `take`. The input is `count divisor`. Take the first `count` naturals divisible by `divisor`, square them, and print them space-separated (or `(none)`), then their sum. Nothing infinite may be materialised.
exam.hint: take must `return` the moment it has enough — that is what stops the infinite source being pulled forever.

flashcards.front: What makes an object iterable?
flashcards.back: A `[Symbol.iterator]()` method returning an iterator — an object with `next()` returning `{ value, done }`.

flashcards.front: What is a generator?
flashcards.back: A `function*` that `yield`s values lazily; calling it returns an iterator that runs the body on demand.

flashcards.front: Why can a generator describe an infinite sequence safely?
flashcards.back: Nothing runs until a value is asked for — `take(naturals(), 5)` computes only five.

flashcards.front: What does `yield*` do?
flashcards.back: Delegates to another iterable, yielding each of its values in turn — handy for recursive tree traversal.

flashcards.front: Can a generator be iterated twice?
flashcards.back: No — it is a one-shot iterator. Call the generator function again for a fresh one.

flashcards.front: What is the `Generator<T, TReturn, TNext>` type?
flashcards.back: The yielded type, the final `return` type, and the type `next(value)` accepts.

flashcards.front: What hangs: spreading which kind of iterator?
flashcards.back: An infinite one — `[...naturals()]` never finishes.

flashcards.front: Why is `queue.shift()` a trap in BFS?
flashcards.back: `shift` is O(n) — it moves every remaining element. Use a head index into the array, or a ring buffer.

flashcards.front: How do you make a `LinkedList<T>` work with `for…of`?
flashcards.back: Give it `*[Symbol.iterator]() { for (let n = this.head; n; n = n.next) yield n.value; }`.

flashcards.front: What does a binary heap give you?
flashcards.back: O(log n) insert and remove-min, with O(1) peek — the engine of a priority queue.

flashcards.front: How does a generic priority queue know what "smaller" means?
flashcards.back: It takes a comparator, `(a: T, b: T) => number`, in its constructor.

flashcards.front: What are iterator helpers (ES2025)?
flashcards.back: `map`, `filter`, `take`, `drop`, `flatMap`, `reduce`, `toArray` directly on iterators — lazy pipelines without writing generators.

flashcards.front: Lazy or eager: `iter.map(f)` on an iterator?
flashcards.back: Lazy — it returns an iterator and runs `f` only as values are pulled.

flashcards.front: How do iterator helpers make infinite sequences safe?
flashcards.back: `take(n)` (or `find`, `some`, a `break`) stops pulling, so only finitely many values are computed.

flashcards.front: How do you use iterator helpers on an `Iterable<T>`?
flashcards.back: `Iterator.from(iterable).map(…)` — plain iterables don't carry the helpers.

flashcards.front: A binary heap's `push`/`pop` cost?
flashcards.back: O(log n) each; `peek` is O(1).

flashcards.front: Comparator contract for a heap or `sort`?
flashcards.back: Negative when `a` should come first, positive when `b` should, zero for a tie.

flashcards.front: How do you keep equal priorities in arrival order in a heap?
flashcards.back: Add an insertion counter and compare it when priorities tie.

project_spec.title: lazy.ts — a lazy pipeline over infinite sources
project_spec.goal: Build pipelines over sequences that never end — natural numbers, Fibonacci, primes — with generators and iterator helpers, so that each pipeline does only the work its `take` asks for. Every step is lazy; nothing is materialised until the end.
requirements: Each input line is a pipeline: `<source> | <step> | <step> …`. Sources: `naturals` (1, 2, 3, …), `fib` (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, …), `primes`, `range <a> <b>` (a ≤ n < b, finite).

Steps: `map square|double|digits` (`digits` = digit sum), `filter even|odd|prime`, `skip <n>`, `take <n>`, `takeWhile below <n>`, `chunk <n>` (groups printed as `[a b]`), `sum` (terminal: prints the total), `count` (terminal).
Without a terminal step print the values space-separated. A pipeline over an infinite source with no `take`, `takeWhile` or finite source before a terminal step or the end prints `refused: infinite`.
Unknown sources or steps print `unknown <word>`.

Use generator functions for the sources and iterator helpers (`map`, `filter`, `drop`, `take`) for the steps; count how many source values were pulled and print `pulled <k>` after each pipeline (except one with an unknown source).
stretch: Add `window <n>` (sliding windows) as a lazy generator step.
Make the step table data — `{ name, arity, apply }` — so adding a step is one entry.
rubric: No `any` anywhere — not even one hidden in a cast
Every function has a typed signature; locals are left to inference
Bad input is handled on purpose, not by accident
Names say what things are, not how they are stored
I could explain every line to someone else

weeks.title: Errors, Result & Resource Management
weeks.goal: Make failure visible in the type: throw for bugs, return a `Result` for failures the caller must handle, and never lose an error.

problems.note: A parser where every malformed token is a failure you must decide how to report.
Validation that finds every violation, not just the first.
A real grammar — and a real set of ways for input to be wrong.

weeks.project: Write a `parse.ts`: a `Result`-based CSV parser that reports every bad line with its line number, never throws, and returns the good rows as typed records.

quiz.question: Under `strict`, what type does `catch (e)` give `e`?
quiz.explanation: Any value can be thrown, so TypeScript refuses to assume `Error`. Narrow with `instanceof` before reading properties.

quiz.question: `try { throw "oops"; } catch (e) { … }` — what is `e`?
options: The string `"oops"` — not an `Error`, and with no stack trace
quiz.explanation: Anything can be thrown. Throw `Error` objects so there's a message and a stack.

quiz.question: `function f() { try { return 1; } finally { console.log("f"); } }` — calling `f()`?
quiz.explanation: `finally` always runs, even after a `return`.

quiz.question: Why set `this.name = "ValidationError"` in a custom error class?
options: So logs and stack traces show which kind of error it is
quiz.explanation: The name prefixes the message in `String(err)` and in stacks.

quiz.question: After `if (e instanceof Error)`, what is `e` (from `catch (e)` under `strict`)?
quiz.explanation: `instanceof` narrows the `unknown` catch variable, so `e.message` is safe.

quiz.question: What is `new Error("load failed", { cause: err })` for?
options: Keeping the original error attached, so the chain can be reported
quiz.explanation: `cause` preserves the low-level reason while the new message says what the program was trying to do.

quiz.question: When should a function throw rather than return a `Result`?
options: For bugs and broken invariants the caller cannot sensibly handle
quiz.explanation: Expected failures (bad input, missing file) belong in the type; programmer errors should fail loudly.

quiz.question: What is wrong with `try { save(); } catch (e) {}`?
options: It silently swallows every error, including bugs
Nothing — it's the idiomatic way to ignore failures
quiz.explanation: An empty catch hides failures you never anticipated. Catch what you can handle; let the rest propagate.

quiz.question: You need to report every invalid field, not just the first. What shape fits?
options: Accumulate errors into an array and return `Result<T, E[]>`
Throw on the first invalid field
Log each error and return the partial object
quiz.explanation: Fail-fast and collect-all are both valid designs — the type should say which one you chose.

quiz.question: What does an `AggregateError` hold?
options: The first error and its cause
The stack traces of every caller
quiz.explanation: `Promise.any` rejects with one when every input fails; you can throw your own for batch validation.

quiz.question: `andThen` (a.k.a. `flatMap`) on a failed `Result` does what?
options: Returns the failure unchanged without calling the function
quiz.explanation: That short-circuit is what lets a chain of fallible steps read as straight-line code.

quiz.question: Why is a tagged union like `{ kind: "not_found" } | { kind: "invalid"; field: string }` a good `E` for a `Result`?
options: The caller can switch on `kind` exhaustively, and it is plain serializable data
quiz.explanation: Error subclasses need `instanceof` and carry stacks you rarely want in a data result; a union is checked by the compiler.

quiz.question: What does `return` inside a `finally` block do to an exception thrown in `try`?
options: Discards it — the function returns normally
quiz.explanation: `finally` overriding control flow hides failures. Keep `finally` for cleanup only.

quiz.question: A `.then` callback throws. What happens?
options: The promise returned by `.then` rejects with that error
quiz.explanation: Inside promise callbacks, `throw` becomes rejection — which is why an unhandled `.then` chain loses errors.

quiz.question: What does `await Promise.resolve(1).finally(() => 99)` give?
quiz.explanation: `finally` is for cleanup; it can't change the result (unless it throws).

quiz.question: A block with `using r` throws, and `r`'s dispose throws too. What reaches the `catch`?
options: A `SuppressedError` with `.error` = the dispose error and `.suppressed` = the original
quiz.explanation: Neither failure is lost.

quiz.question: A `DisposableStack` has one deferred cleanup that throws. What does `dispose()` throw?
quiz.explanation: With several failing cleanups they're chained as SuppressedErrors.

quiz.question: Is `cause` part of `Object.keys(new Error("x", { cause: 1 }))`?
options: No — it's a non-enumerable own property
quiz.explanation: Read it directly (`e.cause`); `JSON.stringify(e)` won't show it.

quiz.question: Why prefer `Result` for parsing user input?
options: Invalid input is expected, and the type makes every caller handle it
quiz.explanation: Exceptions are for the unexpected.

quiz.question: What does `stack.adopt(value, release)` do on a `DisposableStack`?
options: Registers `release(value)` to run at disposal and returns `value`
quiz.explanation: For resources that don't implement `Symbol.dispose` themselves.

quiz.question: Should a dispose method be safe to call twice?
options: No, it should throw the second time
quiz.explanation: Defensive cleanup avoids double-free bugs.

quiz.question: What is `SuppressedError`?
options: The error raised when cleanup fails while another error is already propagating
quiz.explanation: It keeps both the cleanup error and the original.

quiz.question: What should `catch` do with an error it can't handle?
options: Rethrow it (or wrap it with a `cause`)
quiz.explanation: Swallowing unknown errors hides bugs.

quiz.question: How do `try`/`finally` and `using` differ in ordering several resources?
options: `using` releases in reverse order automatically; with `finally` you write the order by hand
quiz.explanation: Nested `finally` blocks are easy to get wrong as resources multiply.

quiz.question: What is `err.cause` typed as?
quiz.explanation: Anything can be a cause; narrow before use.

quiz.question: What does a `Result` type look like as a discriminated union?
options: `{ ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }`
quiz.explanation: The `ok` tag narrows to the right member.

quiz.question: What makes `Result<T, E>` enforce error handling?
options: It is a discriminated union, so `value` is only reachable after checking `ok`
It throws if you ignore the error branch
E defaults to string, which cannot be ignored
quiz.explanation: The `ok` field is the discriminant. On the `false` branch there is no `value` property at all, so skipping the check is a type error rather than a runtime surprise.

quiz.question: When is throwing the better choice over returning a Result?
options: For bugs and unrecoverable invariant violations the caller cannot sensibly handle
quiz.explanation: Expected, recoverable failures belong in the return type. Genuinely exceptional situations — an impossible branch, a broken invariant — should unwind loudly.

quiz.question: When is `x[Symbol.dispose]()` called for `using x = …`?
options: When the enclosing block exits — normally, by return, or by exception
quiz.explanation: Deterministic, like `finally`.

quiz.question: Two `using` declarations in one block are disposed in which order?
quiz.explanation: Last acquired, first released.

quiz.question: What does `using x = undefined` do?
options: Nothing at block exit — `null` and `undefined` are allowed and skipped
quiz.explanation: Handy for optional resources.

quiz.question: Where is `await using` allowed?
options: In async functions and at a module's top level
quiz.explanation: Wherever `await` is.

quiz.question: What is `DisposableStack.prototype.move()` for?
options: Transferring the collected cleanups to a new stack so the current one won't run them
quiz.explanation: Used when setup succeeds and ownership passes to the caller.

quiz.question: A block throws and then a dispose also throws. What propagates?
quiz.explanation: `.error` is the dispose error, `.suppressed` the original.

quiz.question: Why set `name` on an `Error` subclass?
options: It's what `String(e)` and stack traces print
quiz.explanation: `instanceof` works without it; people reading logs don't.

quiz.question: How do you keep the original error when wrapping it?
quiz.explanation: `cause` is part of the standard `Error` constructor (ES2022).

quiz.question: What type is `e` in `catch (e)` under `strict`?
quiz.explanation: `useUnknownInCatchVariables` — anything can be thrown.

quiz.question: What does `AggregateError` hold?
options: A list of errors in `.errors`, plus its own message
quiz.explanation: `Promise.any` throws one when every promise rejects.

quiz.question: A `catch` block receives an error it doesn't understand. What should it do?
quiz.explanation: Handle what you can; let the rest propagate.

quiz.question: When is returning a `Result` better than throwing?
options: For expected failures the caller must handle, like invalid input
quiz.explanation: The compiler then forces the caller to deal with the failure case.

flashcards.front: What is the type of `e` in `catch (e)` under `strict`?
flashcards.back: `unknown` (`useUnknownInCatchVariables`). Narrow it — `e instanceof Error` — before reading `e.message`.

flashcards.front: Throw or return a `Result`?
flashcards.back: Return a `Result` for failures the caller is expected to handle (bad input); throw for bugs and truly exceptional states.

flashcards.front: What is `Error.cause` for?
flashcards.back: Chaining: `throw new Error("load failed", { cause: err })` keeps the original error attached.

flashcards.front: What does `finally` do if the `try` returns?
flashcards.back: It still runs — and a `return` inside `finally` overrides the `try`'s return, which is almost always a bug.

flashcards.front: Write a `Result<T, E>` type.
flashcards.back: `type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };` — a discriminated union on `ok`.

flashcards.front: Why can't you read `r.value` before checking `r.ok`?
flashcards.back: On the failure branch there is no `value` property at all, so the compiler refuses until `ok` has narrowed the union.

flashcards.front: What does `andThen` (flatMap) on a `Result` do?
flashcards.back: Runs the next fallible step on a success; passes a failure through untouched — so a chain of steps reads straight down.

flashcards.front: Why throw `Error` objects instead of strings?
flashcards.back: An `Error` carries a message, a name and a stack; `throw "oops"` carries nothing, and `e instanceof Error` fails for it.

flashcards.front: What is `AggregateError`?
flashcards.back: An error holding several errors in `.errors` — what `Promise.any` rejects with, and handy for batch validation.

flashcards.front: Fail fast or collect all errors?
flashcards.back: Fail fast when later steps depend on earlier ones; collect all when the user should fix everything in one go (form or config validation).

flashcards.front: How do you name a custom error class so logs say what happened?
flashcards.back: `class ValidationError extends Error { name = "ValidationError"; }` — the name prefixes the message in `String(err)` and stacks.

flashcards.front: What is wrong with an empty `catch {}`?
flashcards.back: It swallows every error — including the bugs you never anticipated. Catch only what you can handle.

flashcards.front: What does `using x = r` guarantee?
flashcards.back: `r[Symbol.dispose]()` runs when the block exits, however it exits — in reverse order for several `using`s.

flashcards.front: `await using` — where is it allowed?
flashcards.back: In async functions and at a module's top level (TS2852 elsewhere).

flashcards.front: What is `DisposableStack.move()` for?
flashcards.back: Handing the collected cleanups to a new owner, so the current stack won't run them — the "commit" of a setup.

flashcards.front: How do you chain a low-level error to a high-level one?
flashcards.back: `throw new Error("high-level", { cause: original })` — walk `.cause` to read the chain.

flashcards.front: What does `AggregateError` hold?
flashcards.back: Several errors in `.errors`, plus its own message — e.g. every validation failure, or every rejection from `Promise.any`.

flashcards.front: When does a `Result` beat an exception?
flashcards.back: For expected failures the caller must handle; throw for failures it can't (bugs, lost connections).

weeks.title: Async, Concurrency & Cancellation
weeks.goal: Run async work concurrently on purpose, keep the output deterministic, and stop work you no longer need.

problems.note: Time-ordered state — the shape of every rate limiter.
Incremental computation over a stream of values.
A simulated clock and a pool of workers — concurrency without real timers.

weeks.project: Write a `fetchAll.ts` that loads several simulated resources concurrently, races each against a timeout, and returns a `Result` per resource — no exception escapes.

quiz.question: `async function f() { throw new Error("x"); }` — what does calling `f()` without `await` do?
options: Returns a rejected promise; nothing throws at the call site
quiz.explanation: An async function turns throws into rejections. Unawaited, the rejection goes unhandled.

quiz.question: What does this print? `console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); console.log(4);`
quiz.explanation: Synchronous code first; then microtasks (promise callbacks); then timers.

quiz.question: What does `await 5` evaluate to?
quiz.explanation: Awaiting a non-promise wraps it in a resolved promise and gives the value back.

quiz.question: What does `Promise.all([])` do?
quiz.explanation: With nothing to wait for, it's already done.

quiz.question: What does `Promise.any` do when every promise rejects?
options: Rejects with an `AggregateError` holding all the reasons
quiz.explanation: It resolves on the first success; only total failure rejects.

quiz.question: Type of `await Promise.all([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve("a")])`?
quiz.explanation: `Promise.all` on a tuple keeps each position's type.

quiz.question: What happens to an unhandled promise rejection in modern Node?
quiz.explanation: Since Node 15 the default is to throw. Always `await` or `.catch`.

quiz.question: What does `controller.abort()` on an `AbortController` do?
options: Marks its `signal` as aborted and fires the signal's `abort` event
Kills every pending promise in the process
quiz.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative: work that was handed the signal has to check `signal.aborted` or listen for the event and stop.

quiz.question: What is `AbortSignal.timeout(500)`?
options: A signal that aborts itself after 500 ms
A promise that resolves after 500 ms
A 500 ms delay before the next line
quiz.explanation: It turns a deadline into the same cancellation mechanism as a manual abort.

quiz.question: Ten jobs, but at most two may run at once. What is the usual shape?
options: A pool: start two workers, each takes the next job when it finishes
quiz.explanation: `all` runs everything at once and a loop runs one at a time; a small worker pool is the standard concurrency limit.

quiz.question: What does `Promise.withResolvers()` return?
options: An object with a `promise` and the `resolve` and `reject` functions that settle it
quiz.explanation: It replaces the old pattern of capturing `resolve` from inside `new Promise(...)`.

quiz.question: When does a callback passed to `queueMicrotask` run?
options: After the current synchronous code, before any timer callback
On the next event-loop tick after timers
quiz.explanation: Microtasks — promise reactions included — drain completely before the event loop moves on to tasks like timers.

quiz.question: What can `for await (const x of source)` iterate?
options: An async iterable, or a plain iterable whose items are awaited one by one
quiz.explanation: It uses `Symbol.asyncIterator` when present and otherwise awaits each item of a sync iterable.

quiz.question: What is each element of `await Promise.allSettled(ps)` typed as?
quiz.explanation: It is a discriminated union on `status`; narrow it before reading `value` or `reason`.

quiz.question: What does `await Promise.resolve(Promise.resolve(2))` give?
quiz.explanation: A promise never resolves to another promise.

quiz.question: What does `Promise.race([])` do?
quiz.explanation: An empty race has no competitor to settle it.

quiz.question: Why test async code with a virtual clock?
options: Time advances only when the test says so, making output independent of machine speed
quiz.explanation: Deterministic by construction.

quiz.question: What does a concurrency-limited pool guarantee that `Promise.all(items.map(work))` doesn't?
options: At most k operations are in flight at once
quiz.explanation: `Promise.all` starts everything immediately.

quiz.question: Debounce vs throttle?
options: Debounce waits for a pause, then runs once; throttle runs at most once per interval
quiz.explanation: Search boxes debounce; scroll handlers throttle.

quiz.question: What is the total time of `await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchOne))` versus awaiting inside a loop?
options: The maximum of the individual times, versus the sum of them
The same — Promise.all is just syntax
Depends on the number of CPU cores
quiz.explanation: `.map` starts every promise before `all` waits, so they overlap. Awaiting inside a loop starts each one only after the previous resolves.

quiz.question: How does `Promise.allSettled` differ from `Promise.all` on failure?
options: It never rejects; every entry becomes a fulfilled/rejected record you inspect
It rejects only if every promise fails
It resolves with the successful values and silently drops failures
quiz.explanation: `allSettled` always resolves with one `PromiseSettledResult` per input. That last behaviour — dropping failures — is what `Promise.any` approximates, and it is not what allSettled does.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `Promise.race` and `Promise.any`?
options: race settles with the first promise to settle either way; any waits for the first SUCCESS
any is the async version of race
quiz.explanation: `race` is the timeout pattern precisely because an early rejection wins. `any` ignores rejections until all of them fail, then rejects with an AggregateError.

quiz.question: `setTimeout(f, 0)` and `Promise.resolve().then(g)` are scheduled in that order. Which runs first?
options: `g` — microtasks run before the next timer
quiz.explanation: The whole microtask queue drains before any task.

quiz.question: What runs synchronously when you call an `async` function?
options: Its body up to the first `await`
quiz.explanation: The rest is resumed as a microtask.

quiz.question: Which of these is a microtask?
quiz.explanation: Also `.then` callbacks and `queueMicrotask`.

quiz.question: Why does `items.forEach(async (x) => await save(x))` not wait?
options: `forEach` ignores the promises its callback returns
`forEach` is synchronous only for arrays of numbers
quiz.explanation: Use `for…of` with `await`, or `Promise.all(items.map(…))`.

quiz.question: A synchronous loop runs for two seconds. What happens to a `setTimeout(f, 10)` set before it?
options: It runs after the loop — about two seconds late
quiz.explanation: Nothing interrupts running code; a delay is a minimum.

quiz.question: `Promise.all([slow(), fast()])` — what order are the results in?
options: Input order, regardless of which finished first
quiz.explanation: That's what makes it deterministic to print.

quiz.question: Can you cancel a promise?
options: No — you ask the work to stop via a signal, and it cooperates
Yes, by rejecting it from outside
quiz.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative in JavaScript.

quiz.question: What does `signal.throwIfAborted()` do?
options: Throws the signal's reason if it has been aborted; otherwise nothing
quiz.explanation: The one-line check between steps.

quiz.question: `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` aborts when?
quiz.explanation: Cancel-or-timeout in one signal.

quiz.question: What does `Promise.withResolvers<T>()` return?
quiz.explanation: Settle the promise from outside an executor.

quiz.question: After `Promise.race([work(), timeout])` resolves with the timeout, what is `work()` doing?
options: Still running, unless it was given a signal and checks it
quiz.explanation: Racing chooses a result; it doesn't stop anything.

quiz.question: `controller.abort()` with no argument — what is `signal.reason`?
quiz.explanation: Pass your own reason for a clearer message.

quiz.question: What does `for await (const x of source)` do each iteration?
options: Awaits the next value before running the body
quiz.explanation: Values are pulled one at a time.

quiz.question: What does an `async function*` return?
options: An async generator — an async iterable of its yielded values
quiz.explanation: Consume it with `for await` or `Array.fromAsync`.

quiz.question: A consumer `break`s out of `for await` early. What happens to the generator?
options: Its `return()` is called, so its `finally` blocks run
It keeps running in the background
quiz.explanation: Put cleanup in `finally`.

quiz.question: How do you collect an async iterable into an array?
quiz.explanation: ES2024; also takes a mapping function.

quiz.question: Can you iterate the same async generator object twice?
options: No — it's single-use; call the generator function again
quiz.explanation: Same as sync generators.

quiz.question: Why is async iteration good for paginated APIs?
options: The next page is fetched only when the consumer asks for more
It fetches all pages in parallel
quiz.explanation: Stopping early saves the remaining requests.

exam.title: Concurrent loads with a Result
exam.prompt: `load(id)` resolves to `id * 10` after `id` ms but rejects for a negative id. Run every id concurrently, convert each outcome to a `Result`, and print `id=value` or `id=failed` in input order, then the number that succeeded and their total, space-separated.
exam.hint: allSettled never rejects, so one bad id cannot lose the others; converting each entry to a Result makes the caller handle both branches.

flashcards.front: What does `await` do?
flashcards.back: Pauses the async function until the promise settles, then resumes with its value — or throws its rejection.

flashcards.front: `Promise.all` vs `Promise.allSettled`?
flashcards.back: `all` rejects as soon as one promise rejects; `allSettled` waits for every one and reports each as fulfilled or rejected.

flashcards.front: `Promise.race` vs `Promise.any`?
flashcards.back: `race` settles with the first promise to settle, success or failure; `any` resolves with the first success, rejecting only if all fail.

flashcards.front: Why is `await` inside a `for` loop sometimes slow?
flashcards.back: It runs the operations one after another. Start them all and `await Promise.all(...)` to run them concurrently.

flashcards.front: What goes wrong with `items.forEach(async (x) => { await save(x); })`?
flashcards.back: `forEach` ignores the returned promises — nothing waits for the saves, and their errors go unhandled.

flashcards.front: What is `async function f(): Promise<number>`'s return type if the body returns `5`?
flashcards.back: `Promise<number>` — an async function always returns a promise.

flashcards.front: How do you keep async output deterministic?
flashcards.back: Collect the results and print them in input order — never let completion timing decide the output order.

flashcards.front: How do you add a timeout to a promise?
flashcards.back: Race it against a timer that rejects: `Promise.race([work, timeout(ms)])`, or pass `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` to an API that accepts a signal.

flashcards.front: Print order: `setTimeout(a)`, `Promise.resolve().then(b)`, `console.log(c)`?
flashcards.back: `c`, then `b`, then `a` — synchronous code, then microtasks (promise reactions), then timers.

flashcards.front: How does cancellation work with an `AbortController`?
flashcards.back: `controller.abort()` marks `controller.signal` aborted and fires its `abort` event; the work must check the signal and stop — it is cooperative.

flashcards.front: How do you run 10 jobs with at most 2 at a time?
flashcards.back: A pool: start 2 workers, and have each take the next job index when it finishes, until none are left.

flashcards.front: What does `Promise.withResolvers()` give you?
flashcards.back: `{ promise, resolve, reject }` — a promise plus the functions that settle it, without nesting code in `new Promise(...)`.

flashcards.front: Sync code, microtasks, timers — in which order do they run?
flashcards.back: The current synchronous code, then every microtask (promise callbacks, `await` continuations, `queueMicrotask`), then the next timer.

flashcards.front: What does `await` do to the rest of an async function?
flashcards.back: Schedules it as a microtask once the awaited promise settles; code before the first `await` runs synchronously.

flashcards.front: How do you cancel in-flight async work?
flashcards.back: Pass an `AbortSignal` from an `AbortController`; the work checks it (`throwIfAborted`) and listens for `abort`. Cancellation is cooperative.

flashcards.front: `AbortSignal.any([a, AbortSignal.timeout(ms)])`?
flashcards.back: A signal that aborts when either the caller cancels or the time runs out.

flashcards.front: How do you consume an async generator?
flashcards.back: `for await (const x of gen())`, or `await Array.fromAsync(gen())` for a finite one.

flashcards.front: How do you make async output deterministic in tests?
flashcards.back: Order results by input index (`Promise.all`), and drive time with a virtual clock rather than real timers.

project_spec.title: fetchAll.ts — concurrent loads with limits, timeouts and retries
project_spec.goal: The Month 6 capstone of the async material: load a list of resources with at most two in flight, a per-attempt timeout, and one retry for failures — all on a virtual clock, so every run prints exactly the same thing. Results come back as a `Result` per resource, in input order, however the loads interleave.
requirements: The first input line is `timeout=<ms> retries=<n>`; each later line is `<name> <outcome>:<ms>[,<outcome>:<ms>…]` — the outcome (`ok` or `fail`) and duration of each successive attempt (an attempt beyond the list fails after 1 ms).

Run at most 2 resources at once, starting them in input order. An attempt that hasn't finished by the timeout is cancelled (its timer removed) and counts as a failure `timeout`; a failed attempt is `error`. Failed attempts are retried immediately, up to `retries` extra attempts.
Print `t=<time> <name> attempt <k> <ok|error|timeout>` as each attempt ends.
Then print one line per resource in input order: `<name>: ok after <k> attempt(s)` or `<name>: failed (<last reason>) after <k> attempt(s)`, and finally `done at t=<time>, <ok>/<total> loaded`.
Model each result as `Result<number, string>` and never let the output depend on real time.
stretch: Add jitter to retries without losing determinism (a seeded generator, as in the DSA curriculum).
Stream results as they complete with an async generator, while still offering the in-order summary.
rubric: No `any` anywhere — not even one hidden in a cast
Every function has a typed signature; locals are left to inference
Bad input is handled on purpose, not by accident
Names say what things are, not how they are stored
I could explain every line to someone else
