weeks.title: Capstone & Mock Interview
weeks.goal: Put six months together in one program, then rehearse the interview: TypeScript idioms, a DSA problem in TypeScript, and a type-level puzzle.

problems.note: The hardest design problem in the bank — take your time.

weeks.project: Capstone: build a small typed CLI — a `Result`-based parser, a branded id type, a generic store with an iterator, an ambient declaration for one host global — `strict` and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` clean. Then run a mock interview on yourself: 45 minutes, one idiom question, one problem above, one type puzzle.

quiz.question: An interviewer asks you to type `pipe(f, g, h)`. What is the honest first answer?
options: Overloads for a fixed number of steps — or a variadic tuple type if they want the general version
It cannot be typed in TypeScript
quiz.explanation: Overloads are what most libraries ship; the recursive tuple version exists but is harder to read. Saying which trade-off you are making is the point.

quiz.question: You are asked to explain `unknown` vs `any` in one sentence. Which is best?
options: `unknown` makes you prove what a value is before using it; `any` turns checking off
They are the same, but `unknown` is newer
`any` is for objects and `unknown` for primitives
quiz.explanation: Lead with the consequence for the reader of the code — that is what an interviewer is listening for.

quiz.question: Where do types stop helping in a program that reads JSON?
options: At the boundary: `JSON.parse` returns `any`, so the data must be validated before it gets a type
Nowhere — the compiler checks JSON files
quiz.explanation: Types describe what the code assumes. Untrusted input has to earn its type through a check or a schema.

quiz.question: What does `fs.readFileSync(0, "utf8")` read?
options: All of standard input, as one string
The first line of standard input
quiz.explanation: File descriptor 0 is standard input. The whole input arrives at once; splitting it is up to you.

quiz.question: Why call `.trim()` on the input?
options: To drop the trailing newline and any `\r` from Windows line endings
To convert it to a string
To remove every space inside it
quiz.explanation: Input almost always ends in a newline; leaving it on makes comparisons and printed strings wrong.

quiz.question: `Number("12px")`, `parseInt("12px", 10)` — what do they give?
quiz.explanation: `Number` needs the whole string to be numeric; `parseInt` reads the leading digits and stops.

quiz.question: What does `console.log("sum", 5)` print?
quiz.explanation: Several arguments are joined with a single space.

quiz.question: `const n = 2.5; console.log(n)` prints `2.5`. How do you print `2.50`?
quiz.explanation: `toFixed` returns a string with exactly that many decimals. Converting it back to a number loses the trailing zero again.

quiz.question: Why does `input.split(" ")` miscount words in `"a  b"`?
options: Two spaces produce an empty string between them
It doesn't; it returns two words
quiz.explanation: `"a  b".split(" ")` is `["a", "", "b"]`. Splitting on `/\s+/` treats any run of whitespace as one separator.

quiz.question: Which comparison is `true`?
quiz.explanation: Loose equality treats `null` and `undefined` as equal to each other and nothing else — the one widely accepted use of `==`.

quiz.question: How do you test whether `x` is `NaN`?
quiz.explanation: `NaN` is not equal to anything, itself included.

quiz.question: Which value is truthy?
quiz.explanation: Any non-empty string is truthy, whatever it says.

quiz.question: `const n = 0; n || 10` and `n ?? 10` give…
quiz.explanation: `||` falls back on any falsy value; `??` only on `null`/`undefined`.

quiz.question: What does TypeScript say about `3 === "3"` with those declared types?
options: It's a compile error: the types have no overlap
quiz.explanation: TS2367: comparing a `number` and a `string` is always `false`, so the compiler flags it.

quiz.question: `Object.is(0, -0)` and `Object.is(NaN, NaN)`?
quiz.explanation: `Object.is` is `===` with the two corners fixed the other way.

quiz.question: Why is `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` false?
options: Neither 0.1 nor 0.2 has an exact binary representation
quiz.explanation: The stored values are the nearest doubles; their sum is a hair above 0.3.

quiz.question: How should an app store a price of $19.99?
options: As the string `"19.99"` and parse it every time
quiz.explanation: Integer arithmetic is exact; format to dollars only when printing.

quiz.question: `Math.round(-2.5)`?
quiz.explanation: `Math.round` rounds halves towards +∞.

quiz.question: `1n + 1`?
options: A compile error: `bigint` and `number` can't be mixed
quiz.explanation: Mixing needs an explicit conversion (TS2365 at compile time, a TypeError at runtime).

quiz.question: What is `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`?
options: 2^53 − 1, the largest integer every smaller integer is exact below
quiz.explanation: Past it, adjacent integers share one double. `Number.MAX_VALUE` is the largest finite number, a different thing.

quiz.question: Why pass `"en-US"` to `Intl.NumberFormat` in a judged program?
options: So the output doesn't depend on the machine's locale
quiz.explanation: The default locale varies between machines; tests need one fixed format.

quiz.question: What does `/\d+/.test("abc123")` return?
quiz.explanation: Unanchored patterns match anywhere. `^…$` makes it about the whole string.

quiz.question: What does `"a1b22".match(/\d+/g)` return?
quiz.explanation: With `g`, `match` returns every matched string (or `null` when there are none).

quiz.question: Why is `m[1]` typed `string | undefined` under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`?
options: The compiler can't know a group took part in the match
quiz.explanation: Optional groups really can be `undefined`, and index reads are honest under that flag.

quiz.question: In a replacement string, what is `$<year>`?
options: The text of the named group `year`
quiz.explanation: Named groups can be referenced by name in replacements and read from `m.groups`.

quiz.question: Which flag makes `^` and `$` match at each line?
quiz.explanation: `m` is multiline; `s` makes `.` match newlines.

quiz.question: Why build patterns from user text carefully?
options: Characters like `.` and `*` have special meaning and must be escaped
quiz.explanation: Unescaped, `"1.5"` becomes a pattern where `.` matches any character.

quiz.question: What is `"😀".length`?
quiz.explanation: `length` counts UTF-16 code units, and this emoji is a surrogate pair.

quiz.question: Which walks a string by code point?
quiz.explanation: String iteration is by code point; indexing and `split("")` are by code unit.

quiz.question: What splits text into user-perceived characters?
quiz.explanation: Code points aren't enough for flags or accented letters written with combining marks.

quiz.question: Two strings look identical but aren't `===`. What's a likely cause?
options: Different Unicode normalisation — composed vs decomposed accents
quiz.explanation: Normalise both with `s.normalize("NFC")` before comparing.

quiz.question: Why sort names with `localeCompare` rather than the default `sort()`?
options: The default compares code units, putting uppercase first and accents last
quiz.explanation: `localeCompare` orders text the way a reader expects.

quiz.question: What does the `u` flag change in a regex?
options: It treats the pattern and input as code points
quiz.explanation: Without `u`, `.` matches a single code unit and can split an emoji.

quiz.question: What do callers of an overloaded function see?
options: Only the overload signatures — never the implementation signature
quiz.explanation: That's why a call with a union can fail even when the implementation would accept it.

quiz.question: In what order are overloads tried?
options: Top to bottom; the first that fits wins
All at once, merging the results
quiz.explanation: So the most specific overload must be written first.

quiz.question: What does the compiler check about the implementation?
options: Its body against its own signature, and each overload's compatibility with that signature
That each branch returns what the matching overload promises
quiz.explanation: It cannot tell which branch serves which overload, so the promises are yours to keep.

quiz.question: When is a union parameter better than overloads?
options: When the return type does not depend on which argument type was passed
When there are more than two types
quiz.explanation: Overloads earn their keep only by linking input types to output types.

quiz.question: A variable is `string | number`. The overloads accept `string` and `number` separately. Can you call it?
options: No — add an overload that accepts the union
Yes, the compiler splits the call
Yes, if the implementation accepts the union
quiz.explanation: Overload resolution needs one signature that accepts the whole argument type.

quiz.question: What does a closure capture?
options: The variables themselves — later changes are visible to it
A snapshot of the values at creation
quiz.explanation: That's what lets a counter keep counting, and what causes the `var` loop bug.

quiz.question: Why do closures made in `for (var i…)` all see the same `i`?
options: `var` is one function-scoped variable for the whole loop
They don't; each sees its own
quiz.explanation: `let` in the loop header creates a new binding for each iteration.

quiz.question: `const a = makeCounter(); const b = makeCounter();` — do they share a count?
options: No — each call creates a fresh variable
Only if they're called in the same tick
quiz.explanation: Unless the state lives outside the factory, in which case they do.

quiz.question: Where is a `let` declared inside an `if` block visible?
options: From the start of the function, as `undefined`
quiz.explanation: `let`/`const` are block-scoped.

quiz.question: What is the temporal dead zone?
options: The part of a block before a `let`/`const` declaration, where reading it throws
quiz.explanation: TypeScript catches most such reads at compile time (TS2448).

quiz.question: What is the type of `const add = (a: number) => (b: number) => a + b;`?
quiz.explanation: Calling `add(1)` hands back another function, so the return type is itself a function type. Only `add(1)(2)` produces a number.

quiz.question: Why does `['a','b'].map((s) => s.length)` type-check even though `map` passes three arguments to its callback?
options: A function may ignore trailing parameters it does not declare
The extra arguments are silently dropped at runtime only
TypeScript infers the missing parameters as any
quiz.explanation: Function assignability allows FEWER parameters than the target signature — the caller simply passes arguments the callback ignores. Declaring MORE than the signature offers is the error.

quiz.question: In `const shout = pipe<string>(f, g)`, what does `pipe` need to guarantee about `f` and `g`?
options: Both must be (x: string) => string so the output of one feeds the next
f must return the argument type of g, which can differ from string
Neither — pipe erases the types at runtime
quiz.explanation: This `pipe` is typed as `Array<(x: T) => T>`, so every stage takes and returns the SAME T. A pipeline that changes types between stages needs overloads or a more elaborate generic.

quiz.question: What two things does every recursive function need?
options: A base case that stops, and a step that makes the input strictly smaller
A global variable and a return
quiz.explanation: Without either, the recursion never ends.

quiz.question: What happens when recursion goes about ten thousand calls deep in Node?
quiz.explanation: Deep linear recursion should become a loop.

quiz.question: Why does naive `fib(40)` take so long?
options: It recomputes the same values exponentially many times
The stack limit makes it retry
quiz.explanation: Memoising each result makes it linear.

quiz.question: Why annotate a recursive function's return type?
options: Inference can go circular (TS7023), and the annotation documents the contract
quiz.explanation: The return type depends on itself, so TypeScript may give up.

quiz.question: When is recursion clearly better than a loop?
options: For tree-shaped work — nested data, enumerating combinations
quiz.explanation: Linear recursion converts to a loop mechanically; branching recursion doesn't.

quiz.question: What type does `const p = [1, "a"]` get?
quiz.explanation: Array literals infer arrays. Annotate, or use `as const`, to get a tuple.

quiz.question: What is `pair[2]` for `pair: [string, number]`?
quiz.explanation: The length is part of a tuple's type.

quiz.question: Why prefer `readonly [number, number]` for a return type?
options: A mutable tuple still allows `push`, which breaks the length the type promises
Only readonly tuples can be destructured
quiz.explanation: `readonly` removes every mutating method from the type.

quiz.question: What does `[name: string, ...scores: number[]]` describe?
options: A string followed by any number of numbers
An array of strings and numbers in any order
quiz.explanation: A rest element can follow fixed elements.

quiz.question: What is each element of `Object.entries({ a: 1 })`?
quiz.explanation: Entries are key/value pairs as two-element tuples.

quiz.question: What does `xs.toSorted()` do that `xs.sort()` doesn't?
options: Returns a new sorted array and leaves `xs` unchanged
Sorts in place and returns nothing
quiz.explanation: It's the copying counterpart; numbers still need a comparator.

quiz.question: What is `[1, 2, 3].at(-1)` typed as?
quiz.explanation: An index from the end may be out of range.

quiz.question: Why does `new Array(3).map((_, i) => i)` not give `[0, 1, 2]`?
options: The array has holes, and `map` skips holes
quiz.explanation: `Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i)` visits every index.

quiz.question: What does `Object.groupBy(xs, f)` return?
options: An object from each key to the items that produced it
quiz.explanation: `Map.groupBy` is the version that returns a `Map`.

quiz.question: How is `structuredClone(o)` different from `{ ...o }`?
options: It copies nested objects too, not just the top level
quiz.explanation: Spread is shallow; nested objects stay shared.

quiz.question: Which can name a union type?
quiz.explanation: `type Id = string | number`. Interfaces describe object shapes only.

quiz.question: Two `interface Settings` declarations in one scope…
options: merge into one interface with both sets of members
quiz.explanation: Declaration merging — deliberate in library augmentation, accidental elsewhere.

quiz.question: `type T = { id: number } & { id: string }` — what is `T["id"]`?
options: A compile error at the declaration
quiz.explanation: Intersections intersect property types; the conflict only surfaces when a value is built.

quiz.question: What does `class A implements Shape` do at runtime?
options: Nothing — it only asks the compiler to check the class
quiz.explanation: Interfaces and `implements` are erased.

quiz.question: Assigning a variable with extra properties to an interface type…
options: is allowed; the extra properties stay on the object
quiz.explanation: Excess-property errors are only for fresh object literals.

quiz.question: What does `{ [key: string]: number }` promise about `obj["missing"]`?
options: It types it as `number`, although at runtime it's `undefined`
quiz.explanation: Only `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` makes the read honest.

quiz.question: What does `Record<"a" | "b", number>` require?
options: Exactly the keys `a` and `b`, each a number
At least one of the keys
quiz.explanation: A union of literal keys makes the record exhaustive.

quiz.question: `{ x?: number }` vs `{ x: number | undefined }`?
options: The first may omit the key; the second must have it, possibly holding `undefined`
The second may omit the key
quiz.explanation: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` makes the distinction strict.

quiz.question: Why can `"constructor" in {}` be `true`?
quiz.explanation: Use `Object.hasOwn`, `Object.create(null)` or a `Map`.

quiz.question: What does TS7053 usually mean?
options: You indexed an object that has no index signature with an arbitrary `string`
quiz.explanation: Narrow the key to `keyof typeof obj`, or type the object as a `Record`.

quiz.question: What does `a.difference(b)` return?
options: A new set of the members of `a` that are not in `b`
It removes `b`'s members from `a` in place
Members in exactly one of the two
quiz.explanation: The set methods never mutate either operand.

quiz.question: Why can't you write `set.union([1, 2])`?
options: The argument must be set-like (`size`, `has`, `keys`), and an array isn't
quiz.explanation: Wrap it: `set.union(new Set([1, 2]))`.

quiz.question: How are keys compared in a `Set`?
options: SameValueZero — like `===`, but `NaN` equals `NaN`; objects by identity
quiz.explanation: Two equal-looking objects are two different members.

quiz.question: When do you need a `WeakMap` rather than a `Map`?
options: To attach data to objects without keeping them alive
When you need to iterate the entries
quiz.explanation: Entries disappear with their key; the price is no iteration and no `size`.

quiz.question: `Map.groupBy` versus `Object.groupBy`?
options: `Map.groupBy` keeps keys of any type; `Object.groupBy` turns them into property keys
quiz.explanation: Numbers, objects or booleans as keys call for the `Map` version.

quiz.question: `let d = "up"` — what type is `d`?
quiz.explanation: A `let` can be reassigned, so its literal widens.

quiz.question: `const o = { d: "up" }` — what is `o.d`?
quiz.explanation: Object properties are mutable and widen unless you use `as const` or annotate.

quiz.question: What does `as const` do to `[1, 2]`?
quiz.explanation: Literal element types, fixed length, readonly — and nothing at runtime.

quiz.question: `const SIZES = ["S", "M"] as const` — what is `(typeof SIZES)[number]`?
quiz.explanation: Indexing a tuple type with `number` gives the union of its element types.

quiz.question: Is `const x = input as Size` a validation?
options: No — it only tells the compiler to assume it
Yes, it throws on bad values
quiz.explanation: Check the value against the list at runtime to earn the type.

quiz.question: What changes if you write `function isPerson(x: unknown): boolean` instead of `: x is Person`?
options: The function still runs but no longer narrows x at the call site
x is narrowed to any instead of Person
quiz.explanation: Only the `x is T` return type carries narrowing information. With `: boolean` the compiler learns nothing from the `if`, so `x` stays `unknown` inside it.

quiz.question: `function isPerson(x: unknown): x is Person { return true; }` — what does TypeScript do?
options: Accepts it; the compiler trusts the predicate without verifying the body
Errors, because the body does not check any Person fields
Narrows to unknown instead, as a safety fallback
quiz.explanation: A type predicate is an unchecked promise. This is exactly why a predicate should test every field it claims — a sloppy one puts a hole straight through the type system.

quiz.question: What distinguishes `asserts x is string` from `x is string`?
options: The assertion narrows for the rest of the scope by throwing on failure, rather than returning a boolean to test
The assertion works on primitives only
The assertion is checked at runtime by TypeScript
There is no difference other than spelling
quiz.explanation: A predicate answers a question you branch on; an assertion function makes a demand — control only continues past the call when the value really is that type.

quiz.question: After `if (!user) return;`, what does the compiler know about `user`?
options: That it's truthy — `null` and `undefined` are gone
quiz.explanation: Early returns narrow everything after them.

quiz.question: What is `[1, undefined, 2].filter((x) => x !== undefined)` typed as (TS 5.5+)?
quiz.explanation: The arrow is inferred as a type predicate.

quiz.question: What does `asserts v is T` mean in a return type?
options: If the function returns at all, `v` is a `T` from then on
quiz.explanation: It narrows by throwing on failure.

quiz.question: When is a narrowed `let` NOT narrowed inside a callback (TS 5.4+)?
options: When the variable is assigned again after the callback is created
quiz.explanation: The callback might run after that later assignment. Copy the narrowed value to a `const`.

quiz.question: `typeof null` is…
quiz.explanation: Check `v === null` before trusting a `typeof v === "object"` test.

quiz.question: Why must the discriminant be a literal type rather than `string`?
options: Only distinct literal types let the compiler rule out the other union members
String discriminants are slower at runtime
TypeScript forbids string-typed properties in unions
Literal types are required for JSON serialization
quiz.explanation: Narrowing works by elimination: `kind === \"circle\"` can only exclude the rect member if that member's `kind` is the literal `\"rect\"`. With `kind: string` both members still match.

quiz.question: You add a `{ kind: "triangle"; b: number; h: number }` member. What does the `const exhaustive: never = s` line do?
options: It becomes a compile error in every switch that has not handled the new kind
It silently accepts the new member
It throws at runtime when a triangle arrives
It narrows the triangle to never so the switch keeps working
quiz.explanation: That is the point of the pattern: `s` in `default` is now the triangle member, which is not assignable to `never`, so the compiler walks you to every place that needs a new case.

quiz.question: Which is the real advantage of a tagged union over one object with all fields optional?
options: Each branch statically guarantees which fields exist, removing the undefined checks
It uses less memory at runtime
It allows more than one field to be required
It survives JSON.stringify, which optional fields do not
quiz.explanation: With all-optional fields every access needs a runtime guard and the compiler cannot tell a circle from a rect. The tag makes the impossible combinations unrepresentable.

quiz.question: What can you do with a value of type `unknown` before narrowing it?
options: Pass it around or store it — nothing that reads from it
Nothing; it can't even be stored
quiz.explanation: It's the safe top type: everything fits in, nothing comes out unchecked.

quiz.question: What is the return type of a function that always throws?
quiz.explanation: It never produces a value.

quiz.question: Why does `const unhandled: never = s` in a `default` branch catch missing cases?
options: If a case is missing, `s` isn't `never` there, and the assignment fails to compile
quiz.explanation: The type left after all narrowing must be empty.

quiz.question: Which values does the type `{}` accept?
options: Anything except `null` and `undefined` — including numbers and strings
quiz.explanation: Use `object` for non-primitives, `Record<string, never>` for truly empty objects.

quiz.question: A slot typed `() => void` receives `() => 5`. Is that allowed?
options: Yes — `void` means the result is ignored
quiz.explanation: That's why `forEach` callbacks can return things.

quiz.question: Which type describes something you call with `new`?
quiz.explanation: A construct signature is written with `new` in front. A class value has one, and so can any object type.

quiz.question: A slot expects `(value: number, index: number) => void`. Why does `(value) => …` fit?
options: Passing extra arguments to a function that ignores them is harmless
The compiler adds the missing parameter
It doesn't fit; you must declare both
quiz.explanation: A function that takes fewer parameters can always be called with more arguments; the rest are ignored.

quiz.question: What does `this: Account` in a parameter list do at runtime?
options: Nothing — it is erased; it only checks what `this` is at each call site
Adds a first parameter the caller must pass
Creates a new `Account` for each call
quiz.explanation: The `this` parameter is purely a type annotation. `describe("x")` still takes one argument.

quiz.question: Under `strict`, why can't `(e: "click") => void` be assigned to `(e: string) => void`?
options: The slot may pass any string, and the handler only accepts one
Literal types can't appear in parameters
Arrow functions can't be assigned to type aliases
It can; parameters are compared bivariantly
quiz.explanation: Parameters are checked contravariantly: the function must accept everything the slot might pass it.

quiz.question: What is different about an interface method declared as `accept(v: string): void` compared with `accept: (v: string) => void`?
options: The method form's parameters are checked bivariantly, so a narrower implementation slips through
The property form can't be implemented by a class
quiz.explanation: Method syntax keeps an old, deliberate unsoundness. Property syntax gets the strict, contravariant check.

quiz.question: Why is it `ReturnType<typeof parse>` and not `ReturnType<parse>`?
options: `parse` is a value; `typeof` lifts it into the type world
`typeof` calls the function to find its result
quiz.explanation: Utility types take types. `typeof parse` is the function's type.

quiz.question: When does `type _ = Expect<Equal<A, B>>` compile?
options: Only when A and B are the same type
When A is assignable to B
When B is a subtype of A
quiz.explanation: `Expect` requires `true`, and `Equal` is true only for identical types.

quiz.question: What does an unused `// @ts-expect-error` do?
options: It is itself a compile error (TS2578)
It disables checking for the whole file
quiz.explanation: That is what makes it a negative test: if the next line compiles, the directive fails.

quiz.question: Why do misuses under `@ts-expect-error` usually sit inside a function that is never called?
options: The line must compile-fail but must not run
The directive only works inside functions
quiz.explanation: The type checker sees the line; the runtime never executes it.

quiz.question: Why is `[A] extends [B] ? [B] extends [A] ? true : false : false` not an identity check?
quiz.explanation: Mutual assignability is weaker than identity; the generic-function trick in `Equal` is not.

quiz.question: What can a type test NOT tell you?
options: Whether the function returns the right values
quiz.explanation: Types are erased. Values need runtime tests.

quiz.question: What is `typeof unique<string>`?
options: The type of `unique` with its type parameter fixed to `string` (an instantiation expression)
quiz.explanation: Instantiation expressions (TS 4.7) let you test a generic function at a specific type.

quiz.question: What does `strictNullChecks` change about the meaning of `string`?
options: With it on, `string` excludes null and undefined — absence must be written explicitly
quiz.explanation: With the flag off, every type silently includes null and undefined, so no annotation can be trusted. It is the flag the rest of the type system's usefulness rests on.

quiz.question: What does `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` do?
options: Gives `arr[i]` the type `T | undefined`, reflecting that the index may be out of range
Throws at runtime on an out-of-range index
Requires every array access to use .at()
quiz.explanation: It tells the truth about indexing. It is not part of `strict`, and it is usually the most disruptive flag to enable in an existing codebase — and the most valuable.

quiz.question: Why prefer `@ts-expect-error` over `@ts-ignore`?
options: It errors once the underlying problem is fixed, so the suppression cannot outlive its reason
It only works in test files
quiz.explanation: `@ts-ignore` silently hides whatever the next line does forever. `@ts-expect-error` fails when there is no longer an error, forcing the comment to be removed.

quiz.question: What does a `.d.ts` file emit at build time?
options: Nothing — it only describes types the runtime is assumed to provide
A JavaScript stub for each declaration
A module that must be imported
quiz.explanation: Declaration files are pure description. If you declare something the runtime does not actually have, you get a ReferenceError with no compile-time warning.

quiz.question: Why does a file using `declare global` usually need `export {};`?
options: It forces the file to be a module, which `declare global` requires
It prevents the globals from leaking
It is a convention with no effect
quiz.explanation: A file with no imports or exports is a script, and its top-level declarations are already global — so `declare global` is only meaningful (and only legal) inside a module.

quiz.question: Why must module augmentation use `interface` rather than `type`?
options: Interfaces merge across declarations; type aliases cannot be reopened
type is not allowed inside declare module
Interfaces are erased and types are not
quiz.explanation: Declaration merging is an interface-only feature, and it is what lets you add a field to a library's existing type instead of shadowing it.

quiz.question: Which of these survives type stripping unchanged?
options: `function f<T>(x: T): T { return x as T; }`
quiz.explanation: Generics and `as` are only deleted. The other three generate runtime code, so a stripper rejects them.

quiz.question: What does `--erasableSyntaxOnly` do?
options: Reports every construct that would need code generation, such as `enum` and parameter properties
quiz.explanation: It makes the type checker agree with a stripper about what can run.

quiz.question: Why does `verbatimModuleSyntax` require `import type` for type-only imports?
options: A stripper can't tell which imports are types, so the source must say which ones to delete
quiz.explanation: The rule is: what you write is what runs. A type-only import is deleted; any other import is kept.

quiz.question: `const Level = { A: 1, B: 2 } as const; type Level = (typeof Level)[keyof typeof Level];` — what is the type `Level`?
quiz.explanation: `keyof typeof Level` is the keys; indexing by them gives the values' literal types.

quiz.question: Why can't you write `x instanceof User` when `User` is an interface?
options: Interfaces are erased — nothing named `User` exists at runtime
quiz.explanation: `instanceof` needs a runtime constructor. Test a value (`in`, a tag, a validator) instead.

quiz.question: What does `const n = "5" as unknown as number; console.log(n + 1)` print?
quiz.explanation: Assertions never convert. The value is still a string, so `+` concatenates.

quiz.question: In TypeScript 6.0, what is `strict` if a tsconfig doesn't mention it?
quiz.explanation: 6.0 flipped the default. A project that wants the old behaviour has to say `"strict": false`.

quiz.question: Which option did TypeScript 6.0 deprecate?
quiz.explanation: Use `nodenext` for Node and `bundler` for bundled apps.

quiz.question: What does `"ignoreDeprecations": "6.0"` do in TypeScript 7.0?
options: Nothing useful — the deprecated options are removed and are errors
quiz.explanation: It is a 6.0 transition aid. 7.0 has no switch to bring the options back.

quiz.question: What is TypeScript 7.0?
options: The compiler ported to Go — same `typescript` package and `tsc` command, roughly 10× faster
A new language with different syntax
quiz.explanation: The language is the same; the implementation is native.

quiz.question: Which flag is NOT part of `strict`?
quiz.explanation: It's valuable but disruptive, so it is opt-in. So is `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`.

quiz.question: A 6.0 project doesn't list `types`. What happens to the `@types/node` package it has installed?
options: It isn't loaded — the default is now `[]`, so it must be listed
It's an error to have it installed
quiz.explanation: 6.0 changed the default from 'every installed @types package' to none; add `"types": ["node"]`.

quiz.question: What does `satisfies` do that a type annotation does not?
options: It validates the value against the type while keeping the value's own narrower inferred type
It validates the value at runtime
It widens the value to the given type
quiz.explanation: An annotation replaces the inferred type; `satisfies` only checks against it. That is how you keep literal key and tuple information while still enforcing a contract.

quiz.question: With `const routes = { home: "/" } satisfies Record<string, string>`, what is `keyof typeof routes`?
quiz.explanation: The inferred object type is preserved, so its keys are the literal union of what was actually written. With a plain `Record<string, string>` annotation it would have been `string`.

quiz.question: Does `satisfies` help validate JSON arriving from a network call?
options: No — it is erased at compile time and checks nothing at runtime
Yes, it throws when the shape does not match
Yes, but only in strict mode
quiz.explanation: Like every type-level construct it disappears before the code runs. Runtime data still needs a type predicate or a schema validator.

quiz.question: `const bad: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, label: "home" };` errors, but assigning the same object through a variable does not. Why?
options: The excess property check only applies to fresh object literals assigned directly
Variables are always typed as any
The variable version is also an error, just reported later
label is a reserved property name
quiz.explanation: TypeScript treats a directly-assigned literal as a place where extra keys are almost certainly typos, so it checks them. Once the object is widened into a variable, ordinary structural assignability applies.

quiz.question: Two unrelated aliases `type A = { id: number }` and `type B = { id: number }`. Is `const b: B = someA;` legal?
options: Yes — structural typing compares shapes, not declaration names
No — they are different named types
Only when both are interfaces rather than type aliases
quiz.explanation: Nothing links A and B by name, but they have identical members, so each is assignable to the other. This is the core difference from Java's nominal `implements`.

quiz.question: What makes a class NOT purely structural in TypeScript?
options: Having private or protected members, which only match members from the same declaration
quiz.explanation: Private and protected members are tied to their declaring class, so two classes with identical-looking private fields are not interchangeable — the one nominal corner of the type system.

quiz.question: `Dog` is assignable to `Animal`. Which is assignable to which for `type Getter<T> = () => T`?
quiz.explanation: A getter produces `T`, so it is covariant: same direction as `Dog → Animal`.

quiz.question: And for `type Handler<T> = (x: T) => void`?
quiz.explanation: A handler consumes `T`: contravariant. A handler of any animal can handle a dog.

quiz.question: Why is passing `Dog[]` where `Animal[]` is expected unsound?
options: The receiver can push a non-dog into your array
quiz.explanation: TypeScript allows it for convenience; `readonly Animal[]` makes it genuinely safe.

quiz.question: What variance does `{ get(): T; set(v: T): void }` have in `T`?
quiz.explanation: It both produces and consumes `T`, so only the exact same `T` fits.

quiz.question: What does `interface Source<out T>` do?
options: Declares `T` covariant, and the compiler checks that `T` is only produced
quiz.explanation: Variance annotations are checked, erased documentation.

quiz.question: Which declaration gets the strict, contravariant parameter check under `strictFunctionTypes`?
quiz.explanation: Method syntax stays bivariant; property syntax with a function type is checked contravariantly.

quiz.question: What does a brand cost at runtime?
options: Nothing — the intersection is erased and the value stays a plain string or number
One extra object allocation per value
A hidden property is added to each value
A prototype lookup on every access
quiz.explanation: The brand lives entirely in the type system. That is the appeal over a wrapper class: full nominal safety with zero runtime representation.

quiz.question: Why should the constructor function be the ONLY place that writes `as UserId`?
options: It concentrates the unchecked assertion in one validated spot, so the type genuinely implies the invariant
TypeScript only allows one cast per type
Casting elsewhere is a runtime error
The compiler tracks how many casts a program contains
quiz.explanation: The brand is only as trustworthy as the assertions that create it. Scattering casts around means the type no longer proves anything.

quiz.question: How can you check at runtime whether a value is a `UserId`?
options: You cannot directly — you must re-run the validation the constructor performs
quiz.explanation: Since the brand is erased there is nothing to inspect. Runtime questions about a branded value always come back to re-checking the underlying data.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a validator and a parser?
options: A parser returns a more precise type that records the check; a validator returns a boolean
A validator throws, a parser doesn't
quiz.explanation: The parser's return type carries the knowledge forward, so nothing downstream has to recheck.

quiz.question: What does `declare const Brand: unique symbol` emit at runtime?
quiz.explanation: It only creates a type-level unique symbol to key the brand property.

quiz.question: Where should the `as Email` cast appear?
options: Once, inside the parser, right after the check
quiz.explanation: Concentrating the cast in the smart constructor is what makes the brand trustworthy.

quiz.question: Why is `readonly [number, ...number[]]` useful?
options: Its first element is never `undefined`, so code taking it needs no emptiness check
It is faster than an array
quiz.explanation: The non-emptiness is proven once, at construction, and carried in the type.

quiz.question: A parser trims and lower-cases emails. Why?
options: So equal addresses become equal strings — normalising is part of parsing
quiz.explanation: Returning the canonical form removes a whole class of duplicate bugs.

quiz.question: Where in a program should parsing happen?
options: At the boundary, where untyped input enters — once
In every function that uses the value
quiz.explanation: Inside the boundary, the precise types carry the guarantee.

quiz.question: Why derive the type from the schema rather than write both?
options: Two descriptions drift apart; one description can't
quiz.explanation: The validator is the source of truth, and `Infer` computes the type from it.

quiz.question: What does `Infer<typeof User>` give you when `User = obj({ name: str() })`?
quiz.explanation: `Infer` extracts the `T` from a `Schema<T>`.

quiz.question: `const user = JSON.parse(text) as User` — what has been checked?
options: Nothing; the assertion is a promise, erased at runtime
Only the types of the values
quiz.explanation: Assertions never check. A schema does.

quiz.question: Why should a validator collect every issue instead of stopping at the first?
options: So whoever sent bad data can fix all of it in one pass
quiz.explanation: One error at a time makes fixing data a slow loop.

quiz.question: Where should `User.parse` be called?
options: At the boundary where the data enters the program
In every function that uses a user
quiz.explanation: Parse once; inside the boundary the type carries the guarantee.

quiz.question: Which existing libraries work this way?
quiz.explanation: They are schema libraries whose validators also produce static types.

quiz.question: Why is `function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T` better than `function longest(a: { length: number }, b: { length: number }): { length: number }`?
options: The generic returns the caller's exact type instead of collapsing it to { length: number }
The generic is faster at runtime
The non-generic version does not compile
quiz.explanation: Both accept the same arguments. The difference is on the way out: the generic hands back `string` for strings, while the plain signature loses everything except `.length`.

quiz.question: In `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`, what is `T[K]`?
options: An indexed access type — the type of the property named K on T
An array of T indexed by K
quiz.explanation: `T[K]` looks up a property type by name, which is what lets one signature return `string` for `\"name\"` and `number` for `\"age\"`.

quiz.question: What does the default in `function makeBox<T = string>(value: T)` actually do?
options: It supplies T only when inference has nothing to infer from
It makes the value parameter optional
It coerces the argument to string
quiz.explanation: A type-parameter default is not a value default. `makeBox(1)` still infers `T = number`; the default matters for cases like `const b: Box = ...` where no argument drives inference.

quiz.question: What is `T` in `wrap(42)` for `function wrap<T>(x: T)`?
quiz.explanation: Inferred type arguments widen literals like a `let` does, unless the parameter is `const` or constrained.

quiz.question: What does a `const` type parameter change?
options: Arguments are inferred as if written with `as const`, keeping literal and tuple types
quiz.explanation: Added in TS 5.0: `<const T extends readonly string[]>`.

quiz.question: What is `NoInfer<T>` for?
options: Stopping one argument from contributing to `T`, so it is only checked against it
Disabling type checking for an argument
quiz.explanation: TS 5.4. Typical use: a fallback or default that must be one of the inferred options.

quiz.question: `box([])` infers `T` as?
quiz.explanation: There is no element to infer from. Write `box<string>([])`.

quiz.question: Why is `function log<T>(x: T): void` a smell?
options: `T` appears once, so it relates nothing — it's just `unknown`
quiz.explanation: Type parameters exist to connect types: an input to an output, or two inputs.

quiz.question: When does a type parameter default like `<T = string>` apply?
options: When no type argument is given and nothing can be inferred
quiz.explanation: Inference wins when it has candidates; the default fills the gap when it doesn't.

quiz.question: What is `(typeof levels)[number]` when `const levels = ["a", "b"] as const`?
quiz.explanation: `as const` makes the tuple's elements literal types, and indexing the tuple type by `number` unions every element — the standard way to derive a union from a runtime list.

quiz.question: `const levels = ["a", "b"];` — with no `as const` — what is `(typeof levels)[number]`?
quiz.explanation: Without `as const` the array widens to `string[]`, so indexing it by number yields `string` — the literal information is gone before the type-level trick can use it.

quiz.question: How does the type-position `typeof` differ from the runtime `typeof` operator?
options: The type-position one lifts a value into a type; the runtime one returns a string at execution time
They are the same operator used in two places
The type-position one only works on classes
The runtime one is removed by the compiler
quiz.explanation: They share a keyword and nothing else. `type S = typeof settings` computes a type; `typeof x === \"string\"` is a runtime check that happens to also narrow.

quiz.question: `type U = { tags: string[] }`. What is `U["tags"][number]`?
quiz.explanation: `U["tags"]` is `string[]`; indexing an array type by `number` gives its element type.

quiz.question: `const S = ["a", "b"] as const; type T = (typeof S)[number];` — `T` is?
quiz.explanation: `as const` keeps the literals; `[number]` unions the tuple's elements.

quiz.question: What does `User["id" | "email"]` give?
options: The union of both properties' types
An error — keys must be single
quiz.explanation: Indexing with a union key distributes over it.

quiz.question: Why does `Object.keys(obj)` return `string[]` and not `(keyof T)[]`?
options: At runtime an object can have more keys than its type lists
quiz.explanation: Structural typing admits objects with extra properties, so `keyof T` would be a lie.

quiz.question: What is `keyof { [k: string]: number }`?
quiz.explanation: Numeric keys are allowed on a string index signature (they become strings at runtime).

quiz.question: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K)` — what should it return?
quiz.explanation: The indexed access type follows the specific key passed in.

quiz.question: What does `{ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }` produce?
options: Every property of T made required — the built-in Required<T>
Every property of T made optional
A union of T's property types
quiz.explanation: The `-` prefix strips a modifier the source had, so `-?` removes optionality. `-readonly` does the same for readonly.

quiz.question: In a mapped type's `as` clause, what happens to a key you map to `never`?
options: The property is removed from the result — this is how Omit works
quiz.explanation: Key remapping to `never` drops the entry entirely, which is exactly the mechanism behind filtering utilities like `Omit`.

quiz.question: You define `type Getters<T>` that renames keys to `getName`, `getAge`. What exists at runtime?
options: Nothing — you must still build the object yourself; the type only describes it
An object with those methods, generated by the compiler
A proxy that forwards property access
The original object with extra prototype methods
quiz.explanation: Mapped types are erased like every other type. They describe the shape your runtime code is obliged to produce, usually ending in a cast where the loop finishes.

quiz.question: What does `as` do in `{ [K in keyof T as NewKey]: … }`?
options: Chooses a new key for each property
quiz.explanation: The `as` clause computes the output key from the input key `K`.

quiz.question: How do you remove a key in a mapped type?
options: Map it to `never` in the `as` clause
quiz.explanation: A key of `never` produces no property. (A value of `never` would keep the key, with an unusable type.)

quiz.question: Why write `Capitalize<string & K>` instead of `Capitalize<K>`?
options: `keyof T` can include `number` and `symbol`, and `Capitalize` only accepts strings
quiz.explanation: The intersection keeps only string keys.

quiz.question: What is `` `get${Capitalize<"first_name">}` ``?
quiz.explanation: `Capitalize` upper-cases only the first character.

quiz.question: Does `{ [K in keyof T as …]: T[K] }` keep `?` and `readonly` modifiers?
options: Yes — it's still homomorphic over `keyof T`
quiz.explanation: Add `-?` or `-readonly` to remove them explicitly.

quiz.question: A value is assigned to a remapped type that omits `password`. Is the password gone?
options: No — types are erased; the object is unchanged
quiz.explanation: Remove keys at runtime (rest destructuring), then type the result.

quiz.question: What does `infer` do inside a conditional type?
options: Binds a fresh type variable to whatever type matched at that position
Forces TypeScript to re-infer the whole expression
Declares a default for the type parameter
Converts a value into a type
quiz.explanation: `T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T` matches T against 'array of something' and names that something `U` — pattern matching on the type's structure.

quiz.question: `type NonNil<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T`. What is `NonNil<string | null>`?
quiz.explanation: T is a naked type parameter, so the conditional distributes: `string` takes the else branch and `null` becomes `never`, which disappears from the resulting union.

quiz.question: How do you stop a conditional type from distributing over a union?
options: Wrap both sides in a tuple: [T] extends [U] ? X : Y
Use an interface instead of a type alias
quiz.explanation: Distribution requires a bare type parameter on the left. Putting it inside a tuple makes it non-naked, so the check runs once against the whole union.

quiz.question: `type F<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never`. What is `F<string | number>`?
quiz.explanation: A naked type parameter distributes over the union.

quiz.question: How do you stop a conditional type from distributing?
options: Wrap both sides in a tuple: `[T] extends [U]`
quiz.explanation: `[T]` isn't a naked type parameter, so the union is checked as a whole.

quiz.question: A distributive conditional type is given `never`. The result is?
quiz.explanation: `never` is the empty union: zero members, zero results.

quiz.question: How is `IsNever<T>` written?
quiz.explanation: The distributive version would return `never` for `never`.

quiz.question: What does `infer U extends string` do?
options: Captures `U` only if it is a `string`, and types it as one in the true branch
quiz.explanation: The constraint is part of the match (TS 4.7+).

quiz.question: Why is `Exclude<"a" | "b", "a">` equal to `"b"`?
options: Each member is tested; `"a"` becomes `never` and vanishes from the union
String literals are compared by length
It's a special case in the compiler
quiz.explanation: `type Exclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T` — distribution does the work.

quiz.question: How many members does `` type T = `${"a" | "b"}-${"x" | "y" | "z"}` `` have?
quiz.explanation: Interpolating unions produces the cross product — 2 × 3 = 6 literal types. This growth is also why deeply nested templates can blow the compiler's limits.

quiz.question: Where can `Capitalize<T>` be used?
options: Only inside template literal types — it is a compiler intrinsic, not a runtime function
Anywhere, including as a runtime helper
quiz.explanation: `Capitalize`, `Uppercase`, `Lowercase` and `Uncapitalize` exist purely in the type system. Capitalizing an actual string at runtime is still your own code.

quiz.question: Why does `function toSize(v: number, u: Unit): Size { return `${v}${u}` as Size; }` need the cast?
options: A template built from a runtime `number` widens to `string`, which the compiler cannot prove matches the pattern
Casts are always required when returning template literals
Unit is a union, and unions cannot be interpolated
quiz.explanation: Type-level interpolation over `${number}` works on literal types. A runtime value produces an ordinary `string`, so you assert the invariant your code maintains.

quiz.question: Why is `type Bad = Bad | string` an error while `type Json = string | Json[]` is fine?
options: A recursive alias must go through an object, array or function so the compiler has something concrete to expand
Bad is missing a base case
type aliases cannot be recursive at all; only interfaces can
quiz.explanation: `Bad` refers to itself immediately with nothing to anchor the expansion. Wrapping the recursion in `Json[]` gives the checker a structure to defer into.

quiz.question: In `type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends object ? DeepReadonly<T[K]> : T[K] }`, what is the base case?
options: A property whose type is not an object, which stops the recursion
quiz.explanation: The conditional decides at each property whether to recurse. Primitives take the else branch and terminate that path.

quiz.question: What does `T extends readonly [unknown, ...infer Rest]` accomplish?
options: Peels the first tuple element and binds the remainder to Rest, enabling recursion over tuples
Checks that T is a readonly array of unknowns
quiz.explanation: It is the type-level equivalent of destructuring a head and tail — the standard step for recursive tuple algorithms, which must shrink toward the empty-tuple base case.

quiz.question: What does TS2589 mean?
options: Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite
A union has too many members
A type is used before it is declared
A generic has too many parameters
quiz.explanation: Usually a non-tail-recursive type, or genuinely infinite recursion.

quiz.question: Which recursive type can go deepest?
options: One whose recursive call is the whole branch, with the result carried in an accumulator
One wrapped in a tuple spread
quiz.explanation: Tail-recursive conditional types are evaluated iteratively, up to 1,000 steps.

quiz.question: A template literal of six 10-member unions is…
options: A million members — TS2590, too complex to represent
quiz.explanation: Unions in template literals multiply. Use a pattern like `` `${number}` ``.

quiz.question: `Split<string>` with no special case returns `[string]`. Why is that wrong?
options: A plain `string` has nothing to parse; the honest answer is `string[]`
quiz.explanation: Check `string extends S` first.

quiz.question: Which is cheaper for the checker?
options: `type C = A & B & …` with many parts
quiz.explanation: Interfaces are cached by name; large intersections are recomputed.

quiz.question: When is complex type-level code worth it?
options: When it catches real mistakes at many call sites of a widely used API
quiz.explanation: Otherwise a plain type and a runtime check are cheaper to read and to check.

quiz.question: What does `abstract area(): number` in a base class require?
quiz.explanation: Missing it is TS2515; the base class itself can't be instantiated (TS2511).

quiz.question: What does the `override` keyword catch?
options: A method meant to replace a base member when no such member exists (e.g. a typo)
quiz.explanation: TS4113. `--noImplicitOverride` makes the keyword required.

quiz.question: How do you stop callers from constructing invalid instances?
options: A `private constructor` plus a `static` factory that validates
quiz.explanation: The factory is the only door, and it can refuse.

quiz.question: Why is calling an overridable method from a constructor risky?
options: Subclass fields aren't initialised yet when the base constructor runs
quiz.explanation: The override sees `undefined` fields.

quiz.question: `private` vs `#private`?
options: `private` is checked only by the compiler; `#private` is enforced at runtime
quiz.explanation: `#` fields are part of JavaScript.

quiz.question: When is composition better than inheritance?
options: When you want to reuse behaviour without coupling to a base class's internals
quiz.explanation: Pass collaborators in; keep `extends` for stable is-a relationships.

quiz.question: What does a standard method decorator receive?
options: The original method and a context object
quiz.explanation: `(value, context)` — `context` has `kind`, `name`, `static`, `private` and `addInitializer`.

quiz.question: `@a @b method() {}` — which decorator is applied first?
quiz.explanation: Decorators are applied bottom-up; the top one's wrapper runs outermost.

quiz.question: What is `@retry(3)`?
options: A decorator factory: `retry(3)` returns the decorator that is applied
quiz.explanation: The outer call takes configuration.

quiz.question: Why can't type stripping run decorators?
options: They execute code at class definition, so deleting them would delete behaviour
quiz.explanation: Like `enum` and parameter properties, they aren't erasable.

quiz.question: Which is the experimental (legacy) method decorator signature?
quiz.explanation: Enabled by `--experimentalDecorators`; different from the standard.

quiz.question: How must a method-decorator wrapper call the original?
options: With the same `this` — e.g. `target.call(this, ...args)` in a `function` wrapper
quiz.explanation: An arrow wrapper can't receive the instance as `this`.

quiz.question: What happens the second time you iterate the SAME generator object?
options: Nothing is produced — a generator object is exhausted after one pass
It yields the values in reverse
quiz.explanation: The generator holds its own position. If callers may iterate more than once, hand back a function that creates a fresh generator each time.

quiz.question: Why does `take(naturals(), 4)` terminate even though `naturals()` never ends?
options: Generators are lazy — naturals only computes a value when take asks, and take stops asking
TypeScript detects the infinite loop and bounds it
naturals() is evaluated eagerly up to a default limit
The spread operator caps at 1000 elements
quiz.explanation: Laziness is the point: production is driven entirely by consumption. Spreading `naturals()` directly, with no `take`, really would hang.

quiz.question: What does `yield*` do?
options: Delegates to another iterable, yielding all of its values in place
Yields an array of the remaining values
Yields a value and immediately returns
quiz.explanation: `yield* other` forwards every value from `other` as if written inline — the standard way to compose generators or expose an internal collection.

quiz.question: Why should `pop()` be typed `T | undefined` rather than `T`?
options: An empty stack really does return undefined, and the type should say so
Generic methods cannot return a bare T
undefined is required for iteration to work
quiz.explanation: Typing it as `T` is a lie that hands the caller an `undefined` the compiler swears is a real value — precisely the class of bug the type system exists to prevent.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `#items` and `private items`?
options: `#items` is private at runtime too; `private` is erased and the field is visible in JavaScript
`#items` cannot be used in a generic class
quiz.explanation: `#` is a real JavaScript private field enforced by the engine. `private` is a compile-time-only marker, so anything ignoring the types can still reach the value.

quiz.question: Why does a generic `SortedList<T>` take a comparator instead of constraining `T extends Comparable`?
options: T is erased at runtime, so ordering must be supplied as a function the class can call
Comparable does not exist in the TypeScript standard library
Constraints cannot be used on classes
Comparators are faster than interface dispatch
quiz.explanation: Both parts are true — there is no built-in Comparable — but the underlying reason is erasure: nothing about `T` survives to run, so the behaviour has to be passed in as a value.

quiz.question: Which of these is lazy?
quiz.explanation: Iterator `map` returns a new iterator and runs nothing until pulled.

quiz.question: What does `take(n)` do to the pipeline?
options: Stops pulling from the source after `n` values
quiz.explanation: It's what makes infinite sources safe.

quiz.question: You call `toArray()` twice on the same iterator. The second result?
options: An empty array — the iterator was consumed
quiz.explanation: Iterators are single-use cursors.

quiz.question: How do you use the helpers on a value typed `Iterable<T>`?
quiz.explanation: `Iterable<T>` only promises `[Symbol.iterator]`.

quiz.question: How do you make a class work with `for…of`?
options: Implement `[Symbol.iterator]()`, often as a generator method
quiz.explanation: `*[Symbol.iterator]() { … yield … }`.

quiz.question: Which call hangs?
quiz.explanation: Spreading tries to collect everything.

quiz.question: Where is the smallest item in a min-heap stored in an array?
quiz.explanation: The heap property puts the minimum at the root.

quiz.question: What are the children of index `i`?
quiz.explanation: Its parent is `(i - 1) >> 1`.

quiz.question: Cost of `push` and `pop`?
quiz.explanation: Each walks one root-to-leaf path.

quiz.question: How do you get the k smallest of n values in O(n log k)?
options: A max-heap capped at k items, popping when it exceeds k
quiz.explanation: Its top is the largest kept value — the one to evict.

quiz.question: Are heaps stable for equal priorities?
options: No — add an insertion counter to the comparison if order matters
quiz.explanation: Swaps reorder equal items.

quiz.question: What does the comparator `(a, b) => b - a` produce?
quiz.explanation: Negative when `a` is larger, so larger items come out first.

quiz.question: Under `strict`, what type does `catch (e)` give `e`?
quiz.explanation: Any value can be thrown, so TypeScript refuses to assume `Error`. You must narrow with `instanceof` (or a type guard) before reading properties.

quiz.question: What makes `Result<T, E>` enforce error handling?
options: It is a discriminated union, so `value` is only reachable after checking `ok`
It throws if you ignore the error branch
E defaults to string, which cannot be ignored
quiz.explanation: The `ok` field is the discriminant. On the `false` branch there is no `value` property at all, so skipping the check is a type error rather than a runtime surprise.

quiz.question: When is throwing the better choice over returning a Result?
options: For bugs and unrecoverable invariant violations the caller cannot sensibly handle
quiz.explanation: Expected, recoverable failures belong in the return type. Genuinely exceptional situations — an impossible branch, a broken invariant — should unwind loudly.

quiz.question: When is `x[Symbol.dispose]()` called for `using x = …`?
options: When the enclosing block exits — normally, by return, or by exception
quiz.explanation: Deterministic, like `finally`.

quiz.question: Two `using` declarations in one block are disposed in which order?
quiz.explanation: Last acquired, first released.

quiz.question: What does `using x = undefined` do?
options: Nothing at block exit — `null` and `undefined` are allowed and skipped
quiz.explanation: Handy for optional resources.

quiz.question: Where is `await using` allowed?
options: In async functions and at a module's top level
quiz.explanation: Wherever `await` is.

quiz.question: What is `DisposableStack.prototype.move()` for?
options: Transferring the collected cleanups to a new stack so the current one won't run them
quiz.explanation: Used when setup succeeds and ownership passes to the caller.

quiz.question: A block throws and then a dispose also throws. What propagates?
quiz.explanation: `.error` is the dispose error, `.suppressed` the original.

quiz.question: Why set `name` on an `Error` subclass?
options: It's what `String(e)` and stack traces print
quiz.explanation: `instanceof` works without it; people reading logs don't.

quiz.question: How do you keep the original error when wrapping it?
quiz.explanation: `cause` is part of the standard `Error` constructor (ES2022).

quiz.question: What type is `e` in `catch (e)` under `strict`?
quiz.explanation: `useUnknownInCatchVariables` — anything can be thrown.

quiz.question: What does `AggregateError` hold?
options: A list of errors in `.errors`, plus its own message
quiz.explanation: `Promise.any` throws one when every promise rejects.

quiz.question: A `catch` block receives an error it doesn't understand. What should it do?
quiz.explanation: Handle what you can; let the rest propagate.

quiz.question: When is returning a `Result` better than throwing?
options: For expected failures the caller must handle, like invalid input
quiz.explanation: The compiler then forces the caller to deal with the failure case.

quiz.question: What is the total time of `await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchOne))` versus awaiting inside a loop?
options: The maximum of the individual times, versus the sum of them
The same — Promise.all is just syntax
Depends on the number of CPU cores
quiz.explanation: `.map` starts every promise before `all` waits, so they overlap. Awaiting inside a loop starts each one only after the previous resolves.

quiz.question: How does `Promise.allSettled` differ from `Promise.all` on failure?
options: It never rejects; every entry becomes a fulfilled/rejected record you inspect
It rejects only if every promise fails
It resolves with the successful values and silently drops failures
quiz.explanation: `allSettled` always resolves with one `PromiseSettledResult` per input. That last behaviour — dropping failures — is what `Promise.any` approximates, and it is not what allSettled does.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `Promise.race` and `Promise.any`?
options: race settles with the first promise to settle either way; any waits for the first SUCCESS
any is the async version of race
quiz.explanation: `race` is the timeout pattern precisely because an early rejection wins. `any` ignores rejections until all of them fail, then rejects with an AggregateError.

quiz.question: `setTimeout(f, 0)` and `Promise.resolve().then(g)` are scheduled in that order. Which runs first?
options: `g` — microtasks run before the next timer
quiz.explanation: The whole microtask queue drains before any task.

quiz.question: What runs synchronously when you call an `async` function?
options: Its body up to the first `await`
quiz.explanation: The rest is resumed as a microtask.

quiz.question: Which of these is a microtask?
quiz.explanation: Also `.then` callbacks and `queueMicrotask`.

quiz.question: Why does `items.forEach(async (x) => await save(x))` not wait?
options: `forEach` ignores the promises its callback returns
`forEach` is synchronous only for arrays of numbers
quiz.explanation: Use `for…of` with `await`, or `Promise.all(items.map(…))`.

quiz.question: A synchronous loop runs for two seconds. What happens to a `setTimeout(f, 10)` set before it?
options: It runs after the loop — about two seconds late
quiz.explanation: Nothing interrupts running code; a delay is a minimum.

quiz.question: `Promise.all([slow(), fast()])` — what order are the results in?
options: Input order, regardless of which finished first
quiz.explanation: That's what makes it deterministic to print.

quiz.question: Can you cancel a promise?
options: No — you ask the work to stop via a signal, and it cooperates
Yes, by rejecting it from outside
quiz.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative in JavaScript.

quiz.question: What does `signal.throwIfAborted()` do?
options: Throws the signal's reason if it has been aborted; otherwise nothing
quiz.explanation: The one-line check between steps.

quiz.question: `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` aborts when?
quiz.explanation: Cancel-or-timeout in one signal.

quiz.question: What does `Promise.withResolvers<T>()` return?
quiz.explanation: Settle the promise from outside an executor.

quiz.question: After `Promise.race([work(), timeout])` resolves with the timeout, what is `work()` doing?
options: Still running, unless it was given a signal and checks it
quiz.explanation: Racing chooses a result; it doesn't stop anything.

quiz.question: `controller.abort()` with no argument — what is `signal.reason`?
quiz.explanation: Pass your own reason for a clearer message.

quiz.question: What does `for await (const x of source)` do each iteration?
options: Awaits the next value before running the body
quiz.explanation: Values are pulled one at a time.

quiz.question: What does an `async function*` return?
options: An async generator — an async iterable of its yielded values
quiz.explanation: Consume it with `for await` or `Array.fromAsync`.

quiz.question: A consumer `break`s out of `for await` early. What happens to the generator?
options: Its `return()` is called, so its `finally` blocks run
It keeps running in the background
quiz.explanation: Put cleanup in `finally`.

quiz.question: How do you collect an async iterable into an array?
quiz.explanation: ES2024; also takes a mapping function.

quiz.question: Can you iterate the same async generator object twice?
options: No — it's single-use; call the generator function again
quiz.explanation: Same as sync generators.

quiz.question: Why is async iteration good for paginated APIs?
options: The next page is fetched only when the consumer asks for more
It fetches all pages in parallel
quiz.explanation: Stopping early saves the remaining requests.

exam.title: Capstone: typed record store
exam.prompt: Combine the programme: a branded `RecordId`, a `Result`-returning parser, a generic iterable `Store<T>`, and an ambient host global. The input is `n` then `n` lines of `id value` (ids must match `r-\\d+`). Print `added <id>` or `rejected <line>` per line, then the stored ids space-separated in insertion order, then the store size.
exam.hint: Each piece is one week's idea: the brand proves validation happened, the Result forces the caller to branch, and Symbol.iterator makes the store spreadable.

flashcards.front: Interview: `any` vs `unknown` vs `never`, one line each?
flashcards.back: `any` turns checking off; `unknown` is any value you must narrow before use; `never` is the type with no values — unreachable code, impossible cases.

flashcards.front: Interview: `interface` or `type`?
flashcards.back: Either for object shapes; `interface` can be merged and extended, `type` can also name unions, tuples and mapped types. Pick one convention per codebase.

flashcards.front: Interview: what is structural typing?
flashcards.back: Compatibility is decided by shape, not by name — any value with the right members fits, whatever it was declared as.

flashcards.front: Interview: what does `satisfies` add over an annotation?
flashcards.back: It checks the value against a type but keeps the value's own, narrower inferred type.

flashcards.front: Interview: how do you type a value parsed from JSON?
flashcards.back: As `unknown`, then validate it — a type predicate or a schema — so the type is earned, not asserted.

flashcards.front: Interview: what is a discriminated union for?
flashcards.back: Modelling "one of these cases", each with its own data; switching on the tag narrows, and a `never` check makes the switch exhaustive.

flashcards.front: Interview: how do generics differ from `any`?
flashcards.back: A type parameter links types together (input element type = output element type); `any` throws that information away.

flashcards.front: Interview: what is a branded type?
flashcards.back: A primitive intersected with a phantom tag (`string & { __brand: "UserId" }`) so two structurally identical ids cannot be mixed up.

flashcards.front: Interview: why is `enum` discouraged in modern TypeScript?
flashcards.back: It is not erasable syntax — it emits runtime code — and a literal union (`"a" | "b"`) does the job with no runtime cost.

flashcards.front: Interview: how would you test a type?
flashcards.back: `type _ = Expect<Equal<Actual, Expected>>` for positive claims and `// @ts-expect-error` above a line that must be rejected — both run as part of `tsc`.

flashcards.front: Interview: what does `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` change, and why turn it on?
flashcards.back: Every index read becomes `T | undefined`, so out-of-range reads must be handled — the type finally tells the truth about arrays and records.

flashcards.front: Interview: `Promise.all` or `Promise.allSettled`?
flashcards.back: `all` when one failure should fail the whole operation; `allSettled` when every outcome matters on its own — e.g. reporting each resource.

flashcards.front: Mock interview: how do you open a coding question?
flashcards.back: Restate it, confirm the input/output shapes and edge cases, state a brute force and its complexity, then improve.

flashcards.front: Mock interview: `interface` or `type`?
flashcards.back: Interchangeable for object shapes; `interface` merges and extends cheaply, `type` handles unions, mapped and conditional types. Pick one convention and say why.

flashcards.front: Mock interview: how do you type untrusted JSON?
flashcards.back: Parse to `unknown`, validate at the boundary with a guard or schema, and let the inferred type flow inward — never `as T`.

flashcards.front: Mock interview: what is structural typing's biggest surprise?
flashcards.back: Extra properties pass silently (except fresh literals), so types never guarantee a value has *only* what they list.

flashcards.front: Mock interview: how do you make async output testable?
flashcards.back: Inject the clock and the I/O, order results by input index, and never assert on real timing.

flashcards.front: Mock interview: when would you reach for a branded type?
flashcards.back: When two values share a representation but must never be mixed — ids, units, validated strings — at zero runtime cost.

problem_set.title: Mock type puzzle 1: DeepPartial
problem_set.prompt: Write `DeepPartial<T>`: every property at every depth becomes optional; arrays keep their shape but their elements become deep-partial; functions are left alone.
problem_set.hint: Four cases, in order: functions, arrays, objects, primitives.
hints: Four cases, in order: functions, arrays, objects, primitives.
Arrays: recurse into the element type.
problem_set.starter: type DeepPartial<T> = ____;
problem_set.solution:
type DeepPartial<T> = T extends (...args: never[]) => unknown
  ? T
  : T extends readonly (infer E)[]
    ? DeepPartial<E>[]
    : T extends object
      ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> }
      : T;

project_spec.title: ledger.ts — the arc's final version
project_spec.goal: The six-month arc project, finished: a ledger that loads its sources concurrently with a timeout, parses every row into branded types with `Result`s, keeps its state private in a class, streams statements lazily with a generator, and never lets timing decide what it prints.
requirements: The input has three sections separated by `---` lines: config (`timeout=<ms>`), sources (`<name> <delayMs> <row;row;…>` with rows `YYYY-MM-DD,ACC-123,amount`), and commands.

Load every source concurrently on a virtual clock: a source finishes after its delay, or times out at the timeout (a delay equal to the timeout still loads). Parse each loaded row with `Result`s — `bad date`, `bad account` (three capitals, `-`, three digits), `bad amount` (at most two decimals) — recording errors as `<source>#<row>: <problem>`; add good rows to the ledger in source input order.

Commands: `sources` (`<name>: <k> rows` — `row` for one — or `<name>: timed out`, in input order); `balance <acc>`; `statement <acc> [n]` (the first n lines — all by default — of `<date> <signed amount> <running balance>` in date order, produced by a generator); `top <n>` (accounts by balance, highest first, ties by id); `months` (`<YYYY-MM> in <x> out <y>`, sorted); `errors` (in load order, or `no errors`).
Money prints as `$12.00` / `-$3.50`; a bad account id in a command prints `bad account <x>`, and an unknown one `no account <x>`.
Use a branded `AccountId` and `Cents`, a `Ledger` class with `#private` transactions, and `Result<T, string>` for every parser.
stretch: Split it into modules (`money.ts`, `parse.ts`, `ledger.ts`, `load.ts`, `main.ts`) with `import type` where it applies.
Add `using`-managed resources for the sources and print when each is released.
rubric: Every parser returns a `Result`; nothing in the parsing path throws
Branded `AccountId`/`Cents` are created only by their parsers
The ledger's transactions are `#private`; callers can read, never write
No output depends on real time — only on the virtual clock
No `any` anywhere; every function has a typed signature
