weeks.title: Stacks
weeks.goal: Use LIFO order to match, undo, and find the next greater thing.

problems.note: An auxiliary stack carrying an invariant.

weeks.project: Write a `Rpn.java` evaluating a reverse-Polish expression from stdin, reporting `error` on a malformed one rather than crashing.

quiz.question: Which Java type should you use as a stack?
quiz.explanation: `Stack` extends Vector and is synchronised legacy code; `ArrayDeque` is the modern, faster choice — and `remove(0)` on an ArrayList is O(n).

quiz.question: What makes a stack monotonic?
options: You pop before pushing so the contents stay sorted in one direction
It is backed by a sorted array
quiz.explanation: Popping everything the new element dominates is what makes 'next greater element' linear overall — each element is pushed and popped at most once.

quiz.question: Why does min-stack need a second stack rather than a single min variable?
options: Popping the current minimum has to restore the previous one
quiz.explanation: A lone variable cannot recover the old minimum after a pop. Storing the running minimum alongside each element keeps every operation O(1).

quiz.question: Which structure gives average O(1) lookup by key with NO ordering?
quiz.explanation: HashMap hashes keys to buckets for O(1) average get/put but makes no ordering promise.

quiz.question: You need elements kept in sorted order automatically. Use…
quiz.explanation: TreeSet (a red-black tree) keeps elements sorted; HashSet is unordered.

quiz.question: The modern recommended class for a stack is…
quiz.explanation: `ArrayDeque` is faster and cleaner than the legacy synchronized `Stack` class.

quiz.question: A PriorityQueue always removes…
quiz.explanation: A PriorityQueue is a heap: `poll()` returns the head according to the comparator (smallest by default).

quiz.question: `ConcurrentModificationException` typically means…
options: a collection was structurally modified during iteration
the map ran out of capacity
quiz.explanation: Fail-fast iterators throw it when the backing collection is modified while you're looping over it.

quiz.question: To iterate keys AND values of a Map efficiently, loop over…
quiz.explanation: `entrySet()` gives both key and value per entry, avoiding a second lookup per key.

quiz.question: You store every element you've seen in a hash set while scanning an array of size n. Auxiliary space is:
quiz.explanation: The set can hold up to n distinct elements, so it uses O(n) extra memory.

quiz.question: A recursive function that recurses to a depth of n uses how much space just for the call stack?
quiz.explanation: Each pending call keeps a stack frame alive, so depth-n recursion costs O(n) stack space even with tiny frames.

quiz.question: The 'seen set' trick turns an O(n^2)-time duplicate check into O(n) time. What is it spending to do that?
quiz.explanation: It's a time–space tradeoff: O(n) extra memory (the set) buys the drop from O(n^2) to O(n) time.

quiz.question: Reversing an array 'in place' with two pointers uses how much auxiliary space?
quiz.explanation: In-place means only a constant number of extra variables (the two indices and a temp) → O(1) auxiliary space.

quiz.question: Precomputing a prefix-sum array so each range-sum query is O(1) is an example of:
options: Saving memory at the cost of time
Spending O(n) memory to make queries faster
Reducing both time and space to zero
quiz.explanation: You build an O(n) array once so that later queries drop from O(n) to O(1) — spending memory to buy query speed.

weeks.goal: Always know the current extreme — including with two heaps at once.
weeks.project: Write a `Huffman.java` that reads weights, repeatedly merges the two smallest, and prints the total merge cost plus the number of merges.

quiz.question: What order does Java's `PriorityQueue` use by default?
options: Natural order — it is a MIN-heap

options: A min-heap of size k, polling whenever it grows past k
quiz.explanation: The min-heap's root is the weakest survivor, so it is exactly the one to evict — O(n log k) instead of O(n log n).

quiz.explanation: The backing array is heap-ordered, not sorted. Printing a PriorityQueue directly is a routine source of confusing output.

quiz.explanation: TreeSet (a red-black tree) keeps elements sorted; HashSet is unordered.

quiz.question: A PriorityQueue always removes…

the map ran out of capacity
quiz.explanation: Fail-fast iterators throw it when the backing collection is modified while you're looping over it.

quiz.question: To iterate keys AND values of a Map efficiently, loop over…
quiz.explanation: `entrySet()` gives both key and value per entry, avoiding a second lookup per key.

quiz.question: What is the best worst-case time achievable by any comparison-based sort?
quiz.explanation: Distinguishing all n! orderings by comparisons needs ≥ log₂(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons — so O(n log n) is the floor.

quiz.question: Quicksort's worst-case time complexity is:
quiz.explanation: With consistently bad pivots (e.g. already-sorted input, naive pivot), partitions are maximally unbalanced → O(n^2).

quiz.question: Which sort is stable AND guarantees O(n log n), at the cost of O(n) extra space?
quiz.explanation: Merge sort is stable with a guaranteed O(n log n), but its merge step needs O(n) scratch space.

quiz.question: Which sort is in-place (O(1) extra) with a guaranteed O(n log n), but not stable?
quiz.explanation: Heapsort sorts in place with a hard O(n log n) guarantee, but its heap operations reorder equal elements → not stable.

quiz.question: How do you make quicksort's O(n^2) worst case astronomically unlikely?
quiz.explanation: A randomized or median-of-three pivot makes consistently bad partitions vanishingly improbable, keeping it near O(n log n).

quiz.question: Merge sort's cost comes from the recurrence T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n). That solves to:

exam.title: Huffman merge cost

quiz.question: Java strings are immutable, so `s = s + "x"`…

weeks.title: Linked Lists
weeks.goal: Pointer surgery: reverse, find the middle, detect a cycle.

problems.note: Fast and slow in one pass.
Two cursors and a dummy head.

weeks.project: Write a `Palindrome.java` that decides whether a linked list reads the same forwards and backwards in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

quiz.question: In `reverse`, why must you save `curr.next` before reassigning it?
options: Overwriting it first loses the rest of the list
quiz.explanation: The saved `next` is the only remaining handle on the untouched tail. When curr falls off the end, prev is the new head.

quiz.question: Why does a dummy head node simplify list building?
options: It removes the special case for inserting the very first node
quiz.explanation: You always append after a real node, then return `dummy.next` — no branch for the empty case.

quiz.question: Why do fast and slow pointers meet inside a cycle?
options: The gap closes by one each step, so the faster one must catch up
They start at the same node
The cycle length is always even
quiz.explanation: Once both are inside the loop the distance shrinks by exactly one per step, so a meeting is guaranteed.

quiz.question: Which structure gives average O(1) lookup by key with NO ordering?
quiz.explanation: HashMap hashes keys to buckets for O(1) average get/put but makes no ordering promise.

quiz.question: You need elements kept in sorted order automatically. Use…
quiz.explanation: TreeSet (a red-black tree) keeps elements sorted; HashSet is unordered.

quiz.question: The modern recommended class for a stack is…
quiz.explanation: `ArrayDeque` is faster and cleaner than the legacy synchronized `Stack` class.

the map ran out of capacity
quiz.explanation: Fail-fast iterators throw it when the backing collection is modified while you're looping over it.

quiz.question: To iterate keys AND values of a Map efficiently, loop over…
quiz.explanation: `entrySet()` gives both key and value per entry, avoiding a second lookup per key.

quiz.question: Objects created with `new` live on the…
quiz.explanation: Objects go on the shared heap; local variables and call frames live on each thread's stack.

quiz.question: The difference between the JDK and the JRE is that the JDK also includes…
quiz.explanation: JRE = run Java; JDK = JRE + `javac` and tools to build it.

quiz.question: Deep infinite recursion typically causes…
quiz.explanation: Each call adds a stack frame; too many exhausts the thread's stack → StackOverflowError.

quiz.question: A memory leak in Java usually means…
options: you still hold references to objects you don't need
quiz.explanation: The GC only frees unreachable objects; lingering references (e.g. in a growing cache) keep them alive.

quiz.question: Bytecode (`.class`) is…
quiz.explanation: `javac` produces platform-independent bytecode; the JVM (optionally JIT-compiling) runs it.

quiz.question: Generational GC is based on the observation that…
quiz.explanation: The weak generational hypothesis: most objects become garbage quickly, so the young generation is collected often and cheaply.

exam.title: Linked list palindrome
exam.prompt: The input is `n` then `n` values forming a linked list. Print `true` if the values read the same forwards and backwards, using O(1) extra space: find the middle with fast/slow, reverse the second half, then compare. Print the list's length on the second line.
exam.hint: Reverse from the slow pointer onward; comparing until the reversed half runs out handles both odd and even lengths.

weeks.title: Binary Trees & Traversals
weeks.goal: Recurse over structure, and know what each traversal order gives you.

problems.note: The simplest recursion on a tree.

weeks.project: Write a `Serialize.java` that prints a tree in preorder with `#` for null, then rebuilds it from that string and prints its inorder to prove the round trip.

quiz.question: Which traversal of a BST produces sorted order?
quiz.explanation: Left subtree, node, right subtree visits keys in ascending order — the property behind kth-smallest and BST validation.

quiz.question: Why is postorder the right shape for 'compute something from both subtrees'?
options: Both children are fully processed before the node combines them
It works only on balanced trees
quiz.explanation: Height, diameter and subtree sums are all postorder aggregations — the node's answer needs its children's answers first.

quiz.question: What does level-order need that depth-first traversals do not?
quiz.explanation: BFS is queue-driven. Processing a whole level at a time means recording the queue size before draining it.

quiz.question: What two ingredients does every correct recursive function need?
options: A base case and a recursive case that shrinks toward it
A hash map and a set
quiz.explanation: A base case tells it when to stop; the recursive case must make progress toward that base case, or it never terminates.

quiz.question: Recursion of depth d uses how much memory just for the call stack?
quiz.explanation: Each pending call keeps a live stack frame, so depth-d recursion costs O(d) stack space.

quiz.question: A recursive function with no reachable base case will most likely:
quiz.explanation: Without a base case (or without progressing toward it), it recurses forever, exhausting the stack — a stack overflow.

quiz.question: The recursive factorial uses O(n) space while the loop version uses O(1). The extra space in the recursive one is:
options: The call stack of n frames
quiz.explanation: The recursion stacks n frames before any returns, costing O(n); the loop keeps a single accumulator, O(1).

quiz.question: Which problem shape is MOST naturally expressed with recursion?
quiz.explanation: Trees are defined recursively (a node plus subtrees), so recursive traversal mirrors the structure directly.

quiz.question: The 'leap of faith' when writing recursion means:
options: Assume the recursive call already correctly solves the smaller subproblem, and just combine it
quiz.explanation: You trust that the recursion handles the smaller input correctly and focus on the combine step — correctness then follows by induction.

exam.title: Serialize and rebuild a tree
exam.prompt: The input is `n` then `n` level-order values with `-1` for a missing node. Print the tree's preorder with `#` for null (space-separated), then its inorder (real values only, space-separated).
exam.hint: Preorder emits the node then both children, so a null slot still contributes a `#`. Inorder skips nulls entirely.

weeks.title: BSTs & Tree DP
weeks.goal: Exploit ordering, and aggregate answers upward through a tree.

problems.note: Ordering turns search into a descent.
Bounds passed down, not just child comparisons.
The hardest version of the same shape.

weeks.project: Write a `BstRange.java` that reads a BST and a range `lo hi` and prints the sum of all keys inside it, pruning subtrees that cannot contribute.

quiz.question: Why is comparing each node only against its children NOT enough to validate a BST?
options: A deep descendant can violate a distant ancestor's bound
quiz.explanation: Pass a (low, high) range down and tighten it at each step — the local check misses violations one level further away.

quiz.question: What does a tree-DP function typically return?
options: Its subtree's answer, while updating a global best on the way up
quiz.explanation: Diameter and max-path-sum both do this: return the best downward path, but combine both sides into the global answer at each node.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case height of an unbalanced BST with n nodes?

quiz.explanation: Sorted insertion degenerates the tree into a linked list, which is why self-balancing trees (Java's TreeMap uses a red-black tree) exist.

quiz.question: What happens to generic type info at runtime?
quiz.explanation: Type erasure removes generic parameters at compile time, so `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` share one runtime class.

quiz.question: PECS says: use `? extends T` when you want to…
quiz.explanation: Producer-Extends: an `? extends T` source produces Ts you read; `? super T` consumes Ts you write.

quiz.question: The diamond operator `<>` lets you…
options: omit repeating the type arguments on the right
quiz.explanation: `new ArrayList<>()` infers the type from the variable declaration, avoiding repetition.

quiz.question: A `raw type` like `List l = new ArrayList();` is discouraged because…
quiz.explanation: Raw types bypass generic checks, reintroducing the ClassCastExceptions generics were meant to prevent.

quiz.question: `<T extends Number>` means T can be…

exam.title: BST range sum
exam.prompt: The input is `n`, then `n` level-order values with `-1` for a missing node (values are positive and form a valid BST), then `lo hi`. Print the sum of every key in `[lo, hi]`, then how many keys were in range — pruning subtrees that cannot contribute.

weeks.title: Sorting & Binary Search
weeks.goal: Order the data, then exploit that order.

problems.note: Binary search on the answer, not the array.
Search a shape rather than a value.

weeks.project: Write a `Bounds.java` implementing lowerBound and upperBound over a sorted array with duplicates, and print how many times a target occurs.

quiz.question: Why write `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` instead of `(lo + hi) / 2`?
options: The naive form can overflow int for large indices
quiz.explanation: A famous bug that sat in the JDK's own binarySearch for years.

quiz.question: For a lower bound, why is the update `hi = mid` rather than `hi = mid - 1`?
options: mid itself may be the answer, so it must stay in the range
quiz.explanation: Half-open `[lo, hi)` with `hi = mid` is the form that reliably finds the FIRST qualifying element.

quiz.question: What does `Arrays.sort` use for an object array?
quiz.explanation: Objects get stability (equal elements keep their relative order); primitives get quicksort, where stability is meaningless.

quiz.question: What must be true of the array for standard binary search to be correct?
quiz.explanation: Binary search relies on order to decide which half to discard. On unsorted data it gives wrong answers.

quiz.question: How many comparisons does binary search need in the worst case for n = 1,000,000?
quiz.explanation: log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20, so ~20 halving steps — that's the whole point of O(log n).

quiz.question: Why compute mid = lo + (hi - lo)/2 instead of (lo + hi)/2?
options: It avoids integer overflow when lo+hi is large
It's required by the sorted order
quiz.explanation: In fixed-width integer languages lo+hi can overflow; lo + (hi-lo)/2 computes the same midpoint without that risk.

quiz.question: 'Binary search on the answer' applies when…
options: Feasibility is monotonic in the candidate answer (if X works, so does every larger X)
quiz.explanation: If the yes/no feasibility of a candidate answer flips once (monotonic), you can binary search the answer value itself.

quiz.question: A binary search loop keeps running forever. The most likely cause is:
options: The range doesn't strictly shrink each iteration (e.g. lo = mid instead of mid+1)
quiz.explanation: If lo or hi can stay put (lo = mid with lo==mid), the range never shrinks and the loop spins. Always move past mid.

quiz.question: To find the FIRST occurrence of a value (not just any), on a match you should:
options: Record the index and keep searching the left half (hi = mid - 1)
quiz.explanation: Don't stop at the first hit — record it and continue left to find an earlier occurrence; the last recorded index is the first occurrence.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of bubble, selection, and insertion sort?
quiz.explanation: All three elementary sorts are O(n^2) in the worst case — that's why they don't scale.

quiz.question: Which quadratic sort is the best practical choice for a small or nearly-sorted array?
quiz.explanation: Insertion sort runs in O(n) on nearly-sorted data with tiny overhead, which is why libraries use it for small runs.

quiz.question: A sort is 'stable' when…
options: equal elements keep their original relative order
it's faster than O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: Stability means equal keys retain their prior order — important when sorting by a secondary key.

quiz.question: Which of these elementary sorts is NOT stable?
quiz.explanation: Selection sort's long-distance swaps can reorder equal elements, so it is not stable.

quiz.question: All three quadratic sorts share which space complexity?
quiz.explanation: Bubble, selection, and insertion sort rearrange the array in place using only O(1) extra memory.

quiz.question: What is the best worst-case time achievable by any comparison-based sort?
quiz.explanation: Distinguishing all n! orderings by comparisons needs ≥ log₂(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons — so O(n log n) is the floor.

quiz.question: Quicksort's worst-case time complexity is:
quiz.explanation: With consistently bad pivots (e.g. already-sorted input, naive pivot), partitions are maximally unbalanced → O(n^2).

quiz.question: Which sort is stable AND guarantees O(n log n), at the cost of O(n) extra space?
quiz.explanation: Merge sort is stable with a guaranteed O(n log n), but its merge step needs O(n) scratch space.

quiz.question: Which sort is in-place (O(1) extra) with a guaranteed O(n log n), but not stable?
quiz.explanation: Heapsort sorts in place with a hard O(n log n) guarantee, but its heap operations reorder equal elements → not stable.

quiz.question: How do you make quicksort's O(n^2) worst case astronomically unlikely?
quiz.explanation: A randomized or median-of-three pivot makes consistently bad partitions vanishingly improbable, keeping it near O(n log n).

quiz.question: Merge sort's cost comes from the recurrence T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n). That solves to:
quiz.explanation: log n levels of recursion, each doing O(n) merging, gives O(n log n).

quiz.question: How can non-comparison sorts beat the O(n log n) comparison-sort lower bound?
options: They don't compare elements at all — they count or bucket by key value
They only work on sorted data
quiz.explanation: The n log n bound only applies to comparison-based sorting. Counting/radix/bucket sort by key value without comparing, so the bound doesn't bind them.

quiz.question: Counting sort's time complexity for n integers in the range [0, k) is:
quiz.explanation: You do O(n) work to tally and O(k) to walk the value range → O(n + k). It's linear when k is comparable to n.

quiz.question: When is counting sort a BAD choice?
options: When the key range k is enormous compared to n (e.g. 32-bit integers)
quiz.explanation: If k ≫ n, the O(k) count array dominates and wastes space/time. Radix sort handles large integer keys instead.

quiz.question: Radix sort requires that the per-digit counting sort be:
quiz.explanation: Each digit pass must preserve the order established by previous (less significant) digits — that requires a stable sort.

quiz.question: Bucket sort achieves expected O(n) time under what assumption about the input?
options: The values are roughly uniformly distributed across the range
n is a power of two
quiz.explanation: Uniform distribution keeps each bucket tiny, so sorting all buckets is linear. Skewed data can pile into one bucket and degrade it.

exam.title: Lower and upper bound
exam.prompt: The input is `n target` then `n` integers sorted ascending (duplicates allowed). Print the first index whose value is >= target, the first index whose value is > target, and how many times target occurs.
exam.hint: The two searches differ by one character: >= for the lower bound, > for the upper. Their gap is the occurrence count.

weeks.title: Greedy & Intervals
weeks.goal: When does taking the locally best choice actually give the global optimum?

problems.note: Sort by END — the classic surprise.
The same shape as interval scheduling.

weeks.project: Write a `Schedule.java` that reads meetings and prints the largest number that can be attended without overlap, plus which ones.

quiz.question: For maximum non-overlapping intervals, what do you sort by?
options: End time — finishing earliest leaves the most room
quiz.explanation: Sorting by start solves MERGING; sorting by end solves SELECTION. Mixing them up is the classic interval mistake.

quiz.question: What must be true for a greedy algorithm to be correct?
options: The locally optimal choice is always part of some global optimum
It runs in O(n log n)
quiz.explanation: This is the exchange-argument property. Without it — coin change with arbitrary denominations, for instance — greedy silently returns a worse answer.

quiz.question: Two intervals overlap when…
quiz.explanation: Whether touching endpoints count as overlapping is a per-problem decision — read the statement rather than assuming.

quiz.question: A problem gives you a SORTED array and asks for a pair summing to a target. The signal points to:
quiz.explanation: 'Sorted' plus 'find a pair' is the classic two-pointers signal: move inward from both ends based on the current sum.

quiz.question: 'Longest contiguous subarray/substring satisfying a condition' most strongly signals:
quiz.explanation: A contiguous run with a validity condition is the sliding-window fingerprint: grow the right edge, shrink the left when it becomes invalid.

quiz.question: You must return the k largest elements of a big stream. Best-matched tool?
options: Sort the whole stream every time
A heap / priority queue of size k
quiz.explanation: A size-k heap keeps the top k without fully sorting everything — the standard 'top k' technique.

quiz.question: The problem asks for ALL permutations of a set. This signals:
quiz.explanation: 'All arrangements/combinations/subsets' means you must explore the full decision tree — that's backtracking.

quiz.question: Constraints say n ≤ 20 and you must consider every subset. What complexity is acceptable here?
options: Exponential like O(2^n) is fine because n is tiny
quiz.explanation: Small n (≤ ~20) is a hint that an exponential/backtracking solution (2^20 ≈ 10^6) is intended and fast enough.

quiz.question: Shortest path in an UNWEIGHTED grid or graph is the signal for:
quiz.explanation: BFS explores in rings of increasing distance, so the first time it reaches a node is via a shortest (fewest-edges) path.

exam.title: Meeting schedule
exam.prompt: The input is `n` then `n` lines of `start end`. Print the largest number of meetings attendable without overlap, then their `start end` pairs one per line in the order chosen. A meeting starting exactly when another ends is fine.
exam.hint: Sort by END time — finishing earliest leaves the most room for what follows. Sorting by start solves a different problem.

weeks.title: Grids & Flood Fill
weeks.goal: Treat a grid as a graph and explore its connected regions.
weeks.project: Write a `Regions.java` that reads a character grid and prints the number of regions and the size of the largest, treating equal adjacent characters as connected.

quiz.question: Why mark a cell visited as you ENQUEUE it rather than when you dequeue it?
options: Otherwise the same cell can be enqueued several times before processing
quiz.explanation: Marking on dequeue lets duplicates pile up in the queue, which can blow up the memory and the running time.

quiz.question: Why is a recursive flood fill risky on a large grid?
options: The recursion depth can equal the number of cells and overflow the stack
quiz.explanation: An explicit stack or a BFS queue has the same complexity without depending on the JVM's stack size.

quiz.question: What is a common trick to avoid a separate visited array?
options: Overwrite each visited cell with a sentinel value in the grid itself
Use a HashSet of coordinates, which is always faster
quiz.explanation: It saves memory and is fine when the grid may be mutated — otherwise copy first or use a boolean array.

quiz.question: You store every element you've seen in a hash set while scanning an array of size n. Auxiliary space is:
quiz.explanation: The set can hold up to n distinct elements, so it uses O(n) extra memory.

quiz.question: A recursive function that recurses to a depth of n uses how much space just for the call stack?
quiz.explanation: Each pending call keeps a stack frame alive, so depth-n recursion costs O(n) stack space even with tiny frames.

quiz.question: The 'seen set' trick turns an O(n^2)-time duplicate check into O(n) time. What is it spending to do that?
quiz.explanation: It's a time–space tradeoff: O(n) extra memory (the set) buys the drop from O(n^2) to O(n) time.

quiz.question: Reversing an array 'in place' with two pointers uses how much auxiliary space?
quiz.explanation: In-place means only a constant number of extra variables (the two indices and a temp) → O(1) auxiliary space.

quiz.question: Precomputing a prefix-sum array so each range-sum query is O(1) is an example of:
options: Saving memory at the cost of time
Spending O(n) memory to make queries faster
Reducing both time and space to zero
quiz.explanation: You build an O(n) array once so that later queries drop from O(n) to O(1) — spending memory to buy query speed.

exam.title: Count regions
exam.prompt: The input is `r c` then `r` rows of `c` characters (no spaces). Adjacent cells (up/down/left/right) holding the SAME character belong to one region. Print the number of regions, then the size of the largest.
exam.hint: Mark each cell seen as you PUSH it, not when you pop it, or the same cell enters the stack several times.

weeks.title: Recursion, Backtracking & Pruning
weeks.goal: Explore a decision tree, undo cleanly, and cut branches that cannot win.
weeks.project: Write a `Sudoku.java` that reads a 9x9 grid and reports whether it is solvable, using constraint checks to prune before recursing.

quiz.question: What distinguishes backtracking from plain recursion?
options: It UNDOES its choice after recursing, so siblings see a clean state
quiz.explanation: The undo step is the definition. Forgetting it is why the second branch of a search returns nonsense.

quiz.question: Why does naive recursive Fibonacci take exponential time?
options: The same subproblems are recomputed along different branches
quiz.explanation: Memoising collapses it to linear. Recognising overlapping subproblems is the step from recursion to dynamic programming.

quiz.question: What is the point of a pruning check?
options: Abandon a branch as soon as it cannot possibly lead to a solution
quiz.explanation: It does not change the worst case, but on real inputs it is often the difference between milliseconds and never finishing.

quiz.question: What two ingredients does every correct recursive function need?
options: A base case and a recursive case that shrinks toward it
A hash map and a set
quiz.explanation: A base case tells it when to stop; the recursive case must make progress toward that base case, or it never terminates.

quiz.question: Recursion of depth d uses how much memory just for the call stack?
quiz.explanation: Each pending call keeps a live stack frame, so depth-d recursion costs O(d) stack space.

quiz.question: A recursive function with no reachable base case will most likely:
quiz.explanation: Without a base case (or without progressing toward it), it recurses forever, exhausting the stack — a stack overflow.

quiz.question: The recursive factorial uses O(n) space while the loop version uses O(1). The extra space in the recursive one is:
options: The call stack of n frames
quiz.explanation: The recursion stacks n frames before any returns, costing O(n); the loop keeps a single accumulator, O(1).

quiz.question: Which problem shape is MOST naturally expressed with recursion?
quiz.explanation: Trees are defined recursively (a node plus subtrees), so recursive traversal mirrors the structure directly.

quiz.question: The 'leap of faith' when writing recursion means:
options: Assume the recursive call already correctly solves the smaller subproblem, and just combine it
quiz.explanation: You trust that the recursion handles the smaller input correctly and focus on the combine step — correctness then follows by induction.

quiz.question: In the recurrence T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n), what does f(n) represent?
options: The work to divide and combine outside the recursive calls
quiz.explanation: f(n) is the non-recursive work per call — splitting the input and combining subresults. a and n/b describe the recursive calls.

quiz.question: Merge sort is T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n). By the Master Theorem this is:
quiz.explanation: log₂2 = 1 so n^c = n, and f(n) = n matches it → Case 2 → O(n log n).

quiz.question: Binary search is T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1). This solves to:
quiz.explanation: a=1, b=2 gives n^0 = 1, and f(n)=O(1) matches → Case 2 → O(1·log n) = O(log n).

quiz.question: The Master Theorem in the a·T(n/b)+f(n) form does NOT directly apply to which recurrence?
quiz.explanation: T(n-1) is a subtract-and-conquer form, not a divide form (n/b). The Master Theorem is for divide recurrences; this one just unrolls to O(n).

quiz.question: T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + O(1) unrolls to which complexity?
quiz.explanation: Doubling the number of calls at each of n levels gives 2^n total — the classic exponential blowup of naive branching recursion.

quiz.question: In the Master Theorem, which case ADDS a logarithmic factor to the result?
quiz.explanation: Case 2 is the balanced case where per-level work is equal across log n levels, contributing the extra log factor (e.g. n log n).

exam.title: Sudoku solvable
exam.prompt: The input is 9 lines of 9 digits, `0` meaning empty. Print `true` if the puzzle can be completed legally and `false` otherwise, then the number of empty cells in the input. Reject an already-illegal board up front — searching one wastes the whole run.
exam.hint: Check the givens first — an illegal board has no solution, and searching for one takes effectively forever. Then undo each placement (`g[r][c] = 0`) when a branch fails.

weeks.title: Dynamic Programming & Complexity
weeks.goal: Find the state, write the recurrence, then decide top-down or bottom-up.
weeks.project: Write a `Knapsack.java` solving 0/1 knapsack bottom-up, printing the best value and the chosen items, with the table reduced to one dimension.

quiz.question: What are the two ingredients of a dynamic-programming solution?
options: A greedy choice and a tie-break
quiz.explanation: Without overlap, memoising buys nothing; without optimal substructure, combining subproblem answers is simply invalid.

quiz.question: What is the difference between memoisation and tabulation?
options: Memoisation is top-down and computes only the states it needs; tabulation is bottom-up and fills them all
quiz.explanation: Top-down is usually easier to derive from the recurrence; bottom-up avoids stack depth and makes rolling-array space savings obvious.

quiz.question: `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) for (int j = i; j < n; j++)` — what is the complexity?
options: O(n²) — roughly n²/2 iterations, and constants are dropped
quiz.explanation: Half of a quadratic is still quadratic. Big-O describes the growth rate, not the constant factor.

quiz.question: In the recurrence T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n), what does f(n) represent?
options: The work to divide and combine outside the recursive calls
quiz.explanation: f(n) is the non-recursive work per call — splitting the input and combining subresults. a and n/b describe the recursive calls.

quiz.question: Merge sort is T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n). By the Master Theorem this is:
quiz.explanation: log₂2 = 1 so n^c = n, and f(n) = n matches it → Case 2 → O(n log n).

quiz.question: Binary search is T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1). This solves to:
quiz.explanation: a=1, b=2 gives n^0 = 1, and f(n)=O(1) matches → Case 2 → O(1·log n) = O(log n).

quiz.question: The Master Theorem in the a·T(n/b)+f(n) form does NOT directly apply to which recurrence?
quiz.explanation: T(n-1) is a subtract-and-conquer form, not a divide form (n/b). The Master Theorem is for divide recurrences; this one just unrolls to O(n).

quiz.question: T(n) = 2·T(n-1) + O(1) unrolls to which complexity?
quiz.explanation: Doubling the number of calls at each of n levels gives 2^n total — the classic exponential blowup of naive branching recursion.

quiz.question: In the Master Theorem, which case ADDS a logarithmic factor to the result?
quiz.explanation: Case 2 is the balanced case where per-level work is equal across log n levels, contributing the extra log factor (e.g. n log n).

quiz.question: Simplify: 4n^2 + 100n + 3000 in Big-O.
quiz.explanation: Keep only the dominant term (n^2) and drop constant factors and lower-order terms → O(n^2).

quiz.question: An algorithm makes two separate full passes over an array of size n, one after the other. Its complexity is:
quiz.explanation: Sequential phases add: n + n = 2n, and constant factors drop, so it's O(n). Nesting (not sequencing) would give O(n^2).

quiz.question: Which growth rate is best (scales best) for large n?
quiz.explanation: Order is O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2). Logarithmic grows slowest, so it scales best.

quiz.question: You combine an O(n) step followed by an O(n log n) sort. Total complexity?
quiz.explanation: Sequential steps add, and the sum is dominated by the larger term: O(n) + O(n log n) = O(n log n).

quiz.question: Doubling n roughly quadruples the running time. Which class is this?
quiz.explanation: For O(n^2), replacing n with 2n gives (2n)^2 = 4n^2 — four times the work. That ×4 fingerprint means quadratic.

quiz.question: The problem says n can be up to 200,000 and the time limit is tight. Which target complexity is the safe aim?
quiz.explanation: At n = 2×10^5, O(n^2) is ~4×10^10 operations — far too slow. O(n log n) (~3.5 million) comfortably fits, so aim there or better.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of two nested loops that each run from 0 to n-1?
quiz.explanation: Nesting multiplies: n iterations × n iterations = n^2 → O(n^2).

quiz.question: The inner loop runs from i+1 to n-1 (shrinking as i grows). Overall complexity?
options: O(n) — because the inner loop shrinks
O(n^2) — the total is n(n-1)/2, still quadratic
quiz.explanation: Summing the shrinking bounds gives n(n-1)/2 ≈ n²/2. Dropping the constant, that's still O(n^2) — all-pairs work.

quiz.question: A loop that repeatedly halves n until it reaches 1 runs in:
quiz.explanation: Halving 16→8→4→2→1 takes log₂ n steps, so it's O(log n).

quiz.question: For the recurrence T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + O(n), the total time is:
quiz.explanation: Two half-size subproblems plus linear work per level, over log n levels of n total work, gives O(n log n) — the merge-sort recurrence.

quiz.question: Appending to a dynamic array that doubles when full has which amortized cost per append?
quiz.explanation: Occasional O(n) doublings are rare enough that n appends cost ~2n total, i.e. O(1) amortized each.

quiz.question: Unless stated otherwise, 'the time complexity' of an algorithm refers to its:
quiz.explanation: By convention, an unqualified complexity is the worst case — the guarantee that holds for every input of size n.

exam.title: 0/1 knapsack
exam.prompt: The input is `n capacity` then `n` lines of `weight value`. Print the best achievable value, then how much capacity it uses. Fill the table bottom-up with a single rolling row.
exam.hint: Iterate the capacity DOWNWARD so each item is used at most once — an ascending loop turns this into unbounded knapsack.

weeks.title: Graphs & Capstone
weeks.goal: Represent a graph, traverse it, order it, connect it, and weight it.
weeks.project: Capstone: write a `Network.java` that reads a weighted graph and reports whether it is connected, its MST weight, the shortest path between two nodes, and whether it contains a cycle — one program, four algorithms.

quiz.question: When is BFS the right choice over DFS for shortest paths?
options: On unweighted graphs, where the first arrival is already the shortest
quiz.explanation: With weights you need Dijkstra (non-negative) or Bellman-Ford (negatives allowed) — BFS's guarantee depends on every edge costing the same.

quiz.question: What does Kahn's algorithm placing fewer than n vertices tell you?
options: The graph contains a directed cycle
quiz.explanation: Anything left with a non-zero in-degree is trapped in a cycle — which is why the same routine answers both 'topological order' and 'is it acyclic'.

quiz.question: Why can Dijkstra fail on negative edge weights?
options: It finalises a node on first extraction, which a later negative edge could improve
The priority queue cannot hold negatives
quiz.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge n-1 times instead, which is slower but tolerates negatives and detects negative cycles.

quiz.question: A problem gives you a SORTED array and asks for a pair summing to a target. The signal points to:
quiz.explanation: 'Sorted' plus 'find a pair' is the classic two-pointers signal: move inward from both ends based on the current sum.

quiz.question: 'Longest contiguous subarray/substring satisfying a condition' most strongly signals:
quiz.explanation: A contiguous run with a validity condition is the sliding-window fingerprint: grow the right edge, shrink the left when it becomes invalid.

quiz.question: You must return the k largest elements of a big stream. Best-matched tool?
options: Sort the whole stream every time
A heap / priority queue of size k
quiz.explanation: A size-k heap keeps the top k without fully sorting everything — the standard 'top k' technique.

quiz.question: The problem asks for ALL permutations of a set. This signals:
quiz.explanation: 'All arrangements/combinations/subsets' means you must explore the full decision tree — that's backtracking.

quiz.question: Constraints say n ≤ 20 and you must consider every subset. What complexity is acceptable here?
options: Exponential like O(2^n) is fine because n is tiny
quiz.explanation: Small n (≤ ~20) is a hint that an exponential/backtracking solution (2^20 ≈ 10^6) is intended and fast enough.

quiz.question: Shortest path in an UNWEIGHTED grid or graph is the signal for:
quiz.explanation: BFS explores in rings of increasing distance, so the first time it reaches a node is via a shortest (fewest-edges) path.

quiz.question: Which structure gives average O(1) lookup by key with NO ordering?
quiz.explanation: HashMap hashes keys to buckets for O(1) average get/put but makes no ordering promise.

quiz.question: You need elements kept in sorted order automatically. Use…
quiz.explanation: TreeSet (a red-black tree) keeps elements sorted; HashSet is unordered.

quiz.question: The modern recommended class for a stack is…
quiz.explanation: `ArrayDeque` is faster and cleaner than the legacy synchronized `Stack` class.

quiz.question: A PriorityQueue always removes…
quiz.explanation: A PriorityQueue is a heap: `poll()` returns the head according to the comparator (smallest by default).

quiz.question: `ConcurrentModificationException` typically means…
options: a collection was structurally modified during iteration
the map ran out of capacity
quiz.explanation: Fail-fast iterators throw it when the backing collection is modified while you're looping over it.

quiz.question: To iterate keys AND values of a Map efficiently, loop over…
quiz.explanation: `entrySet()` gives both key and value per entry, avoiding a second lookup per key.

exam.title: Capstone: network report
exam.prompt: The input is `n m src dst` then `m` lines of `u v w` (undirected, non-negative weights). Print four lines: whether the graph is connected, the total weight of a minimum spanning tree (or `-1` if disconnected), the shortest distance from `src` to `dst` (or `-1`), and the number of connected components.
exam.hint: Four algorithms, one parse: Kruskal gives the MST and the components, Dijkstra gives the distance. Keep their state separate.
